### Blockit — Flows and friction — 4 findings (1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] The copy's first-run permission set is more invasive than the original's and missing two of its asks: notification-listener is a core gate, notifications and exact-alarm are never asked

Blockit's boarding ticket (EVIDENCE.md §3, §8) asks 8 things: POST_NOTIFICATIONS, accessibility, overlay, device admin, usage access, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, battery exemption, and Xiaomi autostart — and the APK contains no NotificationListenerService anywhere; notification silencing is Do-Not-Disturb (ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY), a Premium extra asked for later, not a first-run gate. Monolith's first-run set is differently composed and more invasive: WatchStore.kt:80-99 makes NOTIFICATION_LISTENER one of the counted core four (COUNTED = ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN, NOTIFICATION_LISTENER) that the PARK board pushes on day one — a grant that lets the app read notification content, which the original never requests at all — while the two mundane grants Blockit does ask up front have no first-run ask in Monolith: openFixPane's when() (MainActivity.kt:363-408) has branches for accessibility/usage/admin/listener/overlay/battery and no POST_NOTIFICATIONS branch, and no exact-alarm grant exists in the manifest or the FIX routes, so routines are onboarded without the permission Blockit's routine sheet (routine_sheet_body, EVIDENCE.md §7.5) demands before enabling them.

Recommendation: Recompose the first-run ticket to match the original's: demote notification-listener out of the counted core (or drop it for a DND-style approach), and add the missing up-front asks — notifications and exact-alarm — in sequence, the latter gated to when the user first enables a routine, as Blockit does.

#### [HIGH] Blockit pre-announces and explains each grant one at a time; Monolith's first run is one jargon board whose single FIX key fires raw Settings intents with no rationale

Blockit (EVIDENCE.md §8): BoardingActivity runs 4 intro cards first, and card 3 (boarding_intro_*) pre-announces the cost verbatim — 'To really lock your phone, blockit needs %1$d system permissions. I will ask for them one at a time' — then asks each grant behind its own rationale sheet (_sheet_permission.xml), with accessibility behind a dedicated AccessibilityConsentSheet ('Enable session block', body explaining it only brings you back, button 'I agree') and explanatory notes assembled in a fixed order (BoardingActivity lines ~662-702: note_0 haptics → note_block calls always work → note_1 'they light up one by one' → note_3 accessibility never reads screen → note_4 overlay → note_5 battery → note_6 Xiaomi). Total first-run: tear-ticket entry + 4 cards + sign-in + 8 explained asks ≈ 13 sequenced steps. Monolith has no boarding activity at all (AndroidManifest.xml declares a single MainActivity): first run is one LaunchedEffect that auto-opens the PARK drawer over the Deck (MainActivity.kt:311-318), the drawer renders every grant as a bare board row at once, and its only action is a single FIX key for the first missing item (ParkDrawer.kt:412-458, text 'FIX — ${item.boardName}'). Tapping it fires a raw Settings intent with zero per-permission explanation (MainActivity.kt:366-367: ACTION_ACCESSIBILITY_SETTINGS; 368: ACTION_USAGE_ACCESS_SETTINGS). Step count on Monolith's side: 1 board + up to 7 unexplained Settings trips, none of them preceded by what the grant does or why.

Recommendation: Restore a sequenced first-run: state the grant count up front, ask one at a time in Blockit's order, and put a one-paragraph rationale sheet (what it does, what it never does) in front of each Settings trip — accessibility first among them — instead of a bare FIX key.

#### [HIGH] Blockit puts sign-in and the parachute (the escape hatch) before any permission ask; Monolith asks for its four core grants with no account step and no mention of the exit

Blockit (EVIDENCE.md §8, §7.3): the sign-in step comes BEFORE permissions — 'Slide to sign in' with Google (boarding_slide_google) or an explicit guest choice (boarding_guest_*: warns no welcome parachute, data stays on this phone only, 'You can sign in later') — and intro card 4 is THE PARACHUTE, so the user learns the emergency exit exists, and earns the first/welcome parachute (boarding_checkin_*), before a single invasive grant is requested. Monolith inverts and omits both: its manifest/code contains no login/account step at all (no LoginActivity equivalent; grep for sign-in/account in app/src/main/java/com/example returns nothing), and the first-run PARK board (ParkDrawer.kt) asks for ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE ACCESS, DEVICE ADMIN and NOTIFICATION LISTENER (WatchStore.kt:80-99, the counted four) without ever mentioning the emergency-break valve/token that is the user's way out of a session. The copy demands the original's most sensitive grants while skipping the two trust-building steps the original deliberately placed in front of them.

Recommendation: Before the first grant ask, add the equivalent of Blockit's check-in card: explain the emergency exit and its weekly cost, and state the data/account situation plainly. A user who knows how to get out grants accessibility far more willingly than one who does not.

#### [MEDIUM] Blockit ends onboarding with a tour and a pre-set 5-minute first session; Monolith ends it at drawer dismissal, with no tour and no scaffolded first session

Blockit (EVIDENCE.md §5, §8) does not end onboarding at the last grant: it offers a guided tour (17 tour_* strings covering wheel, bag, slider, parachute, routines, tower, nav) and scaffolds the first success — tour_brick_*: 'I set the wheel to 5 minutes… lay the first brick of your tower' — so the first session is pre-configured, short, and almost impossible to fail. Monolith's first run ends the moment the PARK drawer closes for any reason: closePark() calls markParkIntroDone() on every dismissal (MainActivity.kt:280-290), dropping the user onto the full Deck with the dial, loadout and routines all self-service — no tour, no pre-set 5-minute starter session, no guided first brick. The original spends its last onboarding steps manufacturing a first win; the copy spends zero.

Recommendation: After the grants, scaffold the first win the way the original does: pre-set a 5-minute session with a sensible default loadout, walk the user through starting it, and only then hand over the full Deck. Do not treat dismissing the permission drawer as onboarding complete.
### Blockit — Platform execution — 4 findings (1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] Monolith ships an entire NotificationListenerService Blockit proves unnecessary — silence is achieved with DND policy access alone

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §3/§6.9: no NotificationListenerService anywhere in the APK (no component, no notification-listener permission); session silence is Do Not Disturb via the single ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY permission ('Do Not Disturb turns on when the block starts and off when it ends. Calls follow your own Do Not Disturb rules'). Monolith instead declares a third god service at app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:81-91 (MonolithNotificationListener, BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE, directBootAware=true), implemented at app/src/main/java/com/example/service/MonolithNotificationListener.kt:23, which on every post launches an IO coroutine, reads the session and full app table, persists title+body to Room (lines 70-91) and only then calls cancelNotification (line 93). That is one extra special-access Settings grant, one always-bindable service, and a permanent plaintext notification store purchased for a promise the original meets with an OS policy toggle and zero interception machinery.

Recommendation: Delete MonolithNotificationListener, its manifest entry and its permission ask; implement session silence as Blockit does — request ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY and toggle Do Not Disturb for the session window, letting the user's own DND rules govern calls. If a post-session digest is wanted, build it from app-tier metadata only, never intercepted bodies.

#### [HIGH] Two concurrent detection stacks vs one: Blockit's FGS is a timer only, Monolith's specialUse FGS is a second UsageStats polling detector alongside Accessibility

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §6.1-§6.2, §6.5: foreground detection is solely the AccessibilityService (TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED|TYPE_WINDOWS_CHANGED, notificationTimeout=100); PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS is used only as a granted-probe (queryUsageStats INTERVAL_YEARLY, empty=>not granted) with no queryEvents/MOVE_TO_FOREGROUND detection; the sole first-party FGS, LockService, runs only a 1-second ScheduledExecutorService timer and calls startForeground(1, notification, 1024) with foregroundServiceType systemExempted (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SYSTEM_EXEMPTED) plus a retry-without-type fallback. Monolith runs both: MonolithAccessibilityService (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:65-78) AND MonolithShieldService as a specialUse FGS (AndroidManifest.xml:53-62, subtype property 'Active app-blocking focus session timer and usage monitor'), whose loop delays 2000ms per iteration (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/MonolithShieldService.kt:193) over a UsageStats lastTimeUsed guess in app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithRepository.kt:568-575 (INTERVAL_DAILY filtered to last 8s). Monolith also picks the heavier FGS regime: FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE (AndroidManifest.xml:8) gated by an SDK_INT>=UPSIDE_DOWN_CAKE branch at MonolithShieldService.kt:57-62, where Blockit's systemExempted type needs no per-app special-use justification.

Recommendation: Collapse to Blockit's split: AccessibilityService is the only detector, UsageStats demoted to a permission probe, and the foreground service reduced to a timer/session holder. Remove the 2s polling loop and the specialUse subtype; if an FGS type is needed, follow the LockService pattern with a typed startForeground and a no-type fallback instead of an API-level branch that passes 0 below API 34.

#### [HIGH] directBootAware=true is stamped on all eight Monolith components; Blockit concentrates pre-unlock work in a single boot receiver

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §4.2-§4.3: its component inventory records two first-party services and a single BootCompletedReceiver (exported=false, priority Integer.MAX_VALUE) as the one component listening for LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED/BOOT_COMPLETED/USER_PRESENT/USER_UNLOCKED/TIME_SET/TIMEZONE_CHANGED/MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED — boot and pre-unlock re-arming live in exactly one place. Monolith sets android:directBootAware="true" on every component it declares: MainActivity (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:41), MonolithShieldService (:55), MonolithAccessibilityService (:67), MonolithNotificationListener (:83), MonolithBootReceiver (:96), RoutineAlarmReceiver (:111), ReleaseRetryReceiver (:117) and MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver (:124). RoutineAlarmReceiver and ReleaseRetryReceiver have no pre-unlock job at all — they are alarm hints for a credential-protected routine store — yet both are declared runnable before first unlock, alongside a notification listener and an accessibility service, multiplying the pre-unlock execution surface the original keeps to one receiver.

Recommendation: Strip directBootAware from every component except MonolithBootReceiver, following Blockit's one-receiver pattern, and make the remaining services/receivers start only after USER_UNLOCKED. Any component that must survive a locked boot should re-derive its state post-unlock rather than executing in device-protected context by default.

#### [MEDIUM] minSdk 24 vs Blockit's 28: Monolith carries four extra Android generations of compat branches for the same targetSdk 36

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §0: minSdkVersion 28, targetSdkVersion 36, compileSdkVersion 36, shipped as a single 5.69MB DEX in a 6.96MB APK with no native libraries. Monolith matches the target (app/build.gradle.kts:18 targetSdk=36, :13 compileSdk 36) but floors four versions lower at app/build.gradle.kts:17 minSdk=24 (Android 7.0-8.1). The span is paid for in conditional platform code throughout the execution layer: the FGS type exists only from API 34 (MonolithShieldService.kt:57-62), notification-channel creation is re-guarded at API 26 (MonolithShieldService.kt:199), and the sound engine alone branches at API 26/31 repeatedly (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/TactileSoundEngine.kt:524, 539, 561, 586), while modern permissions declared unconditionally in the manifest (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE at AndroidManifest.xml:8, POST_NOTIFICATIONS at :9) do not exist as runtime concepts on the oldest supported devices. Blockit simply does not ship, test or branch for those generations.

Recommendation: Raise minSdk to 28 to match the original's floor, then delete the API 24-27 branches and guards that exist only for those versions and re-audit the remaining SDK_INT checks (several become unconditional). If 24-27 support is a deliberate product choice, record the device share that justifies a 13-level API span against Blockit's 9.
### Blockit — Signature moments — 4 findings (0 critical, 3 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] The copy kept Blockit's procedural synth maths but deleted its actual product: a live ambient soundscape for the whole session

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.9: class h9/c 'SoundEngine' creates an AudioTrack (44,100 Hz, PCM-16, mono) and synthesises sound in code, with named session tiles block_sound_rain=RAIN (free), block_sound_wind=WAVES, block_sound_noise=WHITE NOISE, block_sound_city=CITY, pref keys session_sound/session_sound_on, and the strings claim the sounds are 'generated live, that thin out on their own as the session ends' — i.e. a continuous soundscape that fills the session and fades with it; no audio files exist in the APK. Monolith copied the synthesis technique but inverted its purpose: TactileSoundEngine.kt:30-31 declares 'Zero audio files' AND 'Zero ambient sound mixer loops', its synth loop caps every command at a 160ms transient buffer (TactileSoundEngine.kt:416,460), and every call site is a 6-64ms click/thock (e.g. :637, :841); the longest sound in the app is the 1,000ms seal throw (SEAL_SAMPLES=44,100 at :95). SoundEffectsSetting.kt is a single boolean — there is no sound choice, no rain/waves/noise/city, no session-length audio at all (grep for rain/ambient/session_sound in main sources: zero hits).

Recommendation: Add a continuous procedural session soundscape to TactileSoundEngine: at minimum a free rain generator on a dedicated AudioTrack at 44.1kHz, selectable in-session, with gain/envelope thinning in the final minutes as Blockit does; keep the transient click voices on the existing separate lane so the two never queue against each other.

#### [HIGH] In-session, Blockit keeps a working session screen (+15 hold-to-extend, AUTO DIM, time-left over allowed apps); Monolith collapses it to a 6dp bar and a percentage

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.1/§6.6: the running session is an active screen, not a collapsed readout — layout _overlay_content.xml brings the session screen back in front and 'shows the time left above allowed apps' (overlay_extra_v2), there is an in-session extend verb countdown_extend='+15 min' with extend_hold_hint=HOLD (gated by a parachute aboard, capped: countdown_extend_remaining_full='still 60 min'), a countdown_dim_label='AUTO DIM' for the running countdown, and slide_to_stop as the exit gesture. Monolith's running form deletes the wheel and substitutes a 6dp progress bar plus a percentage: TactileDeckScreen.kt:746-771 renders Box(height=6.dp).fillMaxWidth(progressFraction) and Text('${(progressFraction*100).toInt()}%'). There is no session-extend verb anywhere (grep for extendSession/addMinutes/session-extend in main sources: zero hits — the only extend, MonolithViewModel.kt:1814 extendActiveTaskOvertime, lengthens a task estimate, not the running session), and no auto-dim or time-left-over-other-apps surface in code (grep for dim/screenBrightness: zero hits).

Recommendation: Restore the in-session verbs the original ships: a hold-to-extend (+15 min, cost-gated, with the remaining-cap message), an auto-dim mode for the running countdown, and remaining time rendered on the intercept/overlay surface — instead of reducing a live session to a progress bar and a percent.

#### [HIGH] Blockit's wheel is one notch = one minute with preset and long-press custom tiles to 12h; Monolith's wheel can only stop every 5 minutes and caps a direct choice at 180

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.1: RotaryWheel is a single 328-line custom view whose tour string states the model plainly — tour_wheel_*: 'Each notch is a minute: drag it up or down to choose how long the block lasts' — backed by preset tiles (fifteen=15, thirty=30) and a long-press custom tile that can bind 'any wheel duration from 3 to 12 hours' (custom_editor_hint/custom_info_*); free sessions run to 3 hours on the wheel itself. Monolith's RotaryWheelView (BlockitCoreViews.kt:371) clamps minutesValue to 5..180 (:375), maps it through minutesToAngle (:516: <10 min collapses to a FLOW seat at 108°, numerics start at 126° at 1.8° per minute) and valueForAngle (:524) returns (10 + ((angle-126)/9).roundToInt()*5) — so the wheel can only ever land on 5-minute steps: 7, 22 or 47 minutes are unselectable, there are no preset tiles and no custom-duration binding, and anything past 180 minutes is reachable only indirectly by multiplying the dial with the hub's study-block count rather than by choosing a duration.

Recommendation: Give the wheel 1-minute detents like the original (one notch = one minute over its travel), add the 15/30 preset tiles, and add Blockit's long-press custom tile binding a single explicit duration up to 12 hours — a chosen duration should not require a hidden block-count multiplier to exceed 3 hours.

#### [MEDIUM] Blockit's start, stop and exit are all deliberate slides; Monolith lets a tap commit the seal and demotes exit to a chip

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.1/§7.3 ships three distinct slide gestures as separate layouts/views — _slide_to_start.xml, _slide_to_stop.xml and slide_to_exit, with the exit slide itself carrying the cost (slide_exit_costs='Uses 1 parachute') — the deliberateness of the slide is the ritual, and stopping/exiting are slides of the same physical grammar. Monolith's SlideToStartView prints WORDS_START='SLIDE OR TAP TO START' (BlockitCoreViews.kt:2407) with a dedicated tap path (Mode.MESH) whose plate reads WORDS_UNDO='TAP AGAIN TO UNDO' (:2408, drawn at :1787): a classified tap commits the identical seal a full-track drag does, so the signature gesture is optional. The symmetry is also broken at the other end — Monolith has no slide-to-stop or slide-to-exit view at all; leaving a session is a plain BlockitActionChip ('GRACE WINDOW ABORT' / 'EMERGENCY BREAK VALVE (60S HOLD)') in TactileDeckScreen's pinned stack, with the cost in a badge rather than on the gesture.

Recommendation: Make the full slide the committing gesture again (tap may focus or prime, not seal), and give stop/exit the same slide grammar as start, with the parachute/token cost printed on the exit slide itself as Blockit does — one physical language for entering and leaving a session.
### Blockit — Comparative audit — 4 findings (0 critical, 2 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Monolith replaces Blockit's 3-slot binary Suitcase with a full-catalogue 3-tier rule matrix including a timed peek tier Blockit does not have

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.2: the Bag is a binary allowlist — free tier 1 bag of exactly 3 apps (6 with the bag_six add-on, max 3 bags on Premium); an app is either packed (usable) or bounced, with no graded middle state and no rule for apps outside the slots. Monolith instead gives every installed app a persisted 3-state rule: AppBlockTier LOCKED / PEEK_2M (2-minute peek plus mandatory 20-minute cooldown) / OPEN at app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:13-38, stored per package for the whole catalogue in BlockedAppEntity (MonolithModels.kt:231-249, incl. peek lease/cooldown stamps activePeekUntilElapsedRealtime and lastPeekEndElapsedRealtime). Blockit has no peek/cooldown concept anywhere in the APK — its only mid-session relief is spending a parachute to end the session (§7.3).

Recommendation: Treat the graded tier matrix, not the wheel, as the headline differentiator from the original: Blockit cannot express 'check messages for 2 minutes, then locked again' at all. Protect this model in future fixes — collapsing it back to a binary bag to match Blockit would delete Monolith's clearest structural win.

#### [HIGH] Monolith binds sessions to a task queue with sub-steps and per-session task accounting; Blockit has no task concept at all

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §12 records an observed negative for tasks/to-dos (no task strings or classes in the DEX) and §7.6 shows its only session record is Record(date, time, timeList) — a duration with no work attached. Monolith ships an entire work layer with no counterpart in the APK: FocusTaskEntity with queue status (ACTIVE/QUEUED/DEFERRED/COMPLETED), sub-steps parsed from notesOrSubsteps, actualSecondsSpent and completedInSessionId (MonolithModels.kt:80-129), and sessions carry that bond — intention and taskId on FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:270, 323) plus completedTasksSummary/tasksCompletedCount booked at the ending write (MonolithModels.kt:301-302). A Blockit session can never answer 'what did you work on'; a Monolith session is armed from, billed against, and receipted to a named task.

Recommendation: This is the one place Monolith is a different product category from its model (work queue + blocker, not just a timer) — prioritise making the sequencer surface fully live over cloning more Blockit furniture, since the data model already out-builds the original here.

#### [MEDIUM] Monolith judges routine windows as attendance with frozen window snapshots and an evidence mask; Blockit routines only fire and record nothing

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.5: routines are fire-only — AutoSessionReceiver starts the session, RoutinePreAlertReceiver warns beforehand, and nothing in the APK records whether the user showed up; there is no outcome, judgement or attendance string/class. Monolith's routine windows become judged attendance rows: FocusSessionEntity freezes windowStartMillis/windowEndMillis at materialisation and stamps routineOutcome (ATTENDED/PARTIAL/MISSED/LATE_FIRE) plus an E1-E4 evidenceMask with first/last evidence instants (MonolithModels.kt:309-320), derived by RoutineDerive.kt:53 (WindowJudgement { ATTENDED, PARTIAL, MISSED, HELD, LATE_FIRE, NOT_DELIVERED, UNKNOWN }) and RoutineDerive.kt:79-101. Blockit's Tower can only fall or be repaired after the fact; Monolith keeps a per-window evidentiary record of compliance the original never attempts.

Recommendation: Keep and surface this ledger — it is a system Blockit simply lacks. Its value is currently capped by how little of the judgement reaches a review surface, so wiring the existing ATTENDED/PARTIAL/MISSED record into stats would convert an invisible out-build into a user-visible one.

#### [MEDIUM] Monolith seals each session with a frozen held-apps/sites snapshot, a classified outcome and a numbered receipt; Blockit records only elapsed time

Blockit EVIDENCE.md §7.6/§12: a finished session leaves only a per-day Record of time segments and a generic share text ('I just completed a distraction-free session…'); there is no seal moment, no record of what was blocked, and no classification of how the session ended. Monolith freezes the enforcement set into the session row at birth — heldAppsAtSeal/heldSitesAtSeal written exactly once inside startSession's transaction from the same snapshot that deactivates the predecessor (MonolithModels.kt:325-332; MonolithRepository.kt:1375-1391) — classifies the ending once from a fixed vocabulary (ReceiptState.kt:28-63: ELAPSED_CLEAN, ELAPSED_SHIELD_GAP, VALVE_BROKE, GRACE_CANCEL, ENDED_EARLY, ROUTINE_ATTENDED…) and stamps a claimed receiptNumber on the row inside the claim transaction (MonolithModels.kt:371). The original cannot prove after the fact what a given session held or how it ended; Monolith's row can.

Recommendation: Preserve the seal-snapshot/outcome/receipt-number triple as Monolith's audit-trail advantage over the original — when receipt or stats work is prioritised, read these frozen fields rather than recomputing from live state, which is exactly the discipline Blockit's time-only Record never needed but Monolith's richer claims require.

## Supplement: Forest head-to-head (from its actual APK)

Evidence base: Forest v5.33.0 (cc.forestapp) APK, statically reverse-engineered only — never installed or run. Full evidence: apk-re/forest/EVIDENCE.md. Same rules as the main report: no store-presence or monetisation findings.

### Forest — Head-to-head losses — 8 findings (0 critical, 5 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Forest's scheduled plans carry timed per-target unblock sessions; Monolith's routines have no per-target exemption at all

Forest EVIDENCE.md §6.2: Room table unblock_sessions(id, target_token, target_type, interval_start, interval_end) with UnblockSessionRepository and DetermineShieldUnblockRouteUseCase — a Time Guard plan can exempt one named app or domain for one bounded window inside the schedule, then re-block automatically. Monolith has no equivalent object: RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550) carries only a loadoutName pointer, and the only exemption machinery in the app is the session-scoped 2-minute peek lease for PEEK-tier apps during a manual session. A routine that fires while the user legitimately needs one app for ten minutes offers no targeted hole — it is the whole tier matrix or nothing.

Recommendation: Add a per-target, time-bounded exemption record for routine windows (target package/domain + start/end), evaluated by the shield door alongside the tier matrix, instead of forcing routine users to weaken the whole loadout.

#### [HIGH] One Forest plan blocks apps, whole Play categories and web domains in a single object; Monolith routines point at one of three global presets

Forest EVIDENCE.md §6.2: shield_plans stores settings_application_tokens, settings_category_tokens AND settings_web_domain_tokens in one row, with an RRULE-style schedule_day_recurrence_rule — a plan is a self-contained rule set spanning three target kinds. Monolith's RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-571) stores no targets at all, only loadoutName naming one of three developer-written SmartLoadout presets; categories exist in Monolith only as a catalogue birth-guess/sort key, never as a blocking target, and websites live in a separate global list the routine does not reference. Forest's scheduled blocking is composable per plan; Monolith's is three fixed stencils shared by every routine.

Recommendation: Give routines their own target sets — explicit apps, categories and domains stored on the routine — rather than a pointer to a global preset.

#### [HIGH] Forest uses its notification listener to stop notifications from corrupting detection; Monolith uses its listener to capture notification content — and still gets corrupted by them

Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.3: its only listener service, NotificationBlocker (BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE), exists for detection hygiene — strings 'To avoid misjudgement due to pop-up notifications from other apps' and 'Advanced notification detection' — so a heads-up banner is never mistaken for the user leaving to another app. It holds nothing: no held-notification inbox or content store exists anywhere in the APK. Monolith's MonolithNotificationListener (AndroidManifest.xml) does the opposite job — capturing and storing other apps' notification title+body — while Forest engineered the listener as a shield for its detector, Monolith engineered it as a content vacuum and left its own detection exposed to the same pop-up confusion Forest designed against.

Recommendation: Feed the listener's posting events into the detection path as a 'foreground change was a notification' signal, the way Forest does, before adding any more capture features on top of it.

#### [HIGH] Forest's detector re-checks plan, schedule and entitlement state on every foreground change; Monolith's doors enforce a state they never re-verify

Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.1: the JADX decompile of ForestAccessibilityService shows it Koin-injected with ShieldPlanRepository, SchedulePlanner, UnblockSessionRepository, DetectServiceStateProvider, ServiceLevelManager and a shield-settings check taking (ServiceLevel, ShieldSettings) — checkingCurrentState(currentPackageName) evaluates the live plan + schedule + unblock session + service level at each window change, and Deep Focus is off by default when its permissions are missing (§5.2: 'Since you haven't turned on certain permissions, the Deep focus is turned off by default'). Monolith's accessibility door and shield door enforce from session state latched at arm time; nothing in either service re-reads the current plan-equivalent or degrades the session's claims when a grant disappears underneath it.

Recommendation: Make both Monolith doors evaluate current grant/plan state per intercept and stamp the session with the degraded truth when a component grant is gone, rather than enforcing — and certifying — a stale snapshot.

#### [HIGH] Every dead Forest session names its killer: Plants.die_reason plus a 'Why tree withered' screen; Monolith's session record has no culprit field

Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: the Plants table carries die_reason TEXT and has_left, and the string pool has 'Your tree withers due to this app: %1$s', '%1$s made our tree wither' and a dedicated 'Why tree withered' / 'Check why tree withered' surface — failure attribution is a stored, per-session fact the user can inspect. Monolith's FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:268-330) records intention, elapsed, tamperDetected, phantomReachesBlocked and an outcome classification about the shield's own behaviour, but no field records which app or action ended the session; the receipt grades the shield, never names the culprit in the session's own record.

Recommendation: Persist a failure-cause field (package + trigger kind) on the session row at finalisation and print it on the receipt, so a broken session explains itself the way a withered tree does.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest's session artefact has a persisted growth-phase state machine and its failures stay on the record permanently; Monolith's tower keeps only successes

Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: the grown result is its own table Trees(id, plant_id, tree_type, is_dead, theme, phase) — phase is a stored state of the artefact, and a killed tree persists with is_dead set, accumulating into the visible forest as history, failures included. Monolith's tower (BlockitTowerViews / BlockitTowerFadersAndCatalogViews) is a brick count derived from completed sessions: a session that breaks leaves no brick, no marker, no artefact — the tower is a success-only ledger, so the user's history of failure is invisible everywhere except outcome codes in the Drawer.

Recommendation: Persist a per-session artefact row with a phase/state (growing, completed, broken, repaired) so failed sessions leave a visible, inspectable trace instead of vanishing from the record.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest sessions can be extended mid-flight through a first-class extension timer; Monolith can only extend the task, never the session

Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: Plants carries extension_timer_id next to timer_id, the timer engine has PlantTimerHandlerImpl with TimerBackupPlugin, and MainPresenter.onExtensionTimerEnded handles the extension as its own timer object with its own lifecycle and backup. Monolith has no session-extension path at all: the only extend verb in the codebase is extendActiveTaskOvertime (MonolithViewModel.kt:1814), which adds overtime to the bound task while the session's targetDurationSeconds (MonolithModels.kt:268) stays whatever was dialled at arm time — a user who under-dialled must break the seal or ride out a session that no longer matches the work.

Recommendation: Add an explicit add-time operation on the active session (new target duration, receipt-visible, signed into the session state) instead of leaving task overtime as the only pressure valve.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest closes each session with a stored, fact-based reflection; Monolith closes with a verdict slip and nothing the user said

Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: post-session Reflect is a built subsystem — SaveFocusReflectionUseCase, PickFocusSessionFactUseCase, LoadPlantRecordsInsightUseCase, ReflectGuidanceComposer, PlantRecordsFactMemory and ReflectionHistoryMemory, with the string 'Your first Reflect is saved. A little story to go with your trees!' — the app picks a fact from the finished session and stores the user's reflection against that plant. Monolith's finish path produces only the receipt: outcome code, times, held counts. No per-session reflection, note or user-authored line is stored against a FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:268-330 has no such column).

Recommendation: Store one user-authored reflection (plus one auto-picked session fact) on the session row at finish, and surface them together in the Drawer day view.
### Forest — Visual design — 4 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Forest ships a real animation runtime — Rive state machines and Lottie — as design infrastructure; Monolith hand-rolls every motion in Canvas code

Forest EVIDENCE.md §14/§16: a dedicated animation stack — com.seekrtech.rivecmp (162 classes), Rive assets for the moments that matter (plant_success.riv, cta.riv, main_page_ic.riv, onboard_deep_focus_walkthrough.riv, subscription_walkthrough.riv), InteractiveRiveAnimationView/BreatheRiveView interactive views, Lottie compositions and a seasonal SnowfallView. Motion is authored as state-machine assets, not code. Monolith has no animation asset or runtime of any kind: every moving thing — wheel, tower, sleds, seal-shot — is drawn frame-by-frame in custom Canvas views (the 2,416-line BlockitCoreViews god-file), so each new moment costs bespoke draw code and per-frame allocation instead of an authored asset.

Recommendation: Adopt an asset-based animation format (Rive or Lottie) for the seal, growth and intercept moments, and stop spending Canvas draw code on choreography.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest's type system is one full family plus a dedicated numerals face; Monolith splits three unrelated families across surfaces

Forest EVIDENCE.md §14: assets/font holds the Source Sans Pro family as 12 TTFs (full weight and italic range) plus roboto_medium_numbers.ttf — numerals, the most-read glyphs in a timer app, get their own purpose-cut face. Monolith's res/font is three unrelated families in fragments — Sora (4 cuts), Atkinson Hyperlegible (2), Anonymous Pro (2) — assigned per surface: dial numerals in Sora, mono labels in Anonymous Pro, body in Atkinson, with no single family carrying the product and no numerals-specific face for the wheel, desk clock or receipt figures that are the app's most-read numbers.

Recommendation: Consolidate on one family with a full weight range for UI text and cut or adopt a dedicated numerals face for the dial, clock and receipt; retire the third family.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest keys its UI sounds to growth stages (sound_tree0/1/2.ogg); Monolith's seal sound is one frozen waveform for every outcome

Forest EVIDENCE.md §14: res/raw ships discrete, stage-keyed audio assets — sound_tree0.ogg, sound_tree1.ogg, sound_tree2.ogg for the tree's growth stages, plus sound_click1, sound_slide and sound_ring_c — sound design is mapped to the artefact's state. Monolith's entire voice is one procedural synth whose seal throw is deliberately parameter-free and pinned by a golden SHA-256 hash in tests: a 10-minute session, a 4-hour session, a first finish and a hundredth finish are bit-identical audio, and no sound is keyed to any stage of the session's progress.

Recommendation: Introduce a small set of stage-keyed sounds (arm, mid-session milestone, finish, break) as assets or parameterised synth variants, and un-pin the golden hash so the audio can grow up.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest's artefact layer is themeable down to the ground it grows from (land skins); Monolith's tower sits on one fixed canvas treatment

Forest EVIDENCE.md §10.2/§14: a land_skin_items table and a whole stforestkit.landskin module make the forest's ground itself a swappable visual layer, on top of per-species atlas art and Trees.theme per planted tree — the scene composition (species + land + season) is data, not code. Monolith's tower is drawn by TowerView canvas code with hard-coded token colours: one ground, one treatment, forever — the most-viewed surface in the app cannot change its look without a code change, and no user-facing visual variation of it exists.

Recommendation: Separate the tower scene's visual treatment (ground, backdrop, palette variant) into data-driven themes the user can pick, instead of baking the one treatment into draw code.
### Forest — Platform execution — 3 findings (1 critical, 1 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] Forest runs its whole blocking business with no foreground service and no boot receiver of its own; Monolith needs a persistent specialUse FGS, its own boot receiver and a device admin

Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.4/§17: the manifest declares NO app-owned foreground service (no foregroundServiceType anywhere; the only SystemForegroundService is WorkManager's) and NO Forest-owned BOOT_COMPLETED receiver — boot rescheduling is delegated to WorkManager's RescheduleReceiver and Evernote android-job, and timer survival runs on exact alarms (both SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and USE_EXACT_ALARM declared). Monolith's footprint for the same job: MonolithShieldService as a directBootAware foregroundServiceType=specialUse service (AndroidManifest.xml) whose monitor loop polls every 2 seconds (MonolithShieldService.kt:193 delay(2000L)), its own LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED/BOOT_COMPLETED/QUICKBOOT_POWERON receiver, a RoutineAlarmReceiver, a ReleaseRetryReceiver and a DeviceAdminReceiver. Forest proves the category's core loop does not require a permanent foreground-service presence at all.

Recommendation: Re-architect session timing onto exact alarms + WorkManager rescheduling and demote the shield FGS to an on-demand enforcement aid, so the app is not a permanent foreground-service resident.

#### [HIGH] Forest's first tree is planted before any special-access grant exists; Monolith demands six Settings trips before any value

Forest EVIDENCE.md §13: onboarding is a guided first plant with zero special permissions — OnBoardFirstPlantManager/FirstPlantStartFragment start a 10-minute countdown tree inside the tutorial, and permission asks are deferred and pitched per feature afterwards: a PermissionActivity centre, the Deep Focus walkthrough asking for detection grants, Shield onboarding with its own AccessibilityExplanationBottomSheet ('Why Accessibility is needed'), and account creation is not front-gated (guest mode, registration prompted after the first tree). Monolith inverts the order completely: accessibility, usage access, overlay, notification listener, battery exemption and device admin — six separate Settings scavenger trips — stand between install and the first armable session, with no guided first session at the end of them.

Recommendation: Ship a permission-free guided first session (timer-only, no blocking) inside onboarding, and move each special-access ask to the feature that needs it, each behind its own rationale sheet, as Forest does.

#### [MEDIUM] Forest achieves commercial blocking with no DeviceAdmin and no VPN anywhere in the binary; Monolith spends a device-admin slot on an uninstall guard

Forest EVIDENCE.md §3/§17 (negative evidence, searched across manifest + full DEX string pool + class inventory): no DeviceAdmin receiver, no VpnService, no BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN — its enforcement footprint is accessibility + usage stats + overlay + alarms, full stop. Monolith declares a DeviceAdminReceiver in AndroidManifest.xml and carries a device-admin policy set for an uninstall-guard role, i.e. it requests one of Android's most sensitive admin surfaces for a job Forest's manifest proves a top-category blocker never needs to ask for at all.

Recommendation: Drop the device-admin component and its policies; if uninstall friction is wanted, use the accessibility Settings-guard path already built, and cut the admin permission surface entirely.
### Forest — Comparative audit — 4 findings (0 critical, 3 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Where Monolith out-builds Forest: Forest's core loop is honour-system by default — without Deep Focus a plant enforces nothing

Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.2, in Forest's own strings: 'You have already turned off Deep focus, leaving the app will not affect your tree, and your focused time will not be counted towards the leaderboard' and 'Deep focus enabled. You'll be guided back to Forest if you open apps that aren't on your Allow List' — enforcement is an opt-in mode layered on a timer; the default plant is a countdown the user can ignore, and even Deep Focus only 'guides you back' with a reminder interstitial ('Sorry, this app isn't on your Allow List. Return to Forest and stay focused!'). Monolith's armed session always enforces: the Airlock intercepts the blocked app itself, peeks are leased and timed, and the session receipts what actually happened. On the category's central promise — the phone physically stopping you — Monolith's default is the stricter product.

Recommendation: Keep enforcement non-optional in Monolith's positioning and onboarding copy; it is a genuine, provable edge over the category's best-known app.

#### [HIGH] Where Forest is conspicuously worse: its own detector's false alarms kill the user's tree — and erasing the record costs coins

Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.2/§10.1: Forest's help strings admit the failure modes in writing — 'Notifications cause your tree to wither', 'Unable to detect other applications running in the foreground' — i.e. the artefact dies for detection errors the user did not commit, on OEMs Forest knows it mishandles. The withered record then persists, and §10.1 documents RemovePlantByCoinUseCase with the string 'Are you sure to spend %1$d coins to delete this planting record?' — the user pays earned currency to erase a failure Forest's own FAQ attributes to its detector. Monolith's detector failures are real but they are never billed to the user: no currency exists that a broken session can cost, and no record requires payment to remove.

Recommendation: Preserve this asymmetry deliberately: Monolith should keep failure records free to dismiss and never attach a cost — in any currency — to the app's own detection mistakes.

#### [HIGH] Where Monolith out-builds Forest: Forest's focus timer ships inside a 257 MB APK carrying five analytics stacks and four ad networks; Monolith ships none of that

Forest EVIDENCE.md §1/§11.3/§16: the base APK alone is 268,937,682 bytes (~257 MiB) with ~86.9 MB of DEX across 9 files, and the binary embeds AdMob, AppLovin MAX, Facebook Audience Network (its own assets/audience_network.dex), Vungle and InMobi, plus Firebase Analytics/Crashlytics, Amplitude, Snowplow, AppsFlyer attribution and Intercom — a focus timer that watches its user through five analytics pipelines. Monolith ships as one small APK with zero ad SDKs, zero analytics, zero trackers and no account system; its manifest even hard-disables backup (allowBackup=false, AndroidManifest.xml) to keep its 'data on this phone only' claim true. On footprint and data hygiene, the student-built app is the cleaner binary by an enormous margin.

Recommendation: Treat the zero-tracker, local-only footprint as a headline product property (it is verifiably rare in this category) and resist adding analytics SDKs without a specific, user-visible payoff.

#### [MEDIUM] Where Monolith out-builds Forest: a Forest plant cannot block a website at all — web blocking exists only inside separate Time Guard plans

Forest EVIDENCE.md §17 (negative evidence): 'No website-blocking machinery beyond Shield's domain-token lists' — domain tokens live only in shield_plans (§6.2), so the signature flow, a live plant with Deep Focus, has no web layer whatsoever: a user can open any site in a browser mid-plant and the tree only dies if the browser itself is not allowlisted. Monolith's session enforcement includes its blocked-sites list inside the session itself — browser use during a session is policed by domain, not just by the browser's package. For the single most common distraction surface, Monolith's session is the more complete enclosure.

Recommendation: Keep site blocking session-scoped (not plan-scoped) as Monolith already does, and say so in comparative copy; it is a structural edge over Forest's main flow.

### Second-pass findings — 6 findings (0 critical, 4 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

- **[HIGH] Forest's stopwatch mode auto-stops at a cap and withers under 10 minutes; Monolith's stopwatch runs forever with no terminal rule of its own** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: Plants.mode is persisted and stopwatch is a complete terminal rule-set — 'it takes 10 minutes to grow a tree and it automatically stops at %d minutes. If you stop within 10 minutes, you will get a withered tree.' Monolith: startSession derives stopwatch only from durationMinutes<10 and substitutes a 20-minute floor (MonolithRepository.kt:1330-1332, STOPWATCH_MIN_FLOOR_SECONDS at :109); updateSessionProgress's stopwatch branch (MonolithRepository.kt:1970-1984) merely copies verifiedElapsed into the row and returns — it never caps, never auto-ends, and never records a distinct under-minimum outcome. The only clean stopwatch exit is a manual post-floor disarm in MonolithViewModel.kt:2238-2246.
  - Fix: Give count-up mode its own terminal law: store an auto-stop cap on the session row, end the session in updateSessionProgress when the cap is reached, and book a pre-floor stop as a distinct failed/partial outcome instead of leaving the session running indefinitely until the user finds the valve.
- **[HIGH] Forest plants from saved favourites bundling mode, duration and tag; Monolith offers only four hardcoded in-memory presets** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1: SpeciesFavorite(count_mode, tree_type, tag_id, plant_time_in_min, ...) is a persisted table bundling mode + species + tag + duration, launched in one tap via MainViewModel.startPlantingWithFavorite. Monolith's nearest counterpart is a compile-time enum of exactly four presets (MonolithModels.kt:61-71: STOPWATCH_FLOW, POMODORO_25_5, DEEP_50_10, EXAM_90) held only in ViewModel memory (MonolithViewModel.kt:223-224); selectStudyPreset (MonolithViewModel.kt:1459-1463) sets just _dialMinutes and _studyBlocksCount — no persisted user preset, no bundle of intention/profile/loadout/tag, nothing a user can save from a session they actually repeat.
  - Fix: Add a persisted session-preset table (duration, blocks, profile/loadout, intention) with a save-from-current-setup verb and one-tap start, instead of four hardcoded enum rows that cannot learn the user's real recurring sessions.
- **[HIGH] Forest stores enforcement strictness on each plant and pays half reward in its lenient mode; Monolith has one all-or-nothing contract per session** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §5.1-5.2: Plants carries is_deep_focus INTEGER per plant, and the contract is graded per session — Deep Focus on means leaving kills the tree and earns leaderboard credit; off means leaving does not kill it, and the lenient fallback pays 'only half the reward if you leave Forest midway.' Monolith's FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:268-380) has no enforcement-level field at all: every session is the same hard-shield contract, and the only exits are completion, grace cancel, or spending the single weekly emergency token — there is no stored lenient session type and no proportional/partial reward for a session the user declared low-stakes at arm time.
  - Fix: Store an enforcement level on the session row at arm time (strict vs lenient), let lenient sessions be left without the weekly valve, and price their credit proportionally — so the contract is chosen per session instead of one severity fitting every occasion.
- **[HIGH] Forest layers three detection signals (accessibility + UsageEvents stream + task-stack); Monolith's shield door guesses foreground from lastTimeUsed alone** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §3/§4.2: the manifest declares a foreground-detection cluster — PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS plus GET_TASKS and REORDER_TASKS (task-stack detection) — and the DeviceTracker layer ships UsageEventsManager/UsageEventsManagerImpl and UsageStatsMonitor/UsageStatsMonitorImpl under a MonitoringEngine, i.e. a real UsageEvents event-stream path layered underneath the event-driven ForestAccessibilityService (§4.1). Monolith's manifest declares PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS only — no GET_TASKS/REORDER_TASKS — and its code never calls queryEvents: MonolithRepository.kt:564 queryForegroundBlockedApp() runs queryUsageStats(INTERVAL_DAILY) over a 15s window and guesses the foreground app from lastTimeUsed within 8s, a guess the shield loop acts on every 2s (MonolithShieldService.kt:178, delay(2000L) at :193). Where Forest's supplementary path reads an ordered event stream and its manifest keeps a task-stack signal in reserve, Monolith's session-long enforcer has exactly one signal and it is a timestamp heuristic that can name the wrong app or miss a fast app-switch entirely.
  - Fix: Add a UsageEvents (queryEvents) event-stream path as the shield's foreground source and reserve lastTimeUsed polling as fallback only; consider the task-stack permissions as an additional degraded-mode signal.
- **[MEDIUM] Forest treats screen/lock state as a first-class enforcement signal in a separate :watch process; Monolith has no screen-state input anywhere** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.2/§4.4: the APK ships com.seekrtech.screendetector.ScreenDetector with ScreenAction/ScreenActionType, persists a Room screen_event(event_type, timestamp) table alongside app_usage_event, and runs a dedicated :watch process pair — seekrtech.utils.stdevicelockeventmanager.STDLEMService + JobSchedulerService — whose whole job is tracking device-lock events independently of the main process. A full search of Monolith's app/src/main/java and AndroidManifest.xml returns no ACTION_SCREEN_ON/OFF, no USER_PRESENT, no KeyguardManager reference at all: the shield loop (MonolithShieldService.kt:84-193) reads only the session snapshot and the app table, so Monolith cannot distinguish 'user locked the phone and walked away' from 'user is active', cannot feed screen state into session accounting or detection hygiene, and has no watchdog process that survives independently of the process carrying all its enforcement.
  - Fix: Ingest screen-on/off and keyguard state as a first-class signal (a lightweight receiver feeding the session/detection logic), so locked-idle time and screen state stop being invisible to enforcement.
- **[MEDIUM] Forest ships an 'Advanced Detection' fallback and OEM-specific degraded behaviour for when detection fails; Monolith has one fixed detector config and no fallback mode** — Forest EVIDENCE.md §4.2: the APK's own strings admit detector fallibility and design around it — a help string lists devices where Forest cannot detect foreground apps and directs the user to 'turn on the Advanced Detection option', a separate 'Advanced notification detection' string exists, and a Xiaomi-specific string defines degraded behaviour (return to Forest within a few seconds or the tree withers) instead of pretending detection is binary. Monolith ships exactly one fixed detection configuration — app/src/main/res/xml/accessibility_service_config.xml (typeWindowStateChanged|typeWindowContentChanged, notificationTimeout=80) plus the 2s polling loop — with no alternate detection mode, no per-OEM degraded behaviour and nothing a user can switch on when detection misbehaves on their device; the failure mode is silent non-blocking.
  - Fix: Ship a designed fallback: an alternate/advanced detection mode the user can enable, plus explicit degraded behaviour on devices where the primary detector is known to be unreliable, instead of one fixed config that fails silently.
## Supplement: ScreenZen head-to-head (from its actual APK)

Evidence base: ScreenZen (com.screenzen) APK, statically reverse-engineered only — never installed or run. Full evidence: apk-re/screenzen/EVIDENCE.md. Same rules as the main report: no store-presence or monetisation findings.

### ScreenZen — Head-to-head losses — 7 findings (1 critical, 4 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] ScreenZen's trigger is a physical place: a BLE/UWB Halo beacon with inside/outside radius modes; Monolith has no physical-world input of any kind

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §7: Halo is a purchasable hardware beacon — Nordic BLE scanning plus UWB ranging (DiagnosticUwbEvent, UwbGroundTruthRecorder), with block-inside mode ('Apps are blocked when you're inside the halo, like your bedroom or desk'), block-outside mode, and a Zen mode (block-all-except-allowlist), each with per-Halo schedules and radius settings (RemoteHalo$RemoteHaloRadiusSettings). Monolith contains zero Bluetooth, sensor or location code — grep for SensorManager/BluetoothAdapter/Geofence/FusedLocation across app/src/main/java returns nothing — and its only automatic trigger, RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-556), is name + startMinutes + endMinutes + daysMask + loadoutName: clock and weekday, nothing else. A ScreenZen user walks into a room and blocking exists; a Monolith user must have predicted that room on a weekly timetable.

Recommendation: Add a physical trigger surface — at minimum commodity BLE/NFC presence as a routine activator, with inside/outside semantics — so a place, not just a clock, can arm the block.

#### [HIGH] ScreenZen detects from the real UsageEvents event stream on a 500 ms loop; Monolith guesses 'foreground' from lastTimeUsed on a 2-second poll

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §3.2/§3.5: AppObserverService runs a HandlerThread loop with a 500 ms interval field (f16406R0 = 500L) aggregating UsageEvents via helper F4.d (per-app foreground-time maps built from the actual event stream). Monolith's shield door never sees an event: MonolithRepository.kt:572-575 queryForegroundBlockedApp() takes queryUsageStats(INTERVAL_DAILY) and picks the blocked package with the newest lastTimeUsed inside an 8-second window — a recency guess, not a foreground fact — and MonolithShieldService.kt:193 only re-runs that guess every delay(2000L). The rival's detector is both event-true and 4x faster; Monolith can certify an app 'foreground' that was merely used recently, and can miss one that was opened and closed between polls.

Recommendation: Replace the lastTimeUsed guess with UsageEvents aggregation (queryEvents over a rolling window, ACTIVITY_RESUMED/PAUSED pairs) in the shield door, and shorten the poll cadence or drive intercepts from the accessibility door's window events.

#### [HIGH] ScreenZen makes the user type why they are checking — and keeps the history; Monolith's intercept never asks a reason at all

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §4: IntentionalReasonActivity ('Why am I checking?') is a first-class unlock exercise — the reason is typed, stored (IntentionalReasonModel), and past reasons are viewable later (intentional_reason_alternative_def). Monolith's Airlock (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:550-690) is a passive 5-second countdown numeral (88.sp, :636-639) resolved by exactly two chips — RETURN TO FOCUS (:656) and EMERGENCY PEEK (:665) — and no code anywhere asks, records or reviews the user's reason at the moment of temptation (grep for reason-entry UI in the intercept path returns nothing). ScreenZen turns each surrender/return into a written, reviewable record; Monolith records only that an intercept happened.

Recommendation: Add an optional typed-reason step to the Airlock (required for PEEK/LOCKED tiers), persist it against the intercept log, and surface the user's own past reasons on the intercept itself.

#### [HIGH] ScreenZen can become the home screen and delete blocked apps from the drawer; Monolith only catches the tap after the icon is pressed

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §9: LauncherActivity carries a MAIN+HOME intent-filter (disabled by default, opt-in) — a full launcher replacement whose text-first drawer removes app icons ('nothing visually tempts you'), hides strictly blocked apps from the drawer entirely (string_hide_blocked_apps), and badges each app's lock/pause status. Monolith's manifest declares exactly one activity (MainActivity) and no HOME category: every blocked app keeps its icon, name and position in the stock launcher/drawer, fully visible all day, and Monolith's first contact is the post-tap intercept. ScreenZen removes the temptation surface; Monolith polices only the moment after it has already worked.

Recommendation: Ship an optional Monolith launcher (or at minimum a home-screen surface) that hides LOCKED apps and badges PEEK apps, so prevention starts before the tap rather than after it.

#### [HIGH] Halo spaces are shared, with owners who can forbid exceptions; in Monolith the rule-maker and the rule-subject are always the same person

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §7: Halos are multi-user spaces — claim/own/invite/QR-join flows (halo_qr_layout, https://halo.screenzen.co/s/ deep links incl. NFC), owner/member roles with demotion, a 'You're the last owner' guard, owner-enforced strict mode ('Members cannot add exceptions to the blocked apps list'), a public mode for libraries/classrooms where members are visible only when at the Halo, and a group streak per space. Monolith has no multi-user model at all: one device, one user, and every rule protecting that user is editable by that same user in the same app (its entire catalogue lives in the local Room DB behind the single MainActivity). ScreenZen can put enforcement authority in someone else's hands, bound to a place; Monolith cannot express 'someone else set this rule' in any form.

Recommendation: Introduce a delegated-rule concept: an owner-set rule set (starting with shared-space or trusted-person rules) that the device user can view but cannot edit or except.

#### [MEDIUM] ScreenZen's pause screen offers a replacement app to go to instead; Monolith's intercept only ever says no

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §4: ReplacementAppActivity + ReplacementAppModel + bottom_replacement_app_selection let the pause screen offer a substitute app in place of the blocked one — the craving is redirected, not just denied. Monolith has no substitution concept anywhere: grep for replacement/substitute across app/src/main/java finds only an unrelated comment in MonolithRailView.kt:75, and the Airlock's entire vocabulary is RETURN TO FOCUS or EMERGENCY PEEK (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:656-665). A user who opened a blocked app out of a genuine need (messages, maps, payment) is offered no sanctioned alternative destination inside Monolith's friction.

Recommendation: Let each tier/app rule name a replacement app; render it as a third Airlock action that launches the substitute and closes the intercept as a deflection.

#### [MEDIUM] Halo is calibrated like an instrument — hold-to-measure radius, walk-test, edge-flicker smoothing; Monolith's triggers have no calibration concept because they sense nothing

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §7: Halo onboarding includes 'Hold to measure your space' radius calibration (halo_onboard_hold_to_measure), a radius verify walk-test (string_halo_verify_*), floor logic (halo_floor_above/below/same, ceiling-mount guidance), transition-time smoothing explicitly because 'the signal can sometimes flicker near the edge', a Bluetooth-off behaviour policy (Continue/Start/Stop), and sensor fusion across BLE, UWB, barometric altimeter, step detector/counter and activity recognition (HaloSensorBus). Monolith's sensing inventory is the wall clock and a UsageStats recency guess (MonolithRepository.kt:572-575); there is nothing to calibrate, smooth or verify, and its known failure modes (clock travel, polling gaps) are the direct cost of having no physical signal to discipline the digital one.

Recommendation: Whatever trigger surfaces are added, copy the discipline: measured setup, a user-performed verification pass, and hysteresis/smoothing at boundaries instead of raw threshold flips.
### ScreenZen — Visual design — 2 findings (0 critical, 0 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [MEDIUM] ScreenZen lets the user theme the block screen itself — colour schemes and a personal image; Monolith's Airlock is one fixed treatment for every app and every user

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §5/§19: the pause/block screen — the screen its users see most — is user-themeable: ThemeColor model, GroupThemingBottomSheet, group_theming_layout, item_theme_color_layout, plus a personal image chosen through the bundled CanHub cropper, on top of a 679-colour / 1,017-style resource system with Outfit/Rubik/Roboto-Medium type roles. Monolith's Airlock (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt) is a single hard-coded treatment — fixed palette, one 88.sp countdown numeral (:636-639), two text chips — and grep finds no theming, colour-choice or image code for any surface (themecolor/blockScreenColor/custom image: zero hits). The screen Monolith shows at the exact moment of maximum frustration is the one screen it never lets the user make their own.

Recommendation: Give the Airlock a small theme system: a handful of colour treatments and an optional user image/word, applied per tier or per app, stored with the rule.

#### [MEDIUM] ScreenZen teaches with motion — Lottie tutorials and paired light/dark explainer videos; Monolith has no animated teaching layer at all

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §13/§19: seven named Lottie assets teach its core gestures (strict_blocked.json, lock_pause.json, quick_launch_screenzen.json, swipe_down_notification.json, icon_to_text.json, swipe_up_app_drawer.json), and its scariest permission — accessibility — is sold with explainer videos in both light and dark variants (res/raw/accessibility_permission.mp4 / _dark.mp4, ~1.8-1.9 MB each), plus a streamed walkthrough. Monolith ships no Lottie dependency, no res/raw media at all (the directory does not exist), and explains six special-access permissions and an entire invented verb vocabulary (ARM/SEAL/CUE/FORGE) with static text boards only. ScreenZen's design system includes a motion layer whose job is comprehension; Monolith's motion is confined to in-session ornament.

Recommendation: Add a minimal teaching-motion set: one animated explainer per special-access permission and per core verb, in the app's own visual language, shown at first need rather than in a manual.
### ScreenZen — Platform execution — 2 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] ScreenZen's core blocking runs on four special accesses and no notification listener; Monolith gates its promise on six, including the most invasive one

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §2/§14: its onboarding asks, in order, usage access, display-over-other-apps, accessibility, battery exemption — and its 32-permission manifest contains no notification-listener component at all, because its blocking never needs one. Monolith's own guard board counts SIX permission-family items (WatchStore.kt:80-95: ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN, NOTIFICATION_LISTENER, OVERLAY, BATTERY — PERMISSIONS list at :93-95), and the notification listener is not optional garnish: MonolithNotificationListener is a headline manifest service whose grant is one of the four counted guard items. ScreenZen reaches always-on blocking with a smaller special-access footprint and one fewer Settings scavenger trip class; Monolith demands the single most sensitive grant in Android (read every notification) as a core gate.

Recommendation: Demote the notification listener from core gate to an optional, separately-explained enhancement; the block itself should stand on usage + accessibility + overlay like the rival's does.

#### [MEDIUM] ScreenZen's device admin declares an empty policy set — anti-uninstall only, exactly as labelled; Monolith declares a password policy it never exercises

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §3.3: its DeviceAdminService points at res/xml/device_admin_policy.xml containing an EMPTY <uses-policies/> — zero policies exercised; the class only overrides onDisableRequested/onEnabled/onDisabled, and its summary string says plainly 'Active to prevent ScreenZen from being uninstalled.' Monolith ships the same anti-uninstall trick but its app/src/main/res/xml/device_admin_receiver.xml:3-5 declares <limit-password/> inside <uses-policies> — a credential-policy power no Monolith code path ever calls (MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver only warns on disable). The rival proves the feature needs no policy grant at all; Monolith's manifest asks for one anyway, widening its Play-policy and user-trust surface for nothing.

Recommendation: Empty Monolith's uses-policies to match: keep the anti-uninstall receiver, delete the limit-password declaration.
### ScreenZen — Comparative audit — 4 findings (0 critical, 2 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Where Monolith out-builds ScreenZen: it holds other apps' notifications — ScreenZen structurally cannot touch them

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §10/§20: there is no NotificationListenerService anywhere in its manifest or dex inventory and no ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY — its blocking never holds, cancels or even sees another app's notifications; its only notifications are its own. Monolith ships MonolithNotificationListener (AndroidManifest.xml, BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE) which captures incoming notifications during a session and cancels them into a digest (MonolithNotificationListener.kt:93 cancelNotification(sbn.key)) — an entire enforcement surface, silencing the message layer and not just the app layer, that ScreenZen does not attempt. Honest limit: earlier rounds showed Monolith's digest implementation is deeply flawed (dead transcripts, no restore) — but the architecture and the capability exist in Monolith and are absent by design in the rival.

Recommendation: Keep and fix the notification-holding surface — it is a genuine differentiator over this rival; prioritise restore/actionability of held items over new surfaces.

#### [HIGH] Where Monolith out-builds ScreenZen: zero-network privacy — ScreenZen bundles a session-recording SDK, the full Firebase suite and cleartext traffic

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §1/§17/§18: Smartlook session-recording/analytics is its largest third-party presence (1,789 classes, own installer provider and upload job services), alongside Firebase Auth/Firestore/Functions/Storage/Messaging/Crashlytics/App Check, its own analytics endpoint (https://analytics2.screenzen.co/api), cleartextTrafficPermitted="true" in its network security config, and a bare-IP cleartext help page in code (http://173.212.237.16/how_to_screen_record.html). Monolith's manifest declares no INTERNET permission at all, has no account system and no analytics SDK — its data physically cannot leave the phone. None of this is visible from ScreenZen's store page; only the APK shows what an install actually phones home to, and against that baseline Monolith's local-only architecture is a real, ship-ready advantage it never states.

Recommendation: Treat the zero-network posture as a headline product property: state it in-app (PARK's plate already claims on-device-only data) and refuse analytics/session-recording SDKs categorically.

#### [MEDIUM] Where Monolith out-builds ScreenZen: package visibility restraint — a single <queries> intent vs QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §2: its manifest declares android.permission.QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES — the broadest package-visibility grant Android offers, flagged by Play policy. Monolith builds its entire installed-app catalogue through one scoped declaration: AndroidManifest.xml <queries> with a single MAIN/LAUNCHER intent filter — it can only ever see launchable apps, which is exactly its domain, and nothing else on the device. Same feature (an app catalogue to block from), materially smaller visibility footprint, only provable by reading both manifests.

Recommendation: Hold this line: resist any future QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES request; if a feature needs a non-launchable package, query it by exact package name.

#### [MEDIUM] What ScreenZen does conspicuously worse, visible only in the APK: its self-healing watchdog receiver is exported and takes orders from any app

ScreenZen EVIDENCE §3.3: WatchdogReceiver is exported=true with no permission guard and no intent-filter; it reads extras (service_class_name, interval, is_accessibility_service) and restarts the named service class — i.e. any app on the device can send it an explicit intent and direct which of ScreenZen's services to restart, and BootDeviceReceivers is likewise exported=true. Monolith's manifest exports nothing except its launcher activity: MonolithBootReceiver, RoutineAlarmReceiver, ReleaseRetryReceiver and MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver are all exported=false. ScreenZen's resilience machinery doubles as an unauthenticated control surface; Monolith's equivalent receivers cannot be spoken to by other apps at all.

Recommendation: No Monolith change needed — record as a rival weakness. If Monolith ever adds a watchdog receiver, keep it non-exported or signature-permission guarded, unlike the rival's.
