### Second-pass findings — 10 findings (0 critical, 7 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

- **[HIGH] ScreenZen detects Android Advanced Protection and degrades openly; Monolith's accessibility doors just die silently** — ScreenZen EVIDENCE.md §2/§6: the APK declares android.permission.QUERY_ADVANCED_PROTECTION_MODE and ships advanced_protection_* strings stating that under Android Advanced Protection accessibility access is blocked so website/Shorts/Reels blocking cannot run, while app blocking still works — a detected, communicated degraded mode. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml (permissions at lines 7-14) declares no such permission and no code checks the mode, while its website blocker (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:256), Shorts/Reels sniper (:232) and Settings tamper guard (:206) all ride the single accessibility service whose event path early-returns without an active session (:192-195). On an Advanced Protection device those three doors die with the accessibility binding and Monolith has no detection, no fallback and no user-facing notice of which protections are gone.
  - Fix: Declare QUERY_ADVANCED_PROTECTION_MODE, detect the mode at arm time and in the guard board, and surface an explicit degraded-mode state (app blocking live, site/Shorts/guard dead) instead of letting the accessibility-dependent doors fail silently.
- **[HIGH] ScreenZen guards the phone's clock settings as a bypass route; Monolith's Settings guard is blind to the Date & time page** — ScreenZen EVIDENCE.md §4: the APK ships the anti-tamper string info_lock_time_change — 'If you find yourself changing your phone's time to bypass ScreenZen schedules, this will disable your phone's time or time zone settings' — i.e. the rival treats the system clock settings page itself as a tamper surface. Monolith's Settings guard cannot see that page at all: MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:309-327 (isPackageInstallerOrTamperSettings) only fires for com.android.settings when the window text contains 'monolith' (line 320) AND one of force stop/deactivate/uninstall/clear storage/clear data/device admin (lines 321-326) — a Date & time settings screen contains neither, so the user can walk to the clock settings mid-session completely unintercepted, while Monolith's own foreground check is wall-clock based (MonolithRepository.kt:570-575, System.currentTimeMillis window over queryUsageStats).
  - Fix: Extend the Settings guard to treat the Date & time / time-zone settings screens as tamper surfaces during an active session (intercept regardless of whether the page mentions Monolith), matching the rival's explicit clock-tamper countermeasure.
- **[HIGH] ScreenZen enforces the unlock window from inside the app with a floating timer bubble and a pre-relock warning; Monolith's overlay permission creates nothing** — ScreenZen EVIDENCE.md §5: its SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW grant drives a real overlay — layouts overlay_collapsed_bubble / overlay_expanded_bubble / view_bubble_message, a draggable ScreenZen-logo bubble over the unlocked app that expands to show remaining unlock time (app_unlocked_floating_bubble, info_floating_timer_notification) — plus a warning notification before the unlock expires (info_notification_before_time, notification_nbefore_time_nexpires). Monolith declares the same permission (AndroidManifest.xml:11) but creates no overlay window anywhere: the only WindowManager use in the codebase is FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON at ui/components/AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:96, and there is no pre-expiry warning notification. Once Monolith lets a user into an app there is no in-app countdown presence and no warning shot before any re-lock — enforcement exists only at the moment of the next intercept.
  - Fix: Spend the already-declared SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW grant on a floating remaining-time bubble over leased/unlocked apps and fire a warning notification shortly before expiry, so the time-box is visible and announced while the user is inside the app, not only discovered at the next intercept.
- **[HIGH] Halo resolves the vertical problem Monolith cannot sense at all: barometer/altimeter floor disambiguation (above/below/same) plus ceiling-mount guidance, on top of BLE/UWB ranging** — EVIDENCE.md §7: Halo's detection stack is not BLE alone — HaloSensorBus fuses IMU, a barometric pressure/altimeter listener, step-detector/counter and activity-recognition, and places carry explicit vertical logic (halo_floor_above/below/same, 'Ideally mounted near the ceiling, away from the floor below') so a beacon in an upstairs bedroom does not block the downstairs desk through the floor. Monolith has no vertical or physical sensing at all: AndroidManifest.xml:6-14 declares only VIBRATE, FOREGROUND_SERVICE, POST_NOTIFICATIONS, RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS — no BLUETOOTH_SCAN/CONNECT, no ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION — and a codebase search returns 0 references to SensorManager, BluetoothAdapter or NfcAdapter; its only trigger entity, RoutineEntity in MonolithModels.kt:550-571, stores name/startMinutes/endMinutes/daysMask/loadoutName/enabled/pausedUntilMillis and nothing else.
  - Fix: If Monolith ever adds a place trigger, it needs a floor/altitude dimension and mounting guidance from day one, not a flat radius; until then, do not claim place-awareness parity — a clock window cannot distinguish two rooms stacked vertically, let alone two desks in one room.
- **[HIGH] Halo ships a pre-committed failure policy for when its sensor dies (Bluetooth off: Continue/Start/Stop blocking); Monolith's rules carry no fail-open/fail-closed field at all** — EVIDENCE.md §7: every Halo carries an explicit Bluetooth-off behaviour policy (info_bluetooth_off: Continue / Start / Stop blocking when BT is off) — the owner pre-decides whether a dead radio fails open, fails closed, or holds the last state, alongside RemoteHalo interval and transition-time settings. Monolith has no degraded-sensing policy field anywhere: RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-571) has only enabled and pausedUntilMillis, GuardSettingsEntity (MonolithModels.kt:745+) has no fail-mode column, and the manifest (AndroidManifest.xml:6-14) does not even request a radio whose loss could be policy-managed. Its sensing failures therefore default to whatever the code happens to do, not to a choice the user made in advance.
  - Fix: Add an explicit, per-routine degraded-mode choice (hold last state / keep blocking / release) that is stored with the rule and surfaced when a sensor or permission is lost, mirroring the Bluetooth-off policy — a blocker whose failure direction is undecided will fail in the direction the craving prefers.
- **[HIGH] Halo's public mode turns one beacon into an institutional space — presence-gated member visibility and a hidden group streak for libraries/classrooms; Monolith has no place, member or presence entity to build one from** — EVIDENCE.md §7: beyond private sharing, Halo has a public mode for libraries/classrooms (info_halo_public_mode: members are visible only when physically at the Halo, and the group streak is hidden), a per-Halo group streak ('Build a streak as long as you remain a member'), QR/NFC join via https://halo.screenzen.co/s/… with an NDEF_DISCOVERED filter on SplashActivity, and owner/member roles with a 'You're the last owner' guard. Monolith's data model has no place, member, role or presence entity at all — MonolithModels.kt defines only FocusTaskEntity:101, BlockedAppEntity:232, FocusProfileEntity:252, FocusSessionEntity:268, EmergencyBreakSpendEntity:443, InterceptLogEntity:452, CapturedNotificationEntity:463, BlockedSiteEntity:544, RoutineEntity:550, GuardSettingsEntity:745 and DayNoteEntity:794 — and its manifest declares no NFC or account surface, so one phone's owner can never publish a space for a class or household to join by walking in.
  - Fix: A shared-space model needs, at minimum, a place object, a membership/role object, and presence-gated visibility; without those three entities Monolith cannot serve the classroom/library/household use case at all, and should not be positioned for institutional or family deployment.
- **[HIGH] Permission asks are sequenced least-invasive-first in a dedicated funnel; Monolith's board leads with accessibility and counts the uninstall guard as a top-four grant** — ScreenZen APK (EVIDENCE.md §14, §3.1): onboarding is a staged sequence in dedicated components — OnBoardingActivity plus a separate PermissionRequestActivity, with one full-screen layout per grant in escalating order: layout_usage_permission (usage access, string: 'Required to detect when a distracting app is opened to block it. Also used to track screen time.'), then layout_display_over_permission, then layout_accessibility_permission, then layout_battery_permission, landing immediately on app selection into a first group. Optional hardware permissions get a second, later funnel of their own (HaloPermissionRequestActivity, §3.1). Monolith has exactly one activity in its manifest (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:39-51, MainActivity) and no sequence at all: WatchStore.kt:84-100 fixes the board order as ACCESSIBILITY first, DEVICE_ADMIN third, and openFixPane in MainActivity.kt:364-412 fires whichever Settings intent the user taps, in any order. Worse, the counted four (WatchStore.kt:96-100) rank DEVICE_ADMIN — an uninstall guard that blocks nothing — above OVERLAY and BATTERY (counted=false), while deriveWarrant (WatchStore.kt:302-308) proves only accessibility + usage actually gate a session.
  - Fix: Adopt the rival's order as a sequence, not a board: usage access first, overlay second, accessibility third, battery last, ending on app selection; demote device admin out of the counted grants so the count only ever names grants that block something.
- **[MEDIUM] ScreenZen's block screens are dedicated unexported activities; Monolith funnels every intercept through its exported launcher activity** — ScreenZen EVIDENCE.md §3.1/§3.5: its pause/block screens are four dedicated activities in com.screenzen.ui.activity.overlay.* (MathProblemActivity, IntentionalReasonActivity, ReplacementAppActivity, BreathingActivity), every ScreenZen activity except the Splash/launcher is exported=false, and the actual block is a full-screen activity launched by the monitor — a block surface separate from MainActivity (singleTask). Monolith has no block activity at all: both doors construct an Intent to the exported launcher MainActivity (AndroidManifest.xml:42, exported=true, launchMode singleTop) and pass the block as extras — MonolithShieldService.kt:182-190 and MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:416-428 (launchInterceptScreen, FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP, EXTRA_INTERCEPTED_PACKAGE/APP_NAME/BADGE/PATH). The block therefore shares the main activity's lifecycle, back stack and single-top redelivery path with the entire app UI instead of being an isolated, unexported surface whose only job is the intercept.
  - Fix: Move the Airlock intercept into a dedicated, exported=false block activity launched by both doors, so the enforcement surface is isolated from MainActivity's lifecycle, back handling and intent redelivery.
- **[MEDIUM] Halo is backed by a paid ground-truth diagnostics pipeline (ARCore capture, UWB ground truth, 24-hour sensor long-captures, $20 gift-card incentive); Monolith contains zero logging, so its detection failures leave no evidence to fix from** — EVIDENCE.md §7: ScreenZen built a dedicated field-diagnostics programme for Halo — ~80 classes under com.screenzen.haloutils.diagnostic.* including DiagnosticArCapture/DiagnosticSceneRecorder (ARCore point-cloud/depth), UwbGroundTruthRecorder, IMU/altimeter/pedometer recorders, ZlcWriter streams for BLE/IMU/altimeter/pedometer/UWB/lifecycle, 'long capture' bug reports uploading 24 h of sensor readings plus app logs to a Cloud Function endpoint, and a paid incentive (halo_diag_gift_copy: a one-time $20 gift card, gated by feature flag haloDiagnosticGiftCardEnabled). Monolith ships the opposite posture: a codebase search returns 0 uses of android.util.Log, Firebase or Crashlytics in app/src/main/java, so when its 2-second polling shield mis-detects in a real home there is no ground-truth capture, no sensor log, and no way for a user to send evidence — the failure is unreproducible by construction.
  - Fix: Add an opt-in, user-triggered diagnostic capture (recent intercept/shield decisions with timestamps and permission states) that the user can export with a bug report; a sensing product without a ground-truth pipeline cannot improve its detection in the environments where it actually fails.
- **[MEDIUM] Battery step teaches OEM background-killing via dontkillmyapp.com; Monolith's battery fix is a bare intent with a silent fallback to a different Settings screen** — ScreenZen APK (EVIDENCE.md §3.5, §14): its battery step is a dedicated layout (layout_battery_permission / bottom_battery_optimization) with a purpose string (battery_permission = 'Required for ScreenZen to block apps without being disabled.') and onboarding links dontkillmyapp.com (string ans1) — the public database of OEM background-killing behaviour — so the user is taught why the exemption matters on their specific phone brand. Monolith's entire battery surface is a bare intent: MainActivity.kt:392-404 fires ACTION_REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS and, if that throws, silently falls back to a different screen (ACTION_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATION_SETTINGS) — the user cannot tell the two landed in different places. A codebase-wide search finds no dontkillmyapp reference and no OEM-killer explanation anywhere; the grant is just the uncounted BATTERY board row (WatchStore.kt:91).
  - Fix: Give the battery step the rival's treatment: a named purpose sentence ('required so blocking is not disabled'), a dontkillmyapp.com link for OEM-specific instructions, and no silent fallback to a different Settings list.
## Supplement: StayFree head-to-head (from its actual APK)

Evidence base: StayFree (com.burockgames.timeclocker) APK, statically reverse-engineered only — never installed or run. Full evidence: apk-re/stayfree/EVIDENCE.md. Same rules as the main report: no store-presence or monetisation findings.

### StayFree — Head-to-head losses — 8 findings (0 critical, 6 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] StayFree limits are rule objects over apps, websites, categories and brands with three enforcement types and a warning shot; Monolith's limits are app-only numbers nothing enforces

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4.1: Daily Usage Limits (UsageLimitsScreen.kt, 137 limit* string keys) can be set per app, per website, per category and per brand, with three enforcement types — Block, Pop-up, Notification ('Limitation Type'/'Warning Type') — and §10 shows dedicated Warning Before Blocking notifications (plus a Warning Before Sleep Mode channel) that fire before the block lands. Monolith's rule targets are apps only (one blockTier per package) plus a separate flat site list with no limit concept at all, no category or brand target anywhere, and its intercept arrives with no graduated warning type: the Airlock is the first and only signal. StayFree treats a limit as a policy with a target kind, a severity and a preamble; Monolith treats it as a number stored next to an app.

Recommendation: Give limits a target type (app/site/category), an enforcement type (warn-then-block at minimum) and a warning notification before expiry, instead of a silent per-app minute count.

#### [HIGH] Limits on the Go asks for a session cap at the moment the app is opened, then enforces a cool-down before a new session can start; Monolith has no at-the-door negotiation at all

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4.2: opening a selected app/website raises LimitsOnTheGoActivity with a 'Limit this session to …' prompt; at expiry the app is exited/blocked ('You reached the Limit on the Go for this app'), and an optional Cool Down Period then blocks starting a new session for a configured duration. It is schedulable and has its own QS tile and widget. Monolith's only in-the-moment quantity is the peek: a fixed PEEK_DURATION_SECONDS lease referenced at AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:669, identical for every app and every user, never chosen at the door, and when it lapses there is no cool-down object — the 20-minute peek cooldown is a per-app timestamp, not a user-set re-entry lock. StayFree's signature mechanic is a commitment made at the exact second of temptation; Monolith's durations are all decided in advance, in settings, by a calmer self the design never consults again.

Recommendation: Add an at-open session-cap prompt for OPEN/PEEK apps ('how long this time?') with an optional user-set cool-down before the app can be re-entered.

#### [HIGH] StayFree detects foreground apps three ways with a declared fallback when accessibility is off; Monolith's shield is one 2-second polling loop lashed to one accessibility service

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §3: detection is triple-redundant — UsageStats (PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS) as the primary usage tracker, accessibility typeAllMask events for content-level features, and UsageAssistantService, a specialUse foreground service whose declared PROPERTY_SPECIAL_USE_FGS_SUBTYPE text states it 'continuously monitors the current app and system-wide screen time usage'; onboarding states either Usage Assistant or the accessibility service must be enabled, i.e. monitoring survives losing one door. Monolith's shield door is a single monitor loop with delay(2000L) at MonolithShieldService.kt:193 polling a UsageStats guess, plus the accessibility service — if the loop dies, detection dies with it, and there is no third mechanism whose entire job is to keep watching. StayFree engineered for the permission the user revokes; Monolith engineered for the permissions it hopes it keeps.

Recommendation: Give Monolith a degraded-mode detector (a lightweight usage-monitor FGS) that keeps limits and session timing alive when the accessibility binding is lost, instead of total blindness.

#### [HIGH] StayFree blocks individual features inside apps — comments, Explore, Marketplace, Search, Stories, video search — as a user-configurable system; Monolith hardcodes two feeds

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4: InAppBlockingScreen.kt (25 keys) blocks named features inside apps — comments, Explore tab, Marketplace, Reels/Shorts, Search, Spotlight, Stories, video search — with per-feature 'this_application_is_blocked_for_today_in_app_blocking_{feature}' states, plus a dedicated YouTube Plus surface for Shorts and video search. Monolith's entire in-app enforcement is the Shorts & Reels Sniper described at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:26-28: hardcoded internal view IDs and selected-tab text for exactly two feeds, one global Guard switch (shortsReelsSniperEnabled), nothing else inside any app is addressable. StayFree's user can amputate the Explore tab and keep the app; Monolith's user can only take the whole app or the whole feed.

Recommendation: Turn the sniper into a per-app, per-feature rule list (starting with Search, Explore, comments) driven by view IDs the user can toggle, not a single hardcoded pair of feeds.

#### [HIGH] Usage Goals invert the polarity: StayFree sets minimum-time goals for productive apps, websites and brands, with reminders and completion verdicts; Monolith can only ever say 'less'

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §6: Usage Goals (59 keys) are minimum-time targets on productive apps/websites/brands, with a reminder time and Usage Goal Result notifications for completion and failure (usage_goal_is_completed_*/is_not_completed_*). Nothing in Monolith rewards arriving: every verb in the product is restriction — LOCKED, PEEK, OPEN, MISSED — and a session spent on the right app is indistinguishable from a session spent staring at the Deck. There is no entity for 'spend at least 30 minutes on the language app', no reminder toward something, no completion state for a positive target. StayFree's tracker measures approach as well as avoidance; Monolith's richer event log (timestamp, intention, trigger per intercept) is only ever totalled as failure avoided.

Recommendation: Add minimum-time goals on chosen apps with a reminder and a completed/failed verdict on the receipt, so the system can pull toward something, not only push away.

#### [HIGH] StayFree accounts usage by brand — the service, summed across its apps and websites; Monolith can only count packages, so one habit wearing three icons is three unrelated rows

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4/§6: brands are first-class objects (52 brand* keys, AddAppOrBrandLimitBottomSheet.kt, AddWebsiteOrBrandLimitBottomSheet.kt, ReportBrandProblemsDialog.kt) — limits, goals and stats can all target a brand, i.e. every app and website belonging to one service is summed and capped as a single habit. Monolith's accounting unit is the package name: usage comes from queryRealTodayUsageMinutes() at MonolithRepository.kt:531 as a per-package map, the catalogue is per-package rows, and the site list is a separate flat domain list that never merges with app time. A user whose problem is one service spread over an app, a mobile site and a second app must fight it in three places in Monolith and can never see its true total; in StayFree it is one number with one limit.

Recommendation: Introduce a brand/service grouping that merges an app's packages and its domains into one usage total and one rule target.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree's Usage Assistant is a live speedometer in a persistent notification — current app's time today plus device total, refreshed continuously; Monolith shows nothing about usage until the app is opened

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §5: the Usage Assistant persistent notification continuously shows the current app's today-usage and total device usage, with an optional 'total time message every 10 minutes' setting — ambient awareness that works between sessions, with no session armed and no app open. Monolith's only always-on surface is the shield notification, which exists to label a running session and is deleted when the session ends; the moment no session runs, the phone gives back zero information about where time is going, even though the repository can already produce today's per-app minutes (MonolithRepository.kt:531). StayFree put its core metric on the lockscreen-adjacent surface users actually glance at; Monolith keeps its behind a full cold open.

Recommendation: Post a persistent, updating usage readout (current app today + device total) independent of session state.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree turns pickup counts into timed interventions — a Morning Routine barrage after first wake-up use and a Night Owl report of pickups after bedtime; Monolith never acts on the pickup at all

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §5: SettingsMorningRoutineScreen.kt drives repeated notifications for a set duration after the first morning use, counting pickups; SettingsNightOwlScreen.kt notifies 'You've picked up your phone %s times after your %s bedtime' against a configured bedtime. Both are tracker data converted into behaviour at the two weakest moments of the day. Monolith has no morning or night-owl surface: its routines are silent block windows, its day begins whenever the user happens to open the app, and the number of times the phone was picked up after a SLEEP routine began is never counted, let alone reported back the next morning.

Recommendation: Add a night-owl pickup report after SLEEP routines and a short morning check-in sequence after first unlock, fed by the intercept/usage data already collected.
### StayFree — Visual design — 4 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] StayFree ships a real charting system (MPAndroidChart: hourly bars, device-breakdown pies, comparison charts); Monolith renders its richer data as text rows and one 7-day aggregate

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §6/§14: MPAndroidChart (com.github.mikephil) is bundled and drives the Detail screen's Stats tab, hourly and daily breakdowns, device-breakdown (mobile/desktop/web) pie charts and the Global Usage trending/comparison tabs — every usage surface is a chart first. Monolith has no charting library anywhere in gradle/libs.versions.toml and no chart code: its usage and history surfaces are text lists, counters and a Drawer month of rows, despite logging timestamped intercepts with intention and trigger — data with more dimensions than StayFree's, presented with fewer. The visual language of insight in StayFree is graphical; in Monolith the same class of data is a ledger you read, not a shape you see.

Recommendation: Adopt a chart component for per-app history and hourly patterns instead of adding more text rows to the Drawer.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree has a Lottie motion system — nine onboarding slides, permission animations, paired dark/light empty states, even an ambient video; Monolith has no animated illustration assets at all

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §12/§13: assets/animation_slide_1..9.json onboarding slides, Lottie animations for permissions, check, optimise and block-website moments, empty-state animations shipped as dark/light pairs, five semantic sfx .wav files, and lake.mp4 ambient video in res/raw. Monolith's res/ has no raw/ directory and no Lottie dependency in gradle/libs.versions.toml: every visual moment — first run, permission asks, empty catalogue, blocked site — is Canvas geometry and text. Where StayFree illustrates the permission it is about to request, Monolith prints a jargon label for it; the design systems differ not in taste but in whether illustration exists as a material at all.

Recommendation: Introduce a small set of animated illustrations for the permission primer, empty states and the seal moment, in both themes, instead of raw text and canvas shapes.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree ships two interface densities — a Basic UI with one Focus group and an Advanced UI the user graduates to; Monolith presents its full jargon density to everyone from the first second

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4.3/§13: Basic UI is a deliberately reduced interface (single Focus Mode group, less drawer content) and Advanced UI unlocks multiple groups and the full surface — advanced_ui_information_row_focus_mode explicitly sells switching up as growth: 'Switch to the Advanced UI to have multiple Focus Mode groups'. Monolith has exactly one presentation mode: the full board of caps, sleds, matrices and coined surfaces at maximum density for a first-run user and an expert alike, with no simplified mode, no graduation path and no way to hide machinery the user has not grown into. StayFree treats interface complexity as a level; Monolith treats it as a wall.

Recommendation: Add a reduced default interface (one session, one app list, one start control) with the full matrix behind an explicit advanced toggle.

#### [MEDIUM] In StayFree, progression reskins the whole app — seven material themes from Iron to Adamantium earned through use; Monolith's progression never changes how the app looks by one pixel

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §7/§13: Status levels (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Iron, Titanium, Vibranium, Adamantium) unlock whole-app colour themes via ThemePickerDialog — 'new themes will be unlocked automatically' as points accumulate (status_informative_bottom_sheet_text) — so advancement is visible on every screen, every day. Monolith's progression artefacts (tower bricks, curios) live inside their own cabinet surfaces; earn everything or nothing and the Deck, Shield and Airlock look identical, in the same single imposed palette. StayFree made the reward the interface itself; Monolith made it a collection you have to go and visit.

Recommendation: Let long-term progression alter the product's appearance (an earned accent/theme at tower milestones) so progress is ambient, not filed away.
### StayFree — Platform execution — 4 findings (0 critical, 2 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] StayFree asks for two permissions in onboarding and defers the rest to the moment a feature needs them; Monolith demands its whole special-access set before delivering anything

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §12: onboarding asks Usage Access first, then Accessibility — framed as optional-but-recommended, with a second-chance re-prompt page (onboarding_accessibility_second_chance*) and a skip-confirmation sheet — then battery-optimisation. Overlay, notification-listener and POST_NOTIFICATIONS are just-in-time, requested when a feature first needs them (overlay_permission_required_*, notification_listener_permission_required, RequiredPermissionsBottomSheet.kt re-checking when the user visits Usage Limits). Monolith's manifest (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:5-14) fronts PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE and POST_NOTIFICATIONS on top of its accessibility, notification-listener, device-admin and battery grants — a serial Settings scavenger hunt that must be substantially completed before the first session can arm. StayFree sequences trust; Monolith invoices it up front.

Recommendation: Move overlay, notification and battery asks out of first run to the first feature that needs each, with a per-feature rationale sheet and a later re-ask path.

#### [HIGH] StayFree ships a full always-on blocker with no DeviceAdmin, no VPN and no DND permission in its manifest at all; Monolith carries a device-admin surface that exists only as an uninstall guard

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §2 (negative evidence): no BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN receiver, no VpnService, no ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY anywhere in manifest or dex strings — its entire enforcement stack is UsageStats + accessibility + overlay + foreground services. Monolith declares a MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver (AndroidManifest.xml, 'Monolith Uninstall Guard') whose policy file, app/src/main/res/xml/device_admin_receiver.xml:3-5, contains exactly one policy — <limit-password/> — that no code exercises: the admin slot is spent on install friction and Play-policy exposure for a guard that blocks nothing. StayFree is the existence proof that the category's blocking promise does not require the admin permission Monolith asks its users to grant.

Recommendation: Remove the device-admin receiver and its unused limit-password policy; if uninstall protection is ever rebuilt, it must be a mechanism that actually blocks something.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree still installs on Android 5.0 (minSdk 21); Monolith cuts off at minSdk 24 and abandons three Android generations of cheap phones

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §1: minSdk 21, targetSdk 34. Monolith app/build.gradle.kts:17-18: minSdk 24, targetSdk 36. Monolith is more current on target and pays for it with reach: every Android 5.0–7.0 device — disproportionately the second-hand, low-end phones of the students this category serves — cannot install it at all, while a 34.77 MiB rival with a far larger feature surface still bothers to run there. The compat cost StayFree accepted bought it the entire long tail of devices; Monolith's floor was set by template defaults, not by any API its blocking actually needs (its oldest mechanisms — UsageStats, accessibility, overlay — all predate API 24).

Recommendation: Audit the API-24+ calls; if none are load-bearing for the blocking core, lower minSdk or document the deliberate exclusion.

#### [MEDIUM] On package visibility StayFree is the bloated one: it declares QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES while Monolith lists apps through a scoped <queries> block — the one footprint fight Monolith wins cleanly

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §2: QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is declared outright, giving the app visibility of every installed package (a Play-restricted permission) on top of its accessibility firehose. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:16-22 uses a <queries> block scoped to MAIN/LAUNCHER intent — it can enumerate launchable apps, which is all its catalogue needs, without declaring broad package visibility at all. Same feature (an installed-app list), two footprints: the rival took the restricted sledgehammer, the copy took the scoped API. Monolith's manifest is not uniformly the heavier one, and this declaration is the proof.

Recommendation: Keep the scoped <queries> approach and cite it in the Play declaration narrative; do not let any future catalogue feature reach for QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES.
### StayFree — Comparative audit — 4 findings (1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] StayFree is two products in one APK: a blocker wrapped around a Sensor Tower data-collection business that ships its debug screens in the release build; Monolith collects nothing, from anyone, ever

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §9: the APK bundles com.sensortower.usage.* (~174 refs), com.sensortower.accessibility.* (~394) and com.sensortower.network.* (~387), ML Kit OCR for screen-text recognition, collection of ads seen on social sites, purchase and shopping sessions, and debug activities shipped in the production build — DataCollectionDebugActivity, CollectedAdsActivity, CollectedPurchasesActivity, AccessibilityDebugActivity, AiQueryActivity, DataUploadDebugActivity — under an onboarding consent for Sensor Tower 'market research purposes'. Its 34.77 MiB / 3-dex bulk is substantially not the blocker. Monolith's manifest declares no INTERNET permission, no analytics, no ads, no account, and sets allowBackup=false precisely so its 'DATA: ON THIS PHONE ONLY' plate stays true. Against this rival, Monolith's local-only architecture is not a missing feature; it is the entire ethical difference between the two products, visible only inside the APK.

Recommendation: Keep the zero-network, zero-SDK line permanently, and make the contrast a stated design principle: no rival's feature is worth importing its data business.

#### [HIGH] StayFree's accessibility sensor is configured to take screenshots while declaring itself not an accessibility tool; Monolith's service, for all its faults, only watches for the apps it blocks

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §3: res/xml-v22/stayfree_accessibility_service.xml sets canTakeScreenshot='true' and isAccessibilityTool='false' on a service with accessibilityEventTypes=typeAllMask, canRetrieveWindowContent=true and flagReportViewIds — a full-content, screenshot-capable sensor that formally disclaims being an accessibility tool, because its second job is feeding the collection layer (§9: the same service is the web-usage and ads sensor). Monolith's MonolithAccessibilityService exists to detect blocked packages, read the browser URL bar and run the Shorts/Reels sniper: over-broad in its own documented ways, but every capability it holds is pointed at enforcement the user asked for, and it cannot take a screenshot of anything. The rival's most powerful permission is dual-use surveillance; the copy's is single-use, and that restraint is a genuine design virtue the APK comparison exposes.

Recommendation: Never add screenshot or window-content capability beyond the URL bar and view IDs enforcement needs; the single-purpose sensor is a feature, not a limitation.

#### [HIGH] Monolith seals; StayFree merely saves settings — its limits stay editable at any moment behind a 4-digit PIN, with no sealed state, no integrity and no receipt; Monolith's session, once sealed, is a signed fact

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §11: anti-bypass is PIN Protection (27 pin_* keys) or a type-the-text Awareness Challenge gating the editing of Usage Limits, Focus Mode and LOTG settings — the rules are never locked by time or commitment, only by a password the same user knows, and a changed limit leaves no record. There is no session object to seal, nothing signed, no outcome classification, no receipt. Monolith's arm-and-seal model makes a session an immutable, HMAC-signed record with a classified outcome and a numbered receipt: the commitment is temporal and cryptographic, not a settings password. StayFree can be renegotiated in the moment of craving by its own author in seconds; a sealed Monolith session cannot — the original problem this product exists to solve is the one StayFree's model structurally cannot address.

Recommendation: Do not trade the seal for settings-locks in any future simplification; the sealed, signed session is the differentiator against this entire rival class.

#### [MEDIUM] StayFree forbids its own two halves from coexisting — Usage Goals are mutually exclusive with limits, Focus Mode, LOTG and Pause; Monolith composes restriction and intention in a single session

StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4.6: a family of strings (you_cannot_use_<feature>_when_there_is_a_usage_goal, you_cannot_set_usage_limits_when_there_is_a_usage_goal) hard-codes that setting one productive goal disables the entire restriction stack, and vice versa — the product's positive and negative instruments cannot run on the same day. Monolith's session carries an intention and a task binding alongside its block tiers: the user states what the time is for at the same moment the restrictions engage, and routines, tiers and sessions compose (chaotically at times, but they compose). StayFree made approach and avoidance an either/or settings conflict; Monolith made them one act. For a product whose thesis is intention, that composition is the deeper model.

Recommendation: If minimum-time goals are added (see Usage Goals finding), they must live inside the session/intention system, never as a mutually exclusive mode.

#

### Second-pass findings — 8 findings (1 critical, 6 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

- **[CRITICAL] Limits on the Go is a first-class subsystem with its own prompt activity, schedule, QS tile and widget; Monolith's timed allowance is two timestamp columns with no entry point of its own** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §3-§5: LOTG has its own LimitsOnTheGoActivity (the at-open prompt), LimitsOnTheGoScreen/LimitsOnTheGoApps screens, a LimitsOnTheGoTileService QS tile, a 1x1 LOTG widget provider, its own schedules ('Schedule Limits on the Go to activate automatically throughout the day'), a Session Limit notification channel (§10), and a forced state — it cannot be manually disabled while a schedule is active (limits_on_the_go_forced_toast). Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml declares no tile service and no widget provider at all (only MainActivity, the shield/accessibility/notification services and receivers), and the entire timed-allowance machinery is BlockedAppEntity's two Long columns (MonolithModels.kt:240-241) plus MonolithRepository.startPeekLease — reachable only as a side-offer inside an Airlock intercept (MonolithViewModel.kt:138-151 peekOfferFor), never startable, schedulable or toggleable on its own.
  - Fix: Promote the timed allowance to a named, persisted feature: its own settings surface and schedule, a QS tile/widget entry, and a prompt activity that can fire on app-open without first arming a full focus session.
- **[HIGH] StayFree's scheduled modes are forced-on while the schedule runs; Monolith's live routine can be toggled off in one ungated tap** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §5/§11: scheduled Focus Mode and scheduled Limits on the Go cannot be manually disabled while the schedule is active — strings focus_mode_forced_* and limits_on_the_go_forced_toast exist precisely to refuse the off-switch, backed by PIN/AwarenessTextChallenge gating of settings edits. Monolith instead exposes toggleRoutine() as a bare unconditional flip — MonolithViewModel.kt:1515-1519 copies the routine with enabled = !routine.enabled and persists it, with no check that the routine's window is currently live, no PIN, no typed challenge, and no forced-refusal path. The person being blocked can therefore kill the scheduled protection with one tap at exactly the moment it starts to bite.
  - Fix: Refuse routine disable/day-toggle edits while that routine's window is live (or gate them behind the session's existing disarm cost), and surface a forced-active state in the routine UI instead of a live toggle.
- **[HIGH] StayFree blocks on screen content itself — user and premade keyword groups; Monolith can only match packages and URL-bar substrings** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4: BlockKeywordsScreen.kt/BlockKeywordsActivity (21 keys), PremadeKeywordGroup and CommonUtils.getBlockedPremadeKeywordLists, keyword_appeared* strings, an accessibility config of typeAllMask + canRetrieveWindowContent=true + flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows, and ML Kit OCR in the APK — enforcement fires when a blocked word appears in on-screen content, in any app. Monolith's only content match is matchBlockedDomain() at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:67-68, applied solely to the URL-bar text of five hardcoded browsers (detectBlockedBrowserUrl, MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:383-410); its other text scan exists only to spot 'force stop/uninstall' on Monolith's own Settings page. There is no user keyword list anywhere in Monolith's code, so a blocked topic surfacing inside an allowed app — a search, a title, a feed caption — never triggers anything.
  - Fix: Add a user/premade keyword rule type evaluated against retrieved window content (not just browser URL bars), so enforcement can trigger on what is on screen, not only on which package or domain is open.
- **[HIGH] StayFree has an indefinite Pause for apps and websites with no expiry; Monolith has no standing paused state — every tier dies with the session** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4 item 4: Pause Apps / Pause Websites (pause_apps_*, pause_websites_*) is a standalone mechanism that pauses selected apps and websites indefinitely until the user unpauses them — it needs no session, no timer and no daily reset. Monolith's tiers have no equivalent standing state: MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:194-195 returns immediately when there is no active session, and MonolithShieldService.kt:96-100 stops and kills itself the moment getActiveSessionSnapshot() is null, so a LOCKED tier is inert paper between armed sessions and there is no 'paused until I say otherwise' state a user can set once and forget.
  - Fix: Add a session-independent indefinite pause tier for apps and sites that the accessibility door enforces without requiring an armed session, with unpause as the only exit.
- **[HIGH] StayFree's accessibility config retrieves all interactive windows under typeAllMask; Monolith subscribes to two event types and only ever inspects the one active window** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §3: its decoded stayfree_accessibility_service.xml sets accessibilityEventTypes=typeAllMask, accessibilityFlags=flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows|flagReportViewIds, canRetrieveWindowContent=true and notificationTimeout=300, so its detector is subscribed to every event type and can retrieve all interactive windows, not just the focused one. Monolith's res/xml/accessibility_service_config.xml:3-6 subscribes only to typeWindowStateChanged|typeWindowContentChanged with flags flagDefault|flagIncludeNotImportantViews|flagReportViewIds — flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows is absent — and MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:164-195 inspects only rootInActiveWindow for the single event package. A blocked app sitting in the non-focused split-screen pane or a secondary window produces no window Monolith ever looks at, while StayFree's configuration is built to enumerate those windows.
  - Fix: Add flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows to the accessibility config and iterate windows (AccessibilityService.getWindows()) in the event path instead of inspecting only rootInActiveWindow, so non-focused windows are policed.
- **[HIGH] Limits on the Go covers websites as well as apps; Monolith's timed lease is app-only by construction and its website blocker is binary** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §4: LOTG is defined over 'a selected app/website' — at expiry of a website session the site is blocked ('You reached the Limit on the Go for this app'), backed by the accessibility website layer (132 website* keys). Monolith structurally excludes sites from any timed allowance: InterceptPath.canHonourPeekLease is true only for APP_TIER and SHIELD_APP (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:46-57), the SITE door is explicitly one that 'never reads the lease' (MonolithViewModel.kt:131-140 comment on peekOfferFor), and the website model is BlockedSiteEntity with a single field — @PrimaryKey domain (MonolithModels.kt:544-546) — no tier, no lease, no limit. A Monolith user can fully block a site or fully open it; a timed, self-capped visit to a website is impossible.
  - Fix: Give BlockedSiteEntity a tier/limit representation parallel to BlockedAppEntity and let the SITE intercept path honour a lease, so a blocked site can be visited under a chosen cap with a cool-down instead of only all-or-nothing.
- **[HIGH] StayFree's scariest grant is skippable inside onboarding, with a second-chance page; Monolith's accessibility grant is a counted hard gate with no decline path** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §12: its accessibility ask ships with AccessibilitySkipConfirmationBottomSheet.kt and a dedicated onboarding_accessibility_second_chance re-prompt page, and the grant is presented as optional-but-highly-recommended; §3 states the fallback in-product: 'either Usage Assistant or StayFree's accessibility service must be enabled', so declining still leaves a working blocker. Monolith gives its equivalent grant no decline path: WatchStore.kt:81 and :98-101 count ACCESSIBILITY as counted permission #1 of the GUARD 4/4 warrant, so the header can never read complete without it, and the only action offered is the FIX key firing a raw Settings intent (MainActivity.kt:365-366) — grant it or stay permanently unwarranted, with no skip confirmation and no later second-chance surface.
  - Fix: Make accessibility a skippable, re-offerable step: add a skip-confirmation on the board, a later re-prompt when a user first enables an accessibility-dependent feature (Shorts/sites), and a degraded warrant state that can seal an app-only session without it.
- **[MEDIUM] StayFree restarts protection on two boot triggers with no pre-unlock execution; Monolith wakes on six actions and runs its entire component set directBootAware** — StayFree EVIDENCE.md §3: restart after boot/update is one receiver, BootCompletedAndUpdateReceiver, exported=false, subscribed to exactly two actions — BOOT_COMPLETED and MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED — and no component in its manifest is directBootAware. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:95-105 subscribes MonolithBootReceiver to six actions (LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, BOOT_COMPLETED, QUICKBOOT_POWERON, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, TIME_SET, TIMEZONE_CHANGED), and directBootAware='true' is set on effectively the whole component set: MainActivity (:41), MonolithShieldService (:55), MonolithAccessibilityService (:67), MonolithNotificationListener (:83), RoutineAlarmReceiver (:111), ReleaseRetryReceiver (:117) and the device-admin receiver (:124). Monolith therefore executes before first unlock and wakes its stack on every clock/timezone change to achieve the same restart guarantee StayFree gets from two triggers in credential-protected time.
  - Fix: Cut the boot receiver to BOOT_COMPLETED + MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, handle TIME_SET/TIMEZONE_CHANGED inside the already-running shield/routine scheduler instead of a manifest wake, and drop directBootAware from the activity, listener and receivers unless a pre-unlock session-resume requirement is documented for each.
## Supplement: AppBlock head-to-head (from its actual APK)

Evidence base: AppBlock (cz.mobilesoft.appblock) APK, statically reverse-engineered only — never installed or run. Full evidence: apk-re/appblock/EVIDENCE.md. Same rules as the main report: no store-presence or monetisation findings.

### AppBlock — Head-to-head losses — 6 findings (0 critical, 5 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] AppBlock's Strict Mode makes edits tightening-only while it is active; Monolith lets a mid-session loadout tap loosen every app at once

AppBlock EVIDENCE §5: while Strict Mode is active, schedule edits are constrained by design — string schedule_edit_strict_mode_active_hint_banner="Changes can only tighten the rules"; apps can only be added to blocklists or removed from allowlists, never the reverse. Monolith has no such directional invariant anywhere: MonolithViewModel.kt:2098 applySmartLoadout() applies a hand-picked loadout immediately, delegating to MonolithRepository.kt:1126 applySmartLoadout(), which rewrites the blockTier of the app catalogue from the preset — with no check on whether a session is currently sealed and no tightening/loosening direction test. The original this category built treats 'rules may only move toward stricter during enforcement' as a core invariant; Monolith's rule-writing path does not know the concept exists.

Recommendation: Add a direction gate to every rule-writing path (applySmartLoadout, tier cycling, site removal): while a session is active, reject any write that moves an app toward OPEN or removes a blocked site, and surface the refusal in the UI instead of applying silently.

#### [HIGH] AppBlock polices the Recents screen and Settings itself during Strict Mode; Monolith's guard is four installer packages and an English text search

AppBlock EVIDENCE §5.4/§3.1: Strict Mode blocks force stop, floating windows and parts of Settings, and blocks the Recent Apps screen on Xiaomi/POCO/Realme via its accessibility service — whose config packageNames deliberately include com.android.systemui and every major launcher (~42 packages, §3.1) precisely so it can see and intercept those surfaces. Monolith's equivalent guard is MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:311-314, a hardcoded list of four packageinstaller packages, plus :318-323, which dumps the Settings window text and looks for the English substring "uninstall". No Monolith component watches SystemUI or launchers, so the Recents/overview surface — the standard route around an intercept — is entirely unpoliced while a session runs.

Recommendation: Add SystemUI and launcher packages to Monolith's enforcement scope during sessions and intercept the Recents/overview surface explicitly, rather than relying on a 4-package installer list and a locale-dependent text heuristic in Settings.

#### [HIGH] AppBlock's polling service independently enforces the full blocking model, so losing accessibility only degrades web blocking; in Monolith one service death kills sites, Shorts and the Settings guard together

AppBlock EVIDENCE §3.1: it runs two detectors with divided labour — LockAccessibilityService (window/URL/sub-app content) and LockServiceV2, a UsageStats polling service whose manifest PROPERTY_SPECIAL_USE_FGS_SUBTYPE states it mediates 'application usage detection and blocking… Quick Block, blocking schedules and Strict Mode in terms of application blocking'. App blocking therefore survives accessibility loss; only content-level features degrade. Monolith's division is the opposite shape: app blocking sits in MonolithShieldService.kt:193 (delay(2000L) polling loop), while website blocking, the Shorts/Reels sniper and the Settings/uninstall guard are all branches of the single MonolithAccessibilityService — one accessibility death removes three unrelated protections at once, and nothing in the manifest or code reassigns them.

Recommendation: Give the shield's polling door a degraded-mode fallback for at least the Settings/uninstall guard when the accessibility binding is lost, and log/surface which enforcement branches are currently dead instead of presenting a single undifferentiated guard state.

#### [HIGH] AppBlock budgets are pooled across a schedule's apps — one shared usage limit and one combined launch count; Monolith's schema can only express per-app limits

AppBlock EVIDENCE §4.2: a schedule's Usage Limit is 'shared by all apps included in the blocking' (schedule_detail_usage_limit_hint), its Launch Count is 'counted combined across all apps in the schedule' (schedule_detail_launch_count_hint), the end behaviour is selectable (Notification or Pop-up, usage_limit_end_show_as), and a remaining-time notification plus a before-limit warning exist. Monolith's only limit concept is BlockedAppEntity.dailyLimitMinutes (MonolithModels.kt:238), a single per-package integer defaulting to 30 — there is no group, pool or shared-budget entity anywhere in the schema, so '30 minutes of social apps in total' is unrepresentable even before enforcement is considered.

Recommendation: Model a pooled budget (a named app group with a shared daily minutes/launches budget) in the schema, and render remaining pooled budget in the schedule/routine surface the way AppBlock renders its remaining-time notification.

#### [HIGH] AppBlock documents a precedence algebra between overlapping schedule types; Monolith has no rule for which of two live routines wins

AppBlock EVIDENCE §4.2 records explicit cross-type precedence from its strings: Usage Limit and Launch Count are mutually exclusive with each other and with Allowlist mode; a Time schedule overrides limit-based unlocks ('If an app is in a time schedule, it stays blocked during that time even if you unlock it using the Open limit'); a reached usage limit wins over remaining launch allowance; pausing a limit schedule pauses blocking but usage keeps being measured. Monolith has no counterpart: RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-569) is name/start/end/daysMask/loadoutName/enabled/pausedUntil/scheduleEditedAt, and the only 'overlap' logic in the codebase (RoutineDerive.kt:159,215 overlapsAny) judges attendance of windows against sessions — nothing decides which loadout governs when two routine windows are live simultaneously.

Recommendation: Define and document a deterministic precedence rule for simultaneously live routines (e.g. strictest tier wins per app), implement it in the derive layer, and show the merged result in the routine editor the way AppBlock explains its conflicts to the user.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock's schedule pause is a state machine with presets, history and a countdown before resumption; Monolith's pause is one bare timestamp

AppBlock EVIDENCE §4.1/§3.4: a schedule can be paused for a duration or until a date, with pause presets and pause history, a dedicated BeforeProfilePauseEndNotificationService foreground service whose only job is counting down to the pause ending, and the ability to disable pausing entirely from Settings or Strict Mode. Monolith's entire pause model is RoutineEntity.pausedUntilMillis (MonolithModels.kt:561) — a single Long with no presets, no history of past pauses, no warning before the routine resumes, and no way to forbid pausing. The user is never told a paused routine is about to come back, and afterwards there is no record that a pause happened.

Recommendation: Add pause presets and a persisted pause history to routines, and fire a pre-resume notification (AppBlock dedicates a whole countdown service to this) instead of letting a paused routine silently reactivate.
### AppBlock — Visual design — 3 findings (0 critical, 0 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock's whole visual identity is one bundled font and stock Material 3; Monolith ships three type families and a bespoke canvas design language

AppBlock EVIDENCE §14: the APK bundles exactly one font file, assets/fonts/Roboto-Medium.ttf, uses Compose Material 3 token classes, and its block screen is a themed LockActivity/LockActivityV2 — visually, the product is system-default Android with a custom block-screen text field. Monolith, whatever its other faults, ships a real design system: app/src/main/res/font/ holds 8 TTFs across three families (Sora ×4 weights, Atkinson Hyperlegible ×2, Anonymous Pro ×2) plus hand-built Canvas views (rotary wheel, tower, rail). On pure visual identity, the copy is substantially more designed than this rival — AppBlock's polish budget went into feature breadth, not typography or bespoke surfaces.

Recommendation: No action against AppBlock here — record it as a genuine Monolith advantage worth protecting: if Monolith ever adopts stock Material components for speed, it would be surrendering one of the few axes where it visibly out-designs a top rival.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock ships 20 user-selectable launcher icons including disguise options; Monolith offers exactly one fixed icon

AppBlock EVIDENCE §3.5: the manifest declares MainActivity plus MainActivityAlias1…Alias19 — twenty launcher icons, user-selectable in scene.more.settings.icon_select.AppIconSelectActivity ('App icon', 'Extra icon options'). For an app whose presence on the home screen announces 'I have a blocking problem', icon choice is a real privacy/customisation feature. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:33-35 declares a single @mipmap/ic_launcher / ic_launcher_round and the manifest contains no activity-alias at all — the icon is fixed, named and unchangeable.

Recommendation: Ship a small set of activity-alias icon variants (including at least one neutral/disguised option) with an in-app picker; it is a few manifest entries and mipmap sets, and rivals treat it as table stakes.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock teaches its scariest permission with produced light/dark video; Monolith's permission asks are static text on a jargon board

AppBlock EVIDENCE §14/§10: res/raw contains accessibility_permission.mp4 and accessibility_permission_dark.mp4 — matched light- and dark-variant motion explainers embedded in its permission wizard (scene.permission.*), i.e. the accessibility ask is taught with produced media that respects the current theme, and §14 also notes per-surface dark variants elsewhere (dark_map_style.json / map_night.json for its location picker). Monolith has no video or motion explainer anywhere: its special-access asks are presented as text states on the GUARD board and FIX deep-links, in the app's private vocabulary, with the grant's purpose left to the user to infer.

Recommendation: Produce a short theme-matched explainer (video or animated sequence) for at least the accessibility grant, embedded at the ask itself, instead of sending users to a system Settings screen armed only with jargon.
### AppBlock — Platform execution — 3 findings (0 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] AppBlock isolates each enforcement service in its own process; Monolith runs shield, accessibility, notification listener and UI in one shared process

AppBlock EVIDENCE §3: LockAccessibilityService runs in process :AccessibilityService, LockServiceV2 in :LockService, and its two countdown services are separate components again — an accessibility crash or a UI-process kill cannot take the polling enforcer down with it. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:53-92 declares MonolithShieldService, MonolithAccessibilityService and MonolithNotificationListener with no android:process attribute on any of them: all enforcement shares the main application process with MainActivity and the Compose UI, so a single process death — OOM, crash, OEM kill — removes every door simultaneously and the app must rely on sticky-restart luck to get any of them back.

Recommendation: Move at least MonolithShieldService into its own android:process so the session enforcer survives UI-process death, and state per-service liveness separately instead of as one process-wide fact.

#### [HIGH] AppBlock scopes its accessibility subscription to ~42 named packages; Monolith subscribes to window events from every app on the phone

AppBlock EVIDENCE §3.1: its res/xml/serviceconfig.xml sets accessibilityEventTypes=0x821 and an explicit packageNames allowlist of ~42 packages — launchers, SystemUI, ~35 browsers and 3 in-app targets — so the service receives no events at all from the rest of the phone, bounding its tree-walk cost and its exposure by construction. Monolith's app/src/main/res/xml/accessibility_service_config.xml:3-8 declares typeWindowStateChanged|typeWindowContentChanged with NO packageNames restriction, plus flagIncludeNotImportantViews and notificationTimeout=80: it is woken for window changes in every app, including apps it will never police, and pays a recursive tree walk per event for that privilege.

Recommendation: Scope Monolith's accessibility config with a packageNames list covering only what it actually polices (browsers, SystemUI/launchers, installer/Settings, sniper targets) and drop flagIncludeNotImportantViews from branches that never read those nodes.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock declares QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES and sees the whole installed inventory; Monolith restricts itself to launcher-visible apps only

AppBlock EVIDENCE §2: it declares QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, so its app picker, blocklists and statistics cover every installed package. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:12-21 takes the opposite route — PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS plus a <queries> block for MAIN/LAUNCHER intents only — so packages without a launcher entry (in-app surfaces, secondary apps, anything not on the home-screen grid) are invisible to its catalogue: they cannot be listed, tiered or counted, and the catalogue's idea of 'installed apps' is silently 'apps with a launcher icon'.

Recommendation: Declare QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES (with the catalogue's prune safeguards fixed first) so the rule catalogue covers the full package inventory, or explicitly document and surface the launcher-only blind spot in the Shield matrix instead of presenting the list as complete.
### AppBlock — Comparative audit — 3 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] AppBlock's blocker ships three ad networks and syncs usage records to its backend; Monolith ships zero ad/analytics SDKs and no backend at all

Only visible inside the APK (AppBlock EVIDENCE §12.2/§8/§15): the free tier is mediated by AppLovin MAX (2,827 class references, plus its debugger activities), Google AdMob, and Facebook Audience Network — the latter shipped as an extra 5 MB assets/audience_network.dex — backed by AD_ID and five ACCESS_ADSERVICES_* permissions (§2), while its statistics module's records are also synced server-side via ServerSyncWorker to https://api.appblock.app/ (§8, §11). A screen-time cop that sells the user's attention to ad mediation is a real product compromise. Monolith's manifest declares no ad, analytics or account SDK and no backend endpoint; AndroidManifest.xml:24-28 even pins allowBackup=false with full backup/transfer exclusion so its 'DATA: ON THIS PHONE ONLY' plate is mechanically true. On data posture, Monolith is not behind this rival — it is categorically cleaner.

Recommendation: Keep it that way and treat it as a headline product property: any future SDK addition (analytics, crash reporting, sync) should be judged against the fact that the current zero-SDK, zero-backend posture is a genuine competitive edge over AppBlock, not an omission.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock's block is a binary wall with no relief at the intercept itself; Monolith's Airlock has a graduated peek tier AppBlock never built

AppBlock EVIDENCE §14 records an observed absence: no breathing/delay-to-open/wait-timer block-screen mechanic exists in its strings — its LockActivity/LockActivityV2 is an instant wall, and relief exists only at the schedule level (pause the whole schedule, or the emergency-unblock flow, §4.1/§5.3). Monolith's intercept is graduated by design: AppBlockTier.PEEK_2M (MonolithModels.kt:25-31) grants a 2-minute check-in with a mandatory 20-minute cooldown, between LOCKED and OPEN, offered at the moment of temptation in the Airlock. Whatever Monolith's enforcement bugs, its three-state model with a rationed middle tier is a more humane — and more sophisticated — intercept design than anything in AppBlock's APK.

Recommendation: Protect the peek tier as a differentiator: it is one of the few mechanisms Monolith has that a top-three rival demonstrably lacks, and it should be presented (and receipted) as a designed feature rather than treated as a loophole.

#### [MEDIUM] AppBlock ships developer tooling inside its release binary — dev settings, dev events and mock premium/Insights overrides; Monolith ships no in-app developer surface

AppBlock EVIDENCE §14: the production APK contains DeveloperSettingsActivity and DevEventsActivity (plus Doki diagnostics and a TroubleshootingStackActivity), with string-level evidence of developer menus including mock Insights and premium-state overrides shipped in the release build; their reachability is unknown statically, which is itself the problem — the vendor cannot prove from the binary that paying-customer strictness screens and internal override surfaces are walled off. Monolith has no developer activity, dev menu or override surface in its manifest at all (AndroidManifest.xml declares one activity, three services, four receivers, total). On release hygiene of the shipped binary, the student copy is tighter than the commercial original.

Recommendation: No fix needed in Monolith; note the contrast as a standing rule — keep diagnostic/override surfaces out of the release manifest entirely, since AppBlock shows even a mature commercial blocker failing at exactly this.

### Second-pass findings — 7 findings (0 critical, 6 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

- **[HIGH] AppBlock ships dedicated monitor services that watch its own enforcement services; Monolith's only watchdog lives inside the process it is supposed to watch** — AppBlock EVIDENCE.md §3.1-3.2: the APK ships dedicated supervision components — AccessibilityMonitorService (plain service watching that the accessibility service stays alive), NotificationCollectorMonitorService (monitors the notification listener), and CheckGrantedPermissionService declared as a foregroundServiceType=0x800 systemExempted service in coreblock. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:68-112 declares exactly three services (MonolithShieldService, MonolithAccessibilityService, MonolithNotificationListener) and no monitor of any kind; its only liveness machinery is the in-process, in-memory WatchStore singleton, and MonolithShieldService.kt:82 returns plain START_STICKY with no external watcher — when Monolith's single shared process is killed, the thing that would notice the death dies in the same process.
  - Fix: Add an out-of-band supervision path Monolith currently lacks entirely: a separate monitor component (or at minimum a WorkManager/AlarmManager-based dead-man check in a different process) that verifies the accessibility service and notification listener are still bound and re-prompts/re-arms when they are not, instead of relying on an in-memory singleton inside the process being watched.
- **[HIGH] AppBlock re-arms each enforcement service individually on clock changes and holds exact-alarm permission; Monolith has one whole-app receiver and only inexact alarms** — AppBlock EVIDENCE.md §2 and §3.4: the APK declares SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and ships three separate clock-change receivers — a generic TimeChangedReceiver plus LockServiceTimeChangedReceiver running in the :LockService process and AccessibilityTimeChangedReceiver in the :AccessibilityService process — so each enforcement service individually re-arms when the clock is tampered with, layered over Evernote android-job and WorkManager. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:5-13 declares no SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission, its single MonolithBootReceiver (AndroidManifest.xml TIME_SET/TIMEZONE_CHANGED actions) is the only clock-change handling for the whole app, and RoutineScheduler.kt:44 arms its chain with the inexact alarmManager.setAndAllowWhileIdle — no enforcement service in Monolith re-arms itself on a clock change.
  - Fix: Declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, switch routine/enforcement arming to exact alarms, and give the shield and accessibility doors their own TIME_SET/TIMEZONE_CHANGED re-arm receivers so a clock change re-proves each enforcement service individually rather than relying on one whole-app boot receiver and an inexact chain alarm.
- **[HIGH] AppBlock's Strict Mode unlock is temporary and auto-relocks; Monolith's only exit destroys the session outright** — EVIDENCE.md §5.3 item 7: AppBlock ships a dedicated Strict Mode unlock preference ('strict_mode_unlock_prefs_title', subtitle 'Auto lock back after interval') and a changelog entry 'Now you can unlock Strict Mode for a limited time. It re-locks automatically' — a temporary-unlock state with an interval after which the lock re-engages on its own. Monolith's only exit is the opposite shape: MonolithRepository.completeEmergencyBreak() (MonolithRepository.kt:2225) inserts an EmergencyBreakSpendEntity and calls disarmActiveSession()/disarmRoutineSessionByBreak() in the same transaction (lines 2235-2247) — the session is permanently ended, the weekly token is consumed, and no code path re-arms or re-locks afterwards (no relock/temporary-unlock concept exists anywhere in MonolithRepository.kt).
  - Fix: Add a temporary-unlock state to the session model: an unlock expires at a stored timestamp and the shield re-seals automatically, priced separately from (or instead of) the terminal weekly emergency token.
- **[HIGH] AppBlock's emergency exit is a soft-capped, reason-surveyed friction flow that never disappears; Monolith's is a hard 1-per-week cutoff that records nothing** — EVIDENCE.md §5.3 item 5: AppBlock's EmergencyUnblockActivity is a designed state machine, not a binary gate — a wait-on-screen countdown the user must sit through ('emergency_unblock_wait_on_screen_hint'), a final warning that using it resets your progress, a structured post-use reason survey (Urgent access / Blocked something it shouldn't / Hard to stay in control / Didn't work as expected), and a monthly soft cap: after repeated use it says 'This month, you've already used Emergency to disable Strict Mode' and suggests switching access method — the hatch is metered and interrogated but never removed. Monolith's counterpart is a hard binary: EmergencyBreakSpendEntity (MonolithModels.kt:442-449) stores only sessionId, spentAtWallMillis, weekAnchorMillis and heldSeconds (hardcoded 60, MonolithRepository.kt:121) — no reason is ever captured — and completeEmergencyBreak() returns BreakResult.RefusedNoToken once one spend exists in the week (MonolithRepository.kt:2231-2233), so the second emergency in a week has no hatch at all and the first one teaches the app nothing about why it was needed.
  - Fix: Soften the token into a metered emergency path that is always present: a sit-through wait, an explicit progress-loss warning, a mandatory reason capture stored on the spend row, and escalating friction/guidance instead of a hard weekly zero.
- **[HIGH] AppBlock's first permission ask is its cheapest one and it pays off instantly; Monolith's board leads with its scariest grants and pays off nothing** — AppBlock EVIDENCE.md §10: onboarding asks Usage Access alone, embedded as question Q4 'Want to see the reality?' — 'We need the Usage access permission to prepare this report for you' — and immediately converts that single read-only grant into a personalised 7-day report (daily average screen time, most-used apps, unlocks, '%d%% more than your guess'). The blocking permissions (accessibility, overlay, notification access) are deferred until the guided first Quick Block, as step 2 after the user has already chosen apps/websites in step 1, and are followed by a live blocking test. Monolith instead presents all six special accesses as one undifferentiated board whose order literally leads with the most invasive grants: WatchStore.kt:92-99 defines PERMISSIONS in board order ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN, NOTIFICATION_LISTENER, OVERLAY, BATTERY, with the counted four (WatchStore.kt:98-100) being accessibility, usage, device admin and the notification listener; MainActivity.kt:363-408 fires the six FIX trips to Settings panes from that generic board, with no grant producing any value before the full set is in.
  - Fix: Reorder the asks cheapest-first and make the first grant buy something: ask Usage Access first and immediately show the user their own usage picture, defer accessibility/device-admin/notification-listener until a first session is being armed with apps already chosen, and stop leading the board with ACCESSIBILITY and DEVICE_ADMIN.
- **[HIGH] AppBlock's Strict Mode is a schedulable object that follows schedules and attaches per-schedule; Monolith routines carry no lock binding in their schema at all** — EVIDENCE.md §5.1: AppBlock's Strict Mode has three activation bindings implemented as first-class state (backed by a dedicated StrictModeRepository, §11): a manual timer, 'follow schedules' (active whenever any selected schedule is ON, strict_mode_follow_shedules / strict_mode_active_schedules*), and per-schedule attachment ('Strict Mode will be active… whenever this profile is on', strict_mode_profile_premium_only) — the lock automatically engages and disengages with recurring blocking windows without any per-window user action. Monolith's schema has no lock object or lock binding at all: RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-568) carries only name, startMinutes, endMinutes, daysMask, loadoutName, enabled, pausedUntilMillis and scheduleEditedAtMillis — no strict/lock field — so protection exists only as the armed session itself and nothing resembling a lock can be pre-committed to recur alongside a routine.
  - Fix: Give routines an optional enforcement-lock binding in the schema (a lock flag on RoutineEntity whose state is derived from the routine window), so the anti-edit/anti-exit layer engages automatically with every recurring window instead of existing only inside a manually armed session.
- **[MEDIUM] AppBlock reacts to app installs/uninstalls in real time to keep blocklists current; Monolith has no package-change receiver and only discovers new apps on UI-driven catalogue sync** — AppBlock EVIDENCE.md §3.4: the manifest ships AppInstallUninstallReceiver listening for package added/removed so blocklists stay current the moment an app is installed, cloned or removed, alongside UserPresentReceiver and AppUpdatedReceiver. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml declares only four receivers (MonolithBootReceiver, RoutineAlarmReceiver, ReleaseRetryReceiver, MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver) — no PACKAGE_ADDED/PACKAGE_REMOVED/PACKAGE_CHANGED receiver exists anywhere, and MonolithShieldService.kt:171-183 rebuilds its blocked set purely by re-scanning dao.getAllAppsSnapshot() on its 2-second loop, so a newly installed or reinstalled app is invisible to enforcement until a catalogue sync happens to run from the UI layer.
  - Fix: Register a package added/removed/changed receiver that reconciles the app catalogue and the live blocked set at install time, so enforcement reacts to installs and reinstalls in real time instead of discovering them on the next UI-driven catalogue sync.
## Supplement: Opal head-to-head (from its actual APK)

Evidence base: Opal (com.withopal.opal) Android APK, statically reverse-engineered only — never installed or run. Full evidence: apk-re/opal/EVIDENCE.md. Same rules as the main report: no store-presence or monetisation findings.

### Opal — Head-to-head losses — 7 findings (1 critical, 4 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

#### [CRITICAL] Opal blocks with a window it owns; Monolith blocks by launching itself: UsageStats detects, a real overlay draws the block screen, and accessibility is demoted to optional website-only duty

Opal EVIDENCE §3/§6.1-6.2: its own permission strings divide the labour explicitly — Usage Access 'Required to detect which app is open', Display Over Other Apps 'Required to show the block screen', Accessibility 'Optional for website blocking'; the monitor is ForegroundAppMonitorService (specialUse FGS) and the accessibility config (website_detector_config.xml) subscribes only to content/state changes for browser URL reading. Monolith inverts all three assignments: its AccessibilityService is the app detector (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:70, onAccessibilityEvent :164), the 'block' is an Intent that trampolines its own MainActivity into the foreground (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:422), and although SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW is declared (AndroidManifest.xml:11) no overlay window is ever created anywhere in the codebase — the only WindowManager hits are FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON toggles inside the activity (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:96-98). Opal's block therefore survives background-activity-launch restrictions because it never launches an activity; Monolith's entire intercept rides on the single most OEM-fragile door in Android.

Recommendation: Split the doors the way Opal does: keep UsageStats/FGS as the detector, draw the Airlock as a genuine SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay owned by the shield service, and cut the accessibility service down to the website/shorts duties that actually need window content.

#### [HIGH] Opal intervenes during use, not just at launch: the Autofocus overlay floats a live today-total inside the distracting app while Monolith has zero presence once a user is inside any app

Opal EVIDENCE §8.4: autofocus_overlay_* is a floating, draggable overlay shown on Distracting apps displaying time spent today on that app, with 'Hide for 30 minutes' / 'Move to other side', a Settings toggle (settings_autofocus_overlay) and a per-user Room setting (user_settings.autofocusOverlayEnabled). Opal's enforcement model therefore has a continuous in-app awareness layer between 'allowed' and 'blocked'. Monolith's only intervention point is the launch intercept (AirlockInterceptOverlay, AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:550): once an app is OPEN, or a peek lease is running, nothing of Monolith exists inside that app — no elapsed meter, no presence, no escalation — until the lease lapses on paper. Opal also uses the same channel proactively (Autofocus nudges from weather + usage habits, §8.4); Monolith's intercept log is never surfaced back to the user in the moment at all.

Recommendation: Add an in-app meter for PEEK/OPEN exposure: a small overlay (the overlay permission is already declared) showing time-in-this-app during a peek, so the intervention continues after the launch decision instead of ending at it.

#### [HIGH] Opal's rules carry a managedAuthority: a school or family can own rules the device holder cannot edit, with a compliance report and a rationed Sick Day Pass — Monolith's data model has exactly one authority, the person being blocked

Opal EVIDENCE §5/§10.3: blocking_rules stores a managedAuthority column and Room holds managed_rule_details (targetGroupID, scope, blockScope) plus distracting_usage_reports — a per-rule compliance feed. A school Phone Policy is a mandatory allowlist bound to the bell schedule ('This policy is mandatory. Your school receives a daily report for compliance'), and the escape valve is a Sick Day Pass: a limited stock whose reason (Feeling sick / Doctor or dentist / Family emergency / …) and free-text note are explicitly read by the school, with hold-to-leave programme exit that notifies the school immediately. Monolith's rule model has no authority dimension at all: BlockedAppEntity (MonolithModels.kt:232) and RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550) are holder-authored, holder-editable at any unsealed moment, and its one escape (the weekly token + 60s valve) reports to nobody. Opal engineered second-person authority into the schema; Monolith cannot express it.

Recommendation: Add an authority field to the rule/session model — self vs held-by-another — so a rule can be authored by someone other than its subject, and make the emergency exit produce a reason record that authority can read, instead of a purely private token spend.

#### [HIGH] One versioned catalogue entry blocks the app and its website together: Opal ships 21 category files binding packages + domains + a behaviour flag, while Monolith's apps and sites are two disjoint systems and its categories are guessed per-device by substring
