Opal EVIDENCE §7: assets/categories/ ships a versioned catalogue (catalog-manifest.json, 'version':'1.0') with 21 category files; each entry carries id, displayName, behaviour (e.g. 'distracting'), androidPackages[] and domains[] — Instagram is one entry covering com.instagram.android and instagram.com, so a single selection closes both surfaces, and classifications arrive server-seeded (LocalUserServiceClassification) with user override. Monolith keeps the two surfaces in separate universes: BlockedAppEntity (MonolithModels.kt:232) for apps and BlockedSiteEntity (MonolithModels.kt:544) for sites, with separate lists, separate matchers and no shared entry — blocking the Instagram app does nothing to instagram.com. Worse, Monolith's app categories are invented on-device by substring matching on the package/label (MonolithRepository.kt:514-517, categorizePackage), so its 'catalogue' is a guess that differs per phone, where Opal's is a curated, versioned dataset.

Recommendation: Unify the catalogue: one entry per service carrying its packages and its domains, shipped as a versioned dataset in the APK, so selecting a service closes the app and the site in one act and categories stop being per-device substring guesses.

#### [HIGH] Opal Score is a three-signal composite — Sleep, Focus and Rest sub-scores fed by usage harvest, device-state intervals, Activity Recognition and Health Connect — where Monolith's only statistic is its own session ledger

Opal EVIDENCE §9.1: 'Opal Score combines Sleep, Focus, and Rest into one daily score', each sub-score with its own explainer and Poor→Excellent bands; the inputs are implemented, not promised — UsageHarvestWorker writes app_usage_windows into a dedicated ScreenTimeDatabase, Room holds device_state_intervals, and ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION + the Health Connect client supply steps/sitting/standing for the Rest Score, with stats labels including phone-in-bed, first hour awake and weather correlation. Monolith computes exactly one family of numbers: session minutes from its own ledger (sevenDayStats, MonolithViewModel.kt:264-265, fed by repository.compute7DayHistory()). It ingests no body signal, no device-state signal and no rest/sleep signal — a day the user spent well away from a sealed session is indistinguishable from a day in bed scrolling, because Monolith only ever measures itself.

Recommendation: If a score is ever built, copy the input architecture before the arithmetic: harvest whole-device usage windows and device-state intervals continuously, and let rest/activity signals in — a score computed only from sealed sessions will always grade the app, not the user's day.

#### [MEDIUM] Opal's streak is maintained by configuration, not completion: a day with at least one enabled rule counts, with milestone copy to 50 days and an at-risk state — Monolith's tower pays only for finished sessions and floors an empty history at one brick

Opal EVIDENCE §9.2: the streak's at-risk string states the rule outright — 'Don't lose your streak! Enable at least 1 rule to maintain your streak' — backed by home_streak_* milestone copy at 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20, 30 and 50 days, a lost-streak state, and a DailyActiveCheckWorker evaluating the day. The streak therefore rewards keeping protection switched on, a behaviour the user controls even on a bad day. Monolith's tower is completion-only and cosmetic at the floor: bricks derive from focused blocks/days and are coerced to at least 1 (BlockitTowerFadersAndCatalogViews.kt:20, :52-53), so a user who kept every routine armed but finished nothing earns the same invisible nothing as a user who did nothing at all — and a missed day leaves no mark either. Opal designed a streak a struggling user can still keep; Monolith designed a monument only finishers can touch.

Recommendation: Give Monolith a maintenance-based continuity measure alongside the tower: a day on which protection stayed armed counts toward something visible, so continuity survives the days completion doesn't.

#### [MEDIUM] Opal's collectible catalogue is a server-delivered dataset — requirementJSON, a rarity fraction per gem, region- and date-gated requirements, per-language rows — against Monolith's six artifacts hardcoded in a Kotlin list

Opal EVIDENCE §9.3: Room's gemstone_catalog stores name/shortName/description per language, requirementJSON, category, visibility, primary/secondary colours and basePrevalence (validated 'must be a fraction between 0 and 1' — a rarity weight), with gemstone_catalog_manifest holding languages + eTag because the catalogue is fetched and cached from the network; StoredGemstoneRequirementDto supports date, date-range and region-restriction requirement kinds. The collection can grow, rebalance and run region/season-gated drops without an app update. Monolith's entire collectible universe is a literal listOf of six KineticArtifact entries compiled into MonolithModels.kt:799-856 (CurioCatalog), awarded by lot, with no requirements, no rarity, no colours and no way to add a seventh without shipping a new build.

Recommendation: Move the curio catalogue out of code into a data file with requirement and rarity fields, so the collection is a dataset that can grow and gate on behaviour — not a six-line enum that ends the reward loop in a week.
### Opal — Visual design — 2 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Opal's block screen is a curated, previewable gallery of designed screens; Monolith's Airlock is one compiled-in Canvas card that can never be restyled, previewed or swapped

Opal EVIDENCE §6.3: block screens are a design surface in their own right — settings_block_screens ('Personalize your block screens'), a block_screens_section_curated ('Curated by Opal'), named preview pairs (title 'Friendly reminder' / message 'Instagram is distracting'), screens loaded remotely, plus 10 rotating educational variants that teach limits, timers and the Score at the moment of interruption. The most-seen screen in the product is treated as swappable artwork with a gallery and previews. Monolith's equivalent is a single hardcoded composable — AirlockInterceptOverlay (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:550) — one layout, one voice, one numeral, compiled into the binary; there is no variant, no preview, no gallery, and no way for its look to change without a rebuild. Opal designs the interruption as a surface; Monolith prints it as a form.

Recommendation: Make the Airlock a data-driven screen: at minimum two or three designed variants (calm / firm / minimal) rendered from a small spec, previewable from Shield — the intercept is the product's most-seen surface and should not be its least designed.

#### [MEDIUM] Opal ships a produced-media design system — video explainers for its most sensitive features, a Lottie launch animation, CDN video for waiting and detox moments — while Monolith has zero video or animation assets anywhere

Opal EVIDENCE §12: res/raw carries produced media as a deliberate design layer — flower.mp4, intro_autofocus.mp4, intro_blocks_renamed.mp4, intro_score.mp4, and explainer videos for the two moments that most need comprehension, school_mandatory_policy.mp4 and school_privacy.mp4 — plus Lottie launch_animation.json, and CDN-hosted video for the Waiting Room and Digital Detox timers (e.g. touchinggrass.mp4). Sensitive or emotional moments get produced motion media, not text. Monolith contains no res/raw directory, no assets directory and not a single .mp4 or Lottie file in the tree: every surface, including its most sensitive (the permission asks and the intercept), is hand-drawn Canvas/Compose primitives and caps text. One product budgets motion media as a design material; the other has none in the building.

Recommendation: Budget one produced-media moment where comprehension matters most — the permission primer — even as a lightweight in-app animation sequence; text plates are the weakest possible medium for the app's most consequential ask.
### Opal — Platform execution — 2 findings (0 critical, 1 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

#### [HIGH] Opal engineered the return trip from Settings as a service: ReturnAfterPermissionService polls the grant and bounces the user back into the app the moment it lands — Monolith's permission trips are fire-and-forget with no way back

Opal EVIDENCE §4.2: com.withopal.opal.permissions.launcher.ReturnAfterPermissionService is a specialUse foreground service whose own manifest subtype declares its job verbatim — 'Polls a system Settings permission while the user is in the OS Settings deep-link and bounces them back to Opal once the grant lands. Lifetime is bounded by the polling timeout' — supported by a dedicated 'Permission return' notification channel ('Waiting for permission…'). The grant round-trip is a first-class, lifecycle-managed component. Monolith's 139-line manifest contains no such component: its FIX flow fires raw Settings intents and judges the trip after the fact, so the return half of every permission ask — the half where users get lost — is simply not engineered. Opal treats coming back as part of the permission; Monolith treats leaving as the whole flow.

Recommendation: Build the return half: while a FIX trip is outstanding, run a bounded poller on the grant state and bring the user back to the exact board row they left, instead of abandoning them in Settings and re-measuring later.

#### [MEDIUM] Opal sustains always-on blocking with no DeviceAdmin and no battery-exemption ask anywhere in its manifest; Monolith stacks a device-admin 'uninstall guard', a battery prompt and four more special accesses on top

Opal EVIDENCE §3: across all 26 declared permissions and the full component list there is no DeviceAdmin receiver or policy at all, no VPN binding, and no REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS — its always-on rules business runs on UsageStats + overlay + a specialUse FGS without asking to administer the device or to be exempted from battery management. Monolith declares a DeviceAdminReceiver 'Kernel-Level Uninstall Guard' (AndroidManifest.xml:120-130) with a limit-password policy, a battery-exemption prompt, accessibility with full window-content access, a notification listener and overlay — a strictly larger dangerous-capability footprint for a strictly narrower (session-only) enforcement window. Opal's manifest is proof that the category's core promise does not require administering the user's phone; Monolith asks for the keys anyway.

Recommendation: Audit the manifest against Opal's as the reference footprint: drop the device-admin receiver and the battery-exemption ask unless each can name an enforcement behaviour that dies without it.
### Opal — Comparative audit — 4 findings (0 critical, 0 high, 4 medium, 0 low)

#### [MEDIUM] The flagship's Android build is as absent from the home screen as Monolith: Opal's APK contains no widget provider and no Quick Settings tile at all

Opal EVIDENCE §4.3/§14 (observed as absence): the APK has no APPWIDGET_UPDATE receiver, no widget-provider XML in res/xml (only website_detector_config, backup/data-extraction rules, image_share_filepaths, billing/splits files) and no TileService — Opal on Android ships zero home-screen or shade presence, whatever its iOS build offers. Monolith is routinely beaten up in this category for lacking a widget, but against Opal's actual Android artifact the score is 0-0: neither product can start or show a session from the home screen. The gap is real for both; it is not a dimension on which Opal's Android engineering is ahead.

Recommendation: No action against Opal parity — but if a widget is built, it leapfrogs Opal's Android build rather than catching it up; prioritise accordingly (a session-start widget would be a genuine Android-side lead over this rival).

#### [MEDIUM] Opal's Location rule is vapour at the manifest level: the rule builder offers a Location condition while the APK holds zero location permissions and no evidenced enforcement mechanism

Opal EVIDENCE §3/§8.1: 'Location — e.g at Home' (home_condition_location) is one of the rule conditions offered in the Home builder, yet the decoded manifest's 26 permissions contain no ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION and no ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION, and the evidence file records the enforcement mechanism as [unknown] — there is no geofence, Wi-Fi or cell-based trigger evidenced anywhere in the APK. An advertised trigger type ships with no visible means to fire. Monolith's trigger vocabulary is far narrower — clock and weekday mask only (RoutineEntity, MonolithModels.kt:550) — but every trigger it prints is backed by a real scheduler path; it does not sell conditions it cannot sense. On honesty-of-surface, the copy beats the flagship here.

Recommendation: Hold Monolith's line as features grow: never render a trigger or condition in the UI before its sensing path exists in the manifest and the scheduler — Opal's Location rule is the cautionary example.

#### [MEDIUM] On sound, the copy out-engineers the flagship: Opal's entire audio asset base is three gem-crack .ogg files, while Monolith ships an 857-line procedural PCM synthesizer with per-event voices

Opal EVIDENCE §12: the only sound assets in the APK are res/raw/crack_small.ogg, crack_medium.ogg and crack_large_success.ogg — three recordings in service of one animation; there is no sound library, no session audio, no per-event sound design, and haptics are evidenced only by the VIBRATE permission. Monolith, for all its faults, built TactileSoundEngine.kt — 857 lines (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/TactileSoundEngine.kt) of procedural PCM synthesis giving seals, detents, latches and finishes distinct generated voices with zero audio files. Whatever Monolith wasted that engine on (clicks, mostly), the engineering depth is real and Opal's Android build has nothing comparable: its sound design is a stock effect tied to a collectible animation.

Recommendation: Keep the synth and aim it: Opal proves a flagship can ship with almost no audio, so Monolith's engine is a differentiator only if its voices serve the session (pre-end cues, break latches, seal weight) rather than ornamenting taps.

#### [MEDIUM] Monolith is fully self-sufficient offline; Opal's design surfaces are network-fetched and visibly fail without a connection

Opal EVIDENCE §6.3/§9.3/§12: curated block screens are loaded remotely with an explicit failure state (block_screens_empty — 'Couldn't load block screens. Check your connection…'), the gemstone catalogue is fetched and eTag-cached from a CDN, and Waiting Room / Detox media stream from opal-waiting-room.b-cdn.net and opal-timers.b-cdn.net — core product surfaces degrade or empty out when the network does. Monolith declares no INTERNET permission at all (0 matches in AndroidManifest.xml) and consequently every rule, screen, sound and record works offline, forever, with no account and no server. Against an iOS-first rival whose Android experience is partly streamed, Monolith's sealed-box architecture is a genuine functional advantage on planes, in dead zones and on metered connections — the one axis where its isolation is a feature rather than a limitation.

Recommendation: Protect this as a design constraint in any future feature: if content (catalogues, screens, media) is ever added, bundle it in the APK like the categories-file model — never let a blocking surface acquire a network dependency.


#

### Second-pass findings — 7 findings (1 critical, 4 high, 2 medium, 0 low)

- **[CRITICAL] Opal meters escapes with a per-rule unblock budget and a ledger table; Monolith's peek is an uncounted, inexhaustible cooldown** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §8.2/§6.3/§6.4: unblocks are a budgeted, ledgered economy — a temporary_unblocks Room table, a chosen duration of 1 to 15 minutes, a budget counter printed on the block screen itself ('Unblock (%1$s/%2$s left)', 'No unblocks left (%1$s/%2$s)'), per-app detail showing Opens / Unblocks / time-left, Unblock-all and Reblock verbs, and five rotating unblock-exhausted notification bodies for when the budget runs dry. Monolith's entire peek state is two Long columns on BlockedAppEntity — activePeekUntilElapsedRealtime and lastPeekEndElapsedRealtime (MonolithModels.kt:241-242) — driven by fixed constants PEEK_DURATION_SECONDS=120 and PEEK_COOLDOWN_MILLIS=20 min (MonolithRepository.kt:106-108): no budget, no count, no ledger row per peek, so a user can rotate peeks across every PEEK-tier app indefinitely and nothing in the app ever runs out or can show how many escapes were spent.
  - Fix: Give peeks a per-session/per-day budget with a persisted spend ledger and a visible remaining count on the intercept; a cooldown alone is a rate limit, not an economy, and it cannot produce an exhausted state or an honest receipt of escapes used.
- **[HIGH] Opal re-arms enforcement through an independent WorkManager/receiver layer; Monolith's only reconciler lives inside the shield loop it is supposed to resurrect** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §4.2-4.3/§5: alongside its monitor FGS, Opal's manifest carries a whole independent re-arm layer — BootReceiver on BOOT_COMPLETED and MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, a dedicated NotificationFireReceiver as an explicit alarm target, WorkManager's SystemJobService/SystemForegroundService, plus named workers DailyActiveCheckWorker and UsageHarvestWorker — so rule state is reconciled by persisted, system-managed jobs even if the monitor process is dead. Monolith has no WorkManager at all (no work-runtime dependency in app/build.gradle.kts) and no job services in its manifest: routine reconciliation rides inside the shield's own session loop (MonolithShieldService.kt:91-92 ticks RoutineHeartbeat only every 15th 2s iteration, and MonolithShieldService.kt:97 stops the service entirely when no session is active), opportunistic ticks piggybacked on notification posts (MonolithNotificationListener.kt:56), and a single inexact alarm chain (RoutineScheduler.kt:44, setAndAllowWhileIdle). If the shield process dies and that one alarm chain breaks, nothing independent ever wakes to reconcile routine windows until the user happens to open the app or trigger an event.
  - Fix: Add a persisted job layer (WorkManager periodic work with a unique-work policy) that reconciles routine windows and re-arms alarms independently of the shield service's lifetime, so enforcement recovery does not depend on the very process whose death it is meant to recover from.
- **[HIGH] Opal's Timer is a generated Rule with a detox preset link; Monolith's session is a standalone row every mode must re-implement around** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §8.3: Room table active_timer_sessions stores durationMinutes, blockingRuleID and detoxPresetID — a Timer is materialised as a one-shot Rule, so it inherits the whole rule engine (selections, unblock budgets, Hard Mode, lifecycle states) for free, and Digital Detox (Digital Sabbath, Quiet Day, The Retreat, Touch Grass) is just a preset family over the same object, started by hold-to-start. Monolith has no such unification: FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:268) is a standalone row with intention/profileName/targetDurationSeconds and no rule foreign key or preset link, and routines bolt attendance onto that same row via routineId/window snapshot fields (MonolithModels.kt:303-308) — manual sessions and routine sessions are two hand-wired paths over one table, and there is no detox/long-form mode anywhere in the codebase (zero 'detox' hits in main sources).
  - Fix: Model a started timer as a generated rule/session instance behind one shared enforcement object, so any future mode (detox, exam, wind-down) is a preset over the existing engine instead of a new code path with its own judgement logic.
- **[HIGH] Opal asks permissions last and in value order — Usage first as a benefit, Accessibility third; Monolith's board leads with Accessibility and fires unordered Settings trips** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §11: the conversational onboarding runs greeting, personalisation, a personalised screen-time projection, the gem-crack reveal, a 'How Opal works' walkthrough and creation of a starter rule BEFORE any permission is asked; the asks then run in a graduated order — Usage Access first, framed as a benefit ('Screen time — Lets Opal show you your daily screen time and progress'), then Display over other apps ('gently help you pause'), then Accessibility (website detection), then Notifications ('nudges'). Monolith has no sequence at all: WatchStore.kt:82-87 puts ACCESSIBILITY first in board order, and MainActivity.kt:367-412 (openFixPane) is a flat per-item dispatcher that deep-links whichever missing grant is tapped to its raw Settings pane, with no ordering, no value delivered first, and no framing of why the grant comes at that point.
  - Fix: Adopt a graduated ask order: deliver value and let the user build a first rule before any Settings trip, ask Usage Access first as the stats benefit, and present the remaining grants in dependency order with a one-line payoff attached to each, instead of an unordered FIX dispatcher.
- **[HIGH] Opal's core blocking needs only two required grants and labels the third optional; Monolith counts four grants — including device-admin — before it will call itself guarded** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §6.1 (the app's own permission strings): Usage Access = 'Required to detect which app is open', Overlay = 'Required to show the block screen', Accessibility = 'Optional for website blocking' — core blocking is a two-grant product, and although a NotificationBlockingService exists (§4.2), notification-listener access appears in neither the §11 onboarding asks nor the consolidated Permissions screen, so it is never a setup gate. Monolith's readiness accounting demands double: WatchStore.kt:95-103 defines PERMISSIONS as six items and COUNTED as four (ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN, NOTIFICATION_LISTENER), and MonolithRepository.kt:645-654 (watchGrantQuery) checks device-admin and the notification listener as first-class grants — so a user who grants exactly Opal's required pair still reads GUARD 2/4 and is sent on two more Settings trips, one of them for a device-admin receiver (AndroidManifest.xml:123-137) that Opal does not ship at all.
  - Fix: Shrink the counted gate to the grants blocking actually consumes (Usage Access + Accessibility in Monolith's design); demote the notification listener to an optional enhancement and remove device-admin from the readiness count entirely, matching Opal's required/optional labelling.
- **[MEDIUM] Opal isolates enforcement data in its own Room database, separate from screen-time harvest; Monolith puts rules, sessions and captured notifications in one shared store** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §5: the APK ships two separate Room databases with separate jobs — OpalDatabase holds the enforcement state (blocking_rules, active_timer_sessions, temporary_unblocks, emergency_pass_usages) while a distinct ScreenTimeDatabase holds the harvested analytics (app_usage_windows), fed by its own UsageHarvestWorker. A harvest or analytics-schema failure cannot touch the rules that block. Monolith keeps everything in one database: MonolithDatabase.kt:11-28 puts BlockedAppEntity, FocusSessionEntity, CapturedNotificationEntity, RoutineEntity and GuardSettingsEntity in a single @Database with one sequential migration chain, and the shield's own loop writes session progress into that same store every 2 seconds (MonolithShieldService.kt:108). Enforcement rows, captured notification content and session bookkeeping share one failure and corruption domain.
  - Fix: Split the persistence domains: keep blocking rules, tiers and session state in their own database (or at least their own migration track) isolated from captured notifications and usage analytics, so a fault in the data-collection side can never corrupt or lock the enforcement side.
- **[MEDIUM] Opal sunsets its exact-alarm permission by manifest (maxSdkVersion=32) and schedules via WorkManager; Monolith just omits exact alarms and hand-rolls an inexact AlarmManager chain** — Opal EVIDENCE.md §3 item 7: SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is declared with android:maxSdkVersion="32", so the restricted exact-alarm permission simply ceases to exist on Android 13+ installs, while §4.2 shows the scheduling load carried instead by WorkManager's SystemJobService/SystemForegroundService plus the specialUse ForegroundAppMonitorService. Monolith declares no exact-alarm permission at all (AndroidManifest.xml:6-14) and has no WorkManager dependency anywhere in its build files; its only scheduling mechanism is a hand-rolled inexact chain — RoutineScheduler.kt:41-44 and ReleaseRetryScheduler.kt:39-42 both call AlarmManager.setAndAllowWhileIdle — so Monolith's smaller manifest entry is not a designed sunset, it is an omission whose cost is paid at every routine boundary.
  - Fix: Either declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM capped at maxSdkVersion 32 for legacy devices as Opal does, or move routine/heartbeat scheduling onto WorkManager's platform job scheduler; do not rely on a self-rearming inexact alarm chain as the sole timing mechanism.
## Supplement: one sec head-to-head (from its actual APK)

**Evidence base:** static reverse engineering of one sec v2.9.5 (20905), package wtf.riedel.onesec — see `apk-re/onesec/EVIDENCE.md`. Static analysis only; the APK was never installed or run.

### Head-to-head losses

- **[HIGH] One dedicated BlockActivity in its own task renders all eight block kinds; Monolith's intercept is an overlay composable inside MainActivity itself** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §4/§5: BlockActivity is exported, singleTask, taskAffinity=wtf.riedel.onesec.block, excludeFromRecents=true, and ONE activity renders all eight BlockKind values (Intervention, ReInterventionShield, InstantBlock, RecurringBlock, NHSScheduledBlock, NHSDailyBudget, WebsiteBlocked, AppContent), launched by the accessibility service with explicit extras (packageName, blockKind, className, blockContent). The intercept is a real activity in a separate task that the user cannot Recents-swipe back into the blocked app from. Monolith's intercept is AirlockInterceptOverlay, a composable rendered inside MainActivity's own composition (MainActivity.kt:793), reached by MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:422-429 relaunching MainActivity itself with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK | SINGLE_TOP and intent extras — the 'wall' and the app's home are the same activity, same task, same process state.
  - Fix: Move the intercept out of MainActivity into a dedicated singleTask activity with its own taskAffinity and excludeFromRecents, parameterised by block kind (app, website, in-app section, peek expiry) instead of an in-composition overlay.
- **[HIGH] App, website and in-app-section enforcement all run through one accessibility content-event gate; Monolith runs three separate mechanisms that can disagree** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §5/§8: the accessibility config subscribes TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED | TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED (0x820) with FLAG_REPORT_VIEW_IDS and canRetrieveWindowContent=true, and a single 'Content-event gate' feeds every enforcement type — the launch log line carries class=<window class> and content=<...> so the same door intercepts an app open, a browser URL (blockKind=WebsiteBlocked) or an in-app section like Reels/Shorts (blockKind=AppContent, blockContent extra naming the section). Monolith splits this across three independent mechanisms in MonolithAccessibilityService.kt (app door, hardcoded Shorts/Reels view-ID sniper lists, and a substring URL matcher in a separate service door), each with its own state — the exact architecture that lets its guard board print SHORTS + REELS PAUSED while both keep intercepting.
  - Fix: Unify Monolith's three enforcement branches behind one event gate in the accessibility service that classifies each event once (app / URL / in-app section) and renders one intercept type, so the doors cannot diverge.
- **[HIGH] one sec has a separate Intervention Schedule layer — per-app, per-weekday windows for when friction applies, stored as DayTimeSelection blobs; Monolith friction exists only inside armed sessions and global routines** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §10: a Room schedule table (id, feature, enabled, strict_block, same_on_all_weekdays, per-weekday mon_selection…sun_selection DayTimeSelection TEXT blobs, apps TEXT) backs BOTH intervention schedules and recurring blocks, discriminated by the feature column. The Intervention Schedule limits WHEN interventions apply per app; configured apps in no schedule 'stay on all the time'. Friction timing is a per-app property independent of any session. Monolith has no such layer: its only timing object is RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550-570) — a global window plus a loadoutName string — and outside an armed session or routine window there is no per-app friction schedule at all.
  - Fix: Add a per-app intervention-schedule table (per-weekday time windows per app, independent of sessions) so friction can be timed per app — e.g. Shorts only after 21:00 — without arming a full session or a routine.
- **[HIGH] Re-Intervention is a structured per-app time-budget system (ReInterventionSession, MaxReInterventionTime, per-app Active/Off); Monolith's peek has no per-app budget or re-lock shield** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §17: DEX types re_intervention.ReInterventionSession and re_intervention.MaxReInterventionTime; setup asks 'How much time do you need on %s?' per app, a Max Re-Intervention Time setting offers 'No Limit', Customize carries a per-app Active/Off toggle, and on budget expiry a dedicated shield (blockKind=ReInterventionShield) states 'You'll need to go through another intervention to unlock %s again.' Doom-scroll time inside a target app is budgeted per app and re-locks automatically. Monolith's only in-app time budget is the fixed global PEEK_2M tier (MonolithModels.kt:13-38: 2 minutes plus a mandatory 20-minute cooldown) — one constant for every app, no per-app budget, no max-time policy, and no shield that re-locks a user who stays inside the app past a budget.
  - Fix: Give the peek tier a per-app budget (duration + max renewals per session) with a re-lock shield on expiry, instead of one global 2-minute constant for every app.
- **[HIGH] Strictness in one sec is a persisted per-block property (strict_block column) with a time-boxed, reversible emergency bypass; Monolith's strictness is global and its exit is a weekly token plus a 60-second hold** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §9/§10: strict_block is an INTEGER column on the schedule table; with Strict Block on, pause/stop are removed AND strict mode itself cannot be turned off while the block is active ('Locked by Strict Block' list badge, recurring_block_locked_hint). Scheduled blocks separately get an Emergency bypass that is time-boxed and self-describing ('Bypass active until %1$s') with a 'Keep apps locked' cancel — the exit is per-block, expiring and reversible. Monolith has no per-block strictness property at all: strictness is whatever the current session state is, and the only exits are the global one-per-week emergency token and the 60-second valve hold, neither bound to a specific block nor time-boxed.
  - Fix: Persist strictness on the session/routine row itself, and make the emergency exit a per-session time-boxed bypass with a visible expiry and a cancel, instead of a single global weekly token.
- **[MEDIUM] one sec's accessibility service detects the setup trip itself and pulls the user back to finish it; Monolith's permission recovery is a manual serial loop** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §5: OnesecAccessibilityService tracks that the user visited accessibility settings and re-launches OneSecActivity itself (log: 'Bringing app to foreground (a11y settings opened …s ago)'), closing the grant loop automatically; it also persists last_time_block_app_opened on every block. Monolith has no equivalent service-side recovery: its accessibility service (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:70) never re-surfaces the app after a Settings trip, and recovery is the user manually working a one-at-a-time FIX queue with silent failure on a broken Settings intent.
  - Fix: Have Monolith's accessibility service (and the shield service) detect return-from-Settings and re-surface the app at the exact grant step that was in progress, instead of leaving the user to find their way back.
- **[MEDIUM] one sec tunes the intercept's false positives with dedicated settings — intentional app switching grace (None/1/3/5 min) and ignore-incoming-calls; Monolith's Airlock has no equivalent tuning** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §6: 'Intentional app switching' offers None / 1 minute / 3 minutes / 5 minutes so switching between two target apps does not re-trigger a full intervention (DEX field ignoreIntentionalAppSwitching), and 'Ignore incoming calls' ensures an incoming call inside a blocked app never triggers an intervention. These are first-class settings aimed at the intercept's two most common false positives. Monolith's Airlock (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:550) exposes no grace or switching tuning at all: every entry pays the full wall, and its call handling is a single global bypass switch in the accessibility service rather than a scoped, user-visible setting.
  - Fix: Add an intentional-switching grace window and a scoped ignore-calls option to Monolith's intercept settings, so legitimate navigation between blocked apps stops paying full friction.

### Visual design

- **[MEDIUM] one sec's entire Android brand identity is carried by exactly one bundled font file; Monolith bundles eight TTFs across three families** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §19: the APK contains exactly one font file, res/font/permanent_marker.ttf — a handwritten marker display face used as the brand signature — with all other type served by Compose Material 3 defaults. The whole visual identity is one deliberate typographic choice. Monolith's res/font/ ships eight TTF files (anonymous_pro.ttf, anonymous_pro_bold.ttf, atkinson_hyperlegible.ttf, atkinson_hyperlegible_bold.ttf, and four Sora statics: sora.ttf, sora_bold.ttf, sora_medium.ttf, sora_semibold.ttf) spanning three unrelated families, so the app has no single typographic signature — Canvas, dial numerals and Compose text each speak in a different face.
  - Fix: Pick one display face as Monolith's signature (the dial/receipt voice) and cut the bundle to that family plus one text face; delete the unused statics.
- **[MEDIUM] one sec's design system is typography-led with zero media payload — 230 res entries and no audio or illustration assets at all; Monolith's identity is buried under asset bulk** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §0/§19: the 17.3 MB APK holds 410 zip entries, 230 of them res/, no .mp3/.ogg/.wav anywhere, no bundled illustration system — brand is carried by the marker font, Material 3 colour/style tables and copy. Restraint is the design system. Monolith ships 8 font files as ~80% of its res/ bulk plus a 9.3 MB public/ tree of uncompressed reference images and competitor screenshots tracked in the repo — the visual identity a user actually meets is a 10sp label system, while the bytes went to assets no screen renders.
  - Fix: Set an asset budget for Monolith (fonts + shipped imagery) and delete non-shipping media from the repo; let the receipt/dial typography carry the brand the way one sec lets one font carry it.

### Platform execution

- **[HIGH] one sec enforces with none of the heavy grants: no notification listener, no device admin, no VPN, no DND policy — Monolith demands all of the first two on top of accessibility** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §3/§22: across its 16 manifest permissions there is NO BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE, NO BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN receiver, NO BIND_VPN_SERVICE and NO ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY; enforcement is one accessibility service + overlay permission + Usage Access. The category's best-known friction product never touches the two most invasive Android grants. Monolith declares both: MonolithNotificationListener at AndroidManifest.xml:81-91 and MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver at AndroidManifest.xml:122-136, stacked on top of its accessibility service, overlay and usage-stats grants — two extra special-access Settings trips, and a device-admin consent screen, that one sec's Android app proves unnecessary for the core promise.
  - Fix: Justify or delete Monolith's device-admin receiver, and treat the notification listener as an optional enhancement rather than a core gate — one sec ships the category benchmark with neither.
- **[HIGH] one sec's permission flow is scaffolded step-by-step — privacy pre-ask before accessibility, a tutorial per grant, OEM autostart matched to a 13-package <queries> list; Monolith fires raw Settings intents** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §3/§14: before the accessibility ask, a privacy pre-ask shows chips 'Offline / On-device / Private' with the notice 'One sec does not track or collect personal data'; each grant has dedicated tutorial strings (accessibility: 'Enable Use one sec. Keep one sec shortcut disabled.' plus the warning 'Do NOT choose target apps here.'; overlay is literally 'tutorial_step_2'), and the OEM background/autostart step is backed by a manifest <queries> block naming 13 OEM security/battery packages (com.miui.securitycenter, com.coloros.safecenter, com.huawei.systemmanager, com.iqoo.secure, com.vivo.permissionmanager, com.samsung.android, …) so the app can route each phone brand to its own autostart screen. Monolith's manifest <queries> (AndroidManifest.xml:16-22) covers only launcher intents, and its grants are raw Settings intents behind a jargon board with no per-step tutorial and no OEM routing.
  - Fix: Give each Monolith grant its own tutorial step with the exact toggle name and the mistakes to avoid, add a privacy pre-ask before the accessibility trip, and declare the OEM security-centre packages in <queries> to route autostart setup per brand.
- **[MEDIUM] one sec delegates anti-tamper to Play's PairIP wrapper instead of inventing cryptography; Monolith hand-rolls a forgeable HMAC** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §2: the manifest Application class is com.pairip.application.Application (PairIP — Play's app-protection/licence wrapper, 36 com.pairip.* classes, LicenseActivity, CHECK_LICENSE permission), which bootstraps the real OneSecApplication; integrity and licence enforcement are the platform's problem, maintained by Google. Monolith instead hand-rolled its own session-integrity HMAC in CryptoIntegrityManager.kt — with a hard-coded public fallback key and blank-signature acceptance — spending engineering effort on cryptography that is forgeable by construction, where the benchmark app spends zero lines on it.
  - Fix: Stop extending the hand-rolled HMAC scheme; if integrity ever matters for Monolith's receipts, use Play Integrity / PairIP-style platform attestation and keep the local signature as a checksum only.

### Comparative audit

- **[HIGH] Monolith out-builds one sec on progression: the consumer one sec app has no streaks, no gamification and no score at all — they exist only inside an NHS school-study silo** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §13/§22: 'No streak/gamification in the consumer app (streaks exist only inside the NHS study build-out); no focus-score string/class found — statistics are prevented-count + time-saved + time-spent only.' The streaks, XP, daily budgets and leaderboard live behind study enrolment (blockKinds NHSScheduledBlock/NHSDailyBudget, nhs_study_* strings, research-API Leaderboard models) — a research silo no normal user ever sees. Monolith ships its progression to everyone: the Tower, the CurioCatalog collectibles (MonolithModels.kt:799-856), routine attendance judgements and numbered session receipts. Honest limit: Monolith's ladder is exhausted in under a week — but one sec's consumer ladder does not exist at all.
  - Fix: Keep and deepen Monolith's progression line rather than copying one sec's restraint here; the gap to close is content depth (more curios, tower headroom), not existence.
- **[HIGH] Monolith out-builds one sec on hard blocking: one sec's only hard block (App Block) is explicitly beta in its own APK, with a switch-back escape** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §9: App Block's strings call it a preview — app_block_beta_screen_title = 'Try scheduled blocks (Beta)', subtitle 'Preview our redesigned block screen with scheduled blocks. It's still in beta… You can switch back anytime.', plus a 'Leave Beta Feedback' surface. The mature one sec product is friction-only; scheduled/instant hard blocking is unfinished work on Android. Monolith's core shipped system is exactly that hard blocking: armed sessions with seal proving, routine windows with attendance judgement, and receipted outcomes. On the feature one sec labels beta, Monolith is the more complete product.
  - Fix: Treat hard-session depth (proving, receipts, routine judgement) as Monolith's defensible core in positioning and prioritisation — it is ahead of the category's friction benchmark, whose hard mode is still beta.
- **[MEDIUM] Monolith at least attempts notification silence; one sec's Android app cannot touch other apps' notifications at all** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §18/§22: no NotificationListenerService and no ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY — one sec 'does not read, hold, or block other apps' notifications'; during a one sec intervention or block, a target app's notifications still arrive, buzz and sit in the shade untouched, because the app has no mechanism to do anything else. Monolith declares MonolithNotificationListener (AndroidManifest.xml:81-91) and built a capture/hold/digest pipeline on it. Honest both directions: Monolith's implementation is broken in practice (held notifications alert first and are deleted rather than held, per earlier rounds) — but the surface exists in Monolith and is entirely absent in one sec, whose users get zero notification relief.
  - Fix: Keep the notification-holding ambition — it is a genuine differentiator over one sec — and fix its delivery-order defect (cancel before alert, restore on session end) instead of cutting the feature.
- **[MEDIUM] one sec's Android binary is dominated by a purchases SDK and ships leftover tooling: ~2,486 of 11,490 classes are RevenueCat, and an exported Compose PreviewActivity sits in the production manifest** — one sec EVIDENCE.md §0/§4/§20: of 11,490 DEX classes, com.revenuecat.* alone is ~2,486 — the single largest code mass in the app, larger than all first-party logic combined (only 22 classes keep a wtf.riedel.onesec.* name) — and the manifest declares androidx.compose.ui.tooling.PreviewActivity with exported=true, a Compose tooling activity shipped to production. The flagship's Android build carries packaging sloppiness Monolith does not have: Monolith's manifest (AndroidManifest.xml:39-136) declares only its own activity, three services and four receivers, with no tooling components and no third-party SDK outweighing its own code.
  - Fix: No action for Monolith beyond keeping its manifest clean — record this as evidence that the benchmark's Android packaging is not the gold standard; do not copy its SDK weight.


#

### Second-pass findings — 6 findings (2 critical, 4 high, 0 medium, 0 low)

- **[CRITICAL] Detection hierarchy inverted: one sec hard-gates hard features on passive accessibility events and demotes polling to a named legacy fallback; Monolith's session enforcement IS the polling fallback** — EVIDENCE.md §5: one sec's primary detector is OnesecAccessibilityService (config eventTypes 0x820 = WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED|WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED, passive events); its UsageStats detector is literally named LegacyForegroundService/LegacyBootCompletedService and framed in-string as the inferior 'old legacy approach using the app usage permission', and strings app_block_enable_a11y, block_content_enable_a11y, reintervention_enable_a11y and schedule_enable_a11y hard-gate App Block, in-app-content blocking, Re-Intervention and schedules on the accessibility service — they refuse to run degraded on polling. Monolith inverts this: its accessibility door early-returns unless a session is active (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:194-195, scope.launch snapshot check), while its actual session door is MonolithShieldService's 2s polling loop (MonolithShieldService.kt:193 delay(2000L)) calling MonolithRepository.kt:564-575 queryForegroundBlockedApp(), which guesses the foreground app as the blocked package with the max lastTimeUsed inside an 8-second window — i.e. Monolith's main enforcement is exactly the mechanism one sec demoted to a legacy fallback and refuses to trust for its hard features.
  - Fix: Make the accessibility event path the primary session detector, and hard-gate hard blocking on it like one sec does: if accessibility is dead, surface enforcement as OFF rather than silently certifying a session policed only by a 2s lastTimeUsed guess.
- **[CRITICAL] one sec runs on a tiered permission fallback — UsageStats alone if accessibility is declined — Monolith's warrant is binary OFF without accessibility despite also polling UsageStats** — EVIDENCE.md §5/§14: one sec ships LegacyForegroundService (UsageStats polling, START_STICKY) explicitly framed in-string as the declinable fallback — accessibility_service_learn_more_description calls accessibility 'the best user experience' but lets users 'decline it and use our old legacy approach using the app usage permission'; premium features are individually hard-gated instead (app_block_enable_a11y, block_content_enable_a11y, reintervention_enable_a11y, schedule_enable_a11y), so one grant unlocks features incrementally. Monolith has both detectors too but no degraded mode: WatchStore.kt:296-305 deriveWarrant() returns WarrantState.OFF the moment a11yBound is false, regardless of UsageAccess, so its own 2s UsageStats shield polling can never serve as a standalone legacy tier — a user who declines the most invasive permission gets zero protection, not slower protection.
  - Fix: Add a legacy detection tier: when accessibility is declined but Usage Access is ALLOWED, arm sessions on the shield's UsageStats polling alone and hard-gate only the features that truly need window content (Shorts/Reels sniper, URL/content blocking), mirroring one sec's per-feature enable_a11y gates.
- **[HIGH] Strict Block locks itself in one sec; Monolith's shield stop and uninstall guard are both unconditionally escapable** — EVIDENCE.md §9-§10: one sec's App Block persists a strict_block INTEGER column on its schedule table and defines Strict Block in-string as 'you won't be able to pause/stop an active block. On top of that, you can't turn off the strict mode' (badge 'Locked by Strict Block', hint 'This block is active and locked while Strict Block is on'), enforced by a separate specialUse foreground AppBlockService (startForeground(3), AppBlockServiceChannel, with an explicit startForeground-failure fallback log). Monolith has no equivalent self-locking state: MonolithShieldService.kt:35-46 honours an unconditional ACTION_STOP_SHIELD intent by clearing protecting and stopSelf() with no strictness check, and its supposed uninstall lock, MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver.kt, implements only onDisableRequested() returning a warning string plus WatchStore grant stamps — nothing in either component prevents the stop/deactivation path itself while a session is live.
  - Fix: Add a persisted strict flag on the session/schedule that the stop paths themselves check — ShieldService's ACTION_STOP_SHIELD handler and the device-admin disable path must refuse while strict is active, as one sec's strict_block column refuses even disabling strict mode.
- **[HIGH] The rival's breath is a stored, per-configuration object; Monolith's wall is a composable-local integer 5** — EVIDENCE.md §6: the rival's breath is persistent configuration — DEX fields exerciseDuration and exerciseDurations (plural, per configuration), breathingPhrase (user-editable exercise text, settings_screen_exercise_text_title), a 'breath animation state', and a showBypassExercise flag, with four named duration tiers Short / Medium / Long / Extreme and default copy 'It's time to take a deep breath…'. Monolith's 'Breathing Delay Wall' is not data at all: AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:562-569 hardcodes var countdownSecs by remember { mutableIntStateOf(5) } inside the composable, ticking a bare numeral ('0%d' at line 636); no entity field, preference, or per-app value anywhere stores a wall duration, a phrase, or an animation state, so the signature moment cannot differ between a mild app and the user's worst app.
  - Fix: Promote the wall to a stored per-app configuration object (duration tier, editable phrase, guided breath animation state) read by the Airlock overlay instead of the composable-local constant 5, so friction can be sized per app and the wait carries the guided content its name promises.
- **[HIGH] one sec needs exactly one bound privileged service; Monolith declares three bound privileged components for the same intervention promise** — EVIDENCE.md §3/§22 records checked absences in one sec's manifest: NO BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE, NO BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN receiver, NO BIND_VPN_SERVICE, NO ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY — its only bound service is OnesecAccessibilityService (BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE), yet it still delivers interventions, website blocking, in-app content blocking and scheduled hard blocks (§5/§8/§9). Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml declares three separate bound privileged components: MonolithAccessibilityService at line 66 (BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE), MonolithNotificationListener at line 82 (BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE) and MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver at line 122 (BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN), on top of MonolithShieldService at line 54. Each extra bound component is its own Settings consent trip, its own Play restricted-permission/policy surface, and its own always-bindable attack/privacy surface — machinery one sec proves unnecessary for the core product.
  - Fix: Justify or cut each bound component against the one-service baseline: drop the DeviceAdmin receiver entirely and make the NotificationListener an opt-in session-only component rather than a standing manifest declaration, so the default install exposes one bound service, not three.
- **[HIGH] one sec asks in a fixed value-first sequence ending in a live proof-open; Monolith's six asks are a reactive repair queue with no sequence and no proof** — EVIDENCE.md §14: one sec's app-configuration flow asks in order (1) Accessibility — preceded by a privacy pre-ask with 'Offline / On-device / Private' chips and a dedicated tutorial ('Keep one sec shortcut disabled', 'Do NOT choose target apps here'), (2) Overlay with the reason stated ('necessary to show you the breathing exercise'), (3) Usage, (4) Battery exemption, (5) OEM autostart — then permissions_all_set_title 'You're all set!', first-app selection, and a live proof: onboarding_complete sends the user home to open the target app and intervention_success_title confirms 'one sec works, yay!'. Monolith has no sequenced first-run ask at all: its only permission navigation is openFixPane() in MainActivity.kt:362-410, a reactive per-item repair function that fires a bare Settings intent per missing item (accessibility, usage, a hardcoded DeviceAdminSettings component, notification-listener, overlay, battery) after the fact, with runCatching silently swallowing failures and no step that ever test-opens a blocked app to prove the grants actually intercept.
  - Fix: Replace the reactive FIX queue with a sequenced first-run flow in detection-value order (accessibility with a privacy pre-ask and tutorial, then usage, then the counted extras), and finish it with one sec's proof step: have the user open their first blocked app and show a success confirmation when the intercept actually fires.
## Supplement: YPT (Yeolpumta) head-to-head (from its actual APK)

**Evidence base:** static reverse engineering of YPT (com.pallo.passiontimerscoped) — see `apk-re/ypt/EVIDENCE.md`. Static analysis only; the APK was never installed or run.

### Head-to-head losses

- **[CRITICAL] YPT runs four lock modes plus an in-session allowlist on UsageStats polling and overlay windows alone — no accessibility service, no notification listener, no device admin anywhere in the APK** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2/§3.4/§13: the manifest contains no accessibility service component, no NotificationListenerService and no DeviceAdmin receiver; foreground detection is UsageStatsManager.queryEvents polling and enforcement is real WindowManager overlay windows (service_lock.xml, service_phone_lock.xml, service_school_mode.xml, block_apps_overlay_view.xml). That two-mechanism stack carries Block Apps, Phone Lock, Hard Mode, School Mode and the in-recording allowlist (EVIDENCE.md §4/§5). Monolith cannot block at all without the three most invasive grants Android has: its manifest declares an accessibility service that reads window content (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:66-73), a NotificationListenerService (AndroidManifest.xml:82-89, MonolithNotificationListener.kt:23) and a device-admin receiver (AndroidManifest.xml:120-122) — and still only arms inside a session or routine. The rival proves the entire category of lock modes ships without ever reading another app's windows or notifications.
  - Fix: Treat YPT's stack as the existence proof for a permission diet: prototype enforcement on UsageStats + a real overlay window and demote accessibility to the optional Shorts/site role, so the core lock no longer depends on the grant users fear most.
- **[HIGH] YPT's detection loop special-cases Settings and the package installer by package name — the two apps used to kill a blocker are watched inside the detector itself** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §3.4: const-strings inside BlockAppsService's polling loop special-case com.android.settings and com.google.android.packageinstaller, alongside system-package heuristics (launcher, systemui, inputmethod, vending) and allowed content categories — the kill routes are handled at the detection layer, by the same loop that detects everything else. Monolith's equivalent protection lives in a completely different, fragile place: an English-only text heuristic inside its accessibility service (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt), so if that one service is off, dead or bound to another language, the Settings/installer route is unguarded while the shield still runs on its other door. YPT's coverage survives because it is package identity in the polling loop, not screen text in a second service.
  - Fix: Move Settings and package-installer coverage into Monolith's shield detection loop as package-level rules, so the anti-tamper watch does not depend on the accessibility service being alive and reading English.
- **[HIGH] YPT re-arms its blockers with a dedicated alarm-receiver watchdog that checks for an active block before restarting anything; Monolith's shield restart is START_STICKY and hope** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §3.3: BlockAppsAlarmManager is an alarm receiver whose job is to (re)start BlockAppsService — it checks running state via ActivityManager.getRunningServices and logs 'onReceive: no active block, skip service start', i.e. the watchdog knows whether a block should exist before it acts; a BootCompleteReceiver (BOOT_COMPLETED + QUICKBOOT_POWERON) and a separate HardModeAlarmReceiver complete the pattern. Monolith's shield service has no equivalent: its resilience is START_STICKY with no watchdog or self-rescheduling (MonolithShieldService.kt), and its alarm code exists only for routine boundaries (RoutineScheduler.kt:44, setAndAllowWhileIdle). YPT treats 'the blocker died' as a scheduled, state-checked recovery; Monolith treats it as an OS courtesy.
  - Fix: Copy the pattern: a periodic alarm receiver that reads persisted session state and restarts the shield only when a session is provably active — state-checked re-arming instead of sticky-service hope.
- **[HIGH] YPT turns every study session into a timelapse video with a native encoder; a Monolith session produces only a text slip** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §9: timelapse.TimeLapseEncoderPlugin plus a BitmapRenderer (11 native classes) encode recorded study sessions into timelapse video, shipped with a dedicated help set (timelapse_help_image1-4) and example artwork — the session artefact is a watchable, shareable compression of hours of work. Monolith's only session artefact is its receipt: a text slip of counters in ReceiptSheet, with no image, video or visual record of the session ever produced anywhere in the codebase. The rival understood that proof you can watch beats proof you read; Monolith's richer session data (held apps, deflections, task bonds) is rendered as prose and numbers only.
  - Fix: Render the session's own event log into a visual artefact — even a generated timeline image of seals, deflections and held apps — so a finished session produces something watchable, not just a slip of text.
- **[HIGH] YPT bundles the study material itself: a flashcard system with Q&A, O/X and word card types, Excel import templates and a forgetting-curve spaced-repetition model — Monolith's tasks are bare titles** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §9: assets/flash_card/ ships cover and learn/quiz help artwork, a forgetting_curve_image.png (spaced repetition is a designed mechanic, not a blog claim), and spreadsheet import templates flashcard_{blank,ox,qa,word}_form.xlsx in Korean and English variants — three card types with a bulk-import path, inside the timer app. Monolith's entire study-content model is FocusTaskEntity (MonolithModels.kt:101): a title with substeps (TaskSubStep, MonolithModels.kt:80) and a timer. The app that locks your phone for an exam contains nothing you can actually revise with; YPT's timer and its revision deck are the same product.
  - Fix: If Monolith's sessions are task-bound, give the task an object richer than a title — even a per-task note/checklist content layer — instead of timing work the app knows nothing about.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT's Phone Lock is call-aware at the lock layer — a CallReceiver tracks call start, end and missed calls — while Monolith's call handling is a global bypass inside the accessibility service** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §3.3/§5: phonelock.CallReceiver listens to PHONE_STATE and the native strings onIncomingCallStarted / onIncomingCallEnded / onMissedCall show the lock annotates and rides through calls as first-class events; Phone Lock also keeps a dedicated emergency-exit intent (pref flutter.PHONE_LOCK_EMERGENCY_INTENT, onClick handler phone_lock_emergency). Monolith handles calls in the opposite architecture: a single 'Active Phone & VoIP Call Bypass' check in MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:189 (documented at :22, mirrored in MonolithRepository.kt:548) that suspends enforcement wholesale based on AudioManager mode — one global switch in the scraping service, with no per-call start/end/missed record at the lock layer and no equivalent behaviour if accessibility is dead.
  - Fix: Give the shield its own telephony-state listener that records call start/end/missed against the session, instead of borrowing a global AudioManager-mode bypass from the accessibility service.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT ships a whole tablet study surface — SmartBook ink canvas, PDF support, folders — inside the timer; Monolith has no surface for the work itself** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §9: a SmartBookExplainActivity, a native SmartbookCanvasViewFactory platform view, 16 tabletink classes (pen, highlighter, eraser, lasso, sticker tools), note covers and folders, import flows, and PDF rendering via pdfium — a complete handwritten-notes product living inside the focus timer, with its own onboarding videos (assets/tablet/intro_scene1-3.mp4). Monolith's surface area ends at the block: Deck, Shield, Drawer and the receipt. There is no notes, reading or writing surface of any kind, so the moment a session ends the user must leave for another app to do the studying the session was protecting.
  - Fix: Decide whether Monolith is only a gate or also a desk; if a desk, the cheapest honest step is a session scratchpad/notes surface bound to the active task, so work material lives where the session does.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT keeps a floating Quick Button overlay on top of every app — one tap from anywhere starts recording — because its overlay permission does real work** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §3.2: window.QuickButtonService is a draggable floating button rendered over other apps, persisting its position (location_x/location_y, pref flutter.quickButton) — a permanent, movable control for the study session that lives outside the app. Monolith asks for the same underlying grant and gets nothing from it: SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW is declared at AndroidManifest.xml:11 and users are routed to grant it, yet the codebase creates no overlay window at all — the only WindowManager reference in the app is a FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON toggle in AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:96-98. YPT converts the scariest-looking permission into its most convenient surface; Monolith collects the permission and builds no surface.
  - Fix: Either use the overlay grant for a real floating session control like YPT's Quick Button, or stop asking for it — a granted-but-unused overlay permission is pure trust debt.

### Visual design

- **[HIGH] YPT gives every permission its own illustration — a six-icon explainer set for usage, draw, notifications, calendar, camera and screen-time — while Monolith's permission board is bare jargon text** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §4: assets/icon/permissions/{calendar,camera,draw,notifications,screentime,usage}.png is a dedicated illustrated icon per permission ask, backed by illustrated help artwork for its major features (allowed-apps help images in both languages, assets/study/allowed_apps_en.png and _kr.png). The design system treats 'why does this app need that' as an illustrated product surface. Monolith's permission presentation is a text board of grant states and a FIX key: no per-permission artwork, rationale illustration or visual identity for any of its six special-access asks exists in its resources — the most trust-sensitive screens in the app are its least designed.
  - Fix: Commission a small per-permission illustration set in Monolith's own visual language — one image and one plain-language line per grant — instead of presenting the six Settings trips as a raw status board.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT ships a serialized webtoon inside the app — cover, character profiles, a seven-part story arc — as the narrative skin of its group system; Monolith's visual world has no characters or story at all** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §7: assets/webtoon/ contains a cover, an agreement episode, death_1-7 story panels and profile_1-16 character art — a produced comic with a cast, drawn specifically for this app, wrapped around its study-group feature. Monolith's entire visual vocabulary is typography, canvas geometry and one accent colour: no mascot, character, narrative art or illustrated world exists anywhere in its resources. YPT spends real art budget making an abstract behaviour (study with your group) into a story users inhabit; Monolith asks identical behaviour of the user with no world attached to it.
  - Fix: Monolith does not need a comic, but it needs some authored visual world beyond the dial and the slip — even a small set of recurring illustrated motifs tied to the Tower/Curio system would give its rituals a face.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT produces its instructional art as a variant matrix — Korean and English versions, dark and light versions — where Monolith ships a single hard-coded language and no art variants** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §6/§12: routine help artwork ships as assets/help/routine/{dark,light}/{month,year}_{en,ko}.png — every instructional image produced in four variants (two themes × two languages), and the same _en/_ko duplication runs through its challenge, tutorial and allowed-apps art. Its widgets likewise carry dedicated dark and light background drawables with night variants (drawable-night-v8, color-night-v8). Monolith ships zero locale resources and hard-coded English literals throughout its UI, with a single fixed palette — its design system has no variant dimension at all, neither for language nor, outside the session state, for theme.
  - Fix: Build variant discipline into Monolith's few authored surfaces (receipt, Tower, permission art): if an asset is worth drawing once, its dark/light production should be a system rule, not an accident.
- **[MEDIUM] YPT's type system is one family in nine true weights (Pretendard Thin to Black) plus a dedicated numeric display font for timers; Monolith pins a scattered stack of static cuts** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §12: FontManifest.json shows Pretendard in 9 weights as the single primary family, with E1234 — a dedicated numeric display face — reserved for timer readouts, so digits get their own designed voice without leaving the system. Monolith's typography is assembled from 8 bundled TTF files including four separate static cuts of one variable font (Sora) for Compose text, while its Canvas views load different faces again (Atkinson, Anonymous Pro) — three unrelated type voices, none of them a purpose-chosen numeric face for the countdowns and dials that are the app's main readouts.
  - Fix: Consolidate to one family with real weights and give the session numerals a dedicated display face — the timer readout is Monolith's most-read text and currently inherits whatever the canvas happened to load.

### Platform execution

- **[CRITICAL] YPT's entire blocking product needs exactly two special-access grants — usage access and draw-over-apps; Monolith demands six special-access Settings trips before it blocks anything** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2: of its 37 declared permissions, the enforcement stack consumes PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS and SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW as its only two special-access grants; everything else it asks (POST_NOTIFICATIONS, READ_CALENDAR, CAMERA) is an ordinary runtime permission, several of them situational to optional features. Its permission explainer set (EVIDENCE.md §4) covers exactly usage, draw, notifications, calendar, camera, screen-time. Monolith's manifest tells the opposite story (AndroidManifest.xml:11-13 plus service declarations at :66-122): usage stats, overlay, accessibility, notification-listener, device-admin and battery exemption — six separate special-access grants, each its own Settings scavenger trip, standing between install and the first blocked app. The category's study-volume leader asks for a third of the scary permissions.
  - Fix: Publish an internal permission budget: every special-access grant must name the feature that dies without it. On YPT's evidence, accessibility and notification-listener are the two Monolith grants a redesign should try hardest to make optional.
- **[HIGH] YPT holds both exact-alarm permissions and the battery-exemption permission, so its scheduled locks fire on the minute; Monolith holds neither exact-alarm permission and its routine chain is inexact by construction** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2: the manifest declares SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and USE_EXACT_ALARM together, plus REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS — its HardModeAlarmReceiver and BlockAppsAlarmManager schedule against a platform promise of exactness. Monolith's manifest declares neither exact-alarm permission (permission block, AndroidManifest.xml:6-13), and its scheduler settles for inexact delivery: RoutineScheduler.kt:44 uses setAndAllowWhileIdle for routine boundaries, so the moments a routine is supposed to start and end blocking are approximate by design. YPT's school-hours lock starts at the bell; Monolith's routine starts somewhere near it.
  - Fix: Declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and use exact alarms for routine boundaries and session-critical transitions; inexact delivery is a product decision Monolith never announced to its users.
- **[HIGH] YPT locks its dynamic receivers behind a signature-level self-permission; Monolith's exported main activity consumes intercept intents from any app that cares to send them** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2: the manifest self-declares com.pallo.passiontimerscoped.DYNAMIC_RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED_PERMISSION at signature level, and YPT's own blocking services are all exported=false — the app treats its internal broadcast surface as something to fence by default. Monolith's posture is inverted: its MainActivity is exported and consumes intercept extras handed to it by other components with no signature check or caller verification, so any installed app can feed the Airlock fabricated intercept state. YPT, the sprawling Flutter app with ~124 activities mostly owned by SDKs, still fenced its own receivers; Monolith, a single-purpose security tool, left its front door trusting.
  - Fix: Fence Monolith's internal surface the same way: non-exported receivers by default and a signature-level permission or explicit caller check on any intent that can influence session or intercept state.

### Comparative audit

- **[HIGH] Honest reverse: YPT cannot touch notifications at all — no listener, no DND — so every message, mention and promo still lands mid-study; Monolith's held-notification system, for all its faults, exists** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2/§10: no NotificationListenerService component and no ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY permission exist in the APK; its five notification channels carry only its own status and lock notifications. During a YPT recording the phone is app-locked but notification-live — the single most common study interruption vector is entirely unaddressed by its enforcement stack. Monolith ships a real notification-holding system (MonolithNotificationListener.kt:23, declared at AndroidManifest.xml:82-89) that captures and holds other apps' notifications during a session. Whatever its delivery flaws, the capability is present in Monolith and architecturally absent in the category's biggest study timer.
  - Fix: Record this as a genuine Monolith lead in the comparison set: notification holding is a differentiator worth fixing properly, because the volume leader in the category does not attempt it at all.
- **[HIGH] Honest reverse: YPT has no website blocking of any kind — no VPN, no accessibility URL reading, nothing in native code, strings or assets — while Monolith blocks sites and snipes Shorts/Reels in the browser** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2/§13: no BIND_VPN_SERVICE component, no accessibility service to read a URL bar, and no website-blocking evidence in native code, ARSC strings or asset names — a student studying with YPT can open any website in any browser for the entire session. Monolith enforces on the web layer directly: MonolithAccessibilityService.kt documents an in-browser URL-bar blocker and a YouTube Shorts / Instagram Reels sniper working off view IDs and selected tabs (class documentation at :26-33, matching core at :61), plus its blocked-domain rules. On the surface where distraction actually migrated — the browser and the short-video feed — YPT is defenceless and Monolith is armed.
  - Fix: Keep the browser/Shorts enforcement as a headline capability in any Monolith positioning: it is a real, implemented advantage over YPT, not a roadmap item.
- **[HIGH] Honest reverse on footprint: YPT's base APK is 125 MB with 89,446 classes of which 207 are the developer's own, and carries roughly twenty ad and attribution SDKs with ad-ID permissions inside a study app for students; Monolith's binary is first-party code with no ad SDK and no internet permission at all** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §1/§11: 10 DEX files totalling 89,446 classes against 207 classes under com.pallo.*, a 125,379,837-byte base APK (157 MB as shipped bundle), and an observed mediation stack spanning AdMob, AppLovin MAX, Meta Audience Network, Unity/IronSource, Mintegral, Pangle, Vungle, Chartboost, InMobi, Fyber, Moloco, PubMatic, Amazon APS, Yandex, Kakao AdFit, TNK and more — with ACCESS_ADSERVICES_AD_ID, ACCESS_ADSERVICES_ATTRIBUTION, ACCESS_ADSERVICES_TOPICS and AD_ID declared in the manifest (§2). Monolith declares no INTERNET permission at all (AndroidManifest.xml:6-13) and contains no ad or attribution SDK: every class in its binary is there to block apps or keep records. The data-collection surface a student accepts with YPT simply does not exist in Monolith.
  - Fix: Treat 'no ads, no trackers, no internet permission' as a verifiable product claim for Monolith — it is provable from its manifest in a way YPT's privacy posture is not — and protect it as features are added.
- **[MEDIUM] Honest reverse on network posture: YPT permits cleartext traffic globally while syncing study records to third-party endpoints; Monolith has no network stack to leak through** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §1/§10: usesCleartextTraffic=true in the manifest and a network-security-config whose base config sets cleartextTrafficPermitted=true with system anchors only, while the app syncs accounts, groups and study records to Firebase (project yeolpumta-ko) and Pallo's own API/CDN hosts (alicdn.pallo.cn, pi.pallo.cn and siblings). A study record — when a student studies, for how long, with which group — is permitted to travel unencrypted. Monolith makes no network calls: no INTERNET permission, no sync, no backend, so its session records cannot leave the device in cleartext or at all.
  - Fix: If Monolith ever adds sync, adopt YPT as the cautionary example in writing: cleartext disabled globally from day one, with any exception scoped per-domain and justified.


#

### Second-pass findings — 4 findings (1 critical, 3 high, 0 medium, 0 low)

- **[CRITICAL] YPT's recording is default-deny from a single native allowlist contract with built-in study-tool carve-outs; Monolith's shield is default-allow per-package and its category data never reaches enforcement** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §4/§3.5/§3.4: while recording, 'only allowed apps can be used' and '%1$s app is not allowed. You should add it to allowed apps first'; the native blockers are data-driven from one SharedPreferences contract, flutter.userAllowedApps, plus a serialised blockInfo, and the BlockAppsService loop auto-passes whole function categories (docs/documentsui/drive/file/pdf/reader/office/hancom/powerpoint/viewer/player/video/audio/messaging/authfw) while special-casing com.android.settings and com.google.android.packageinstaller — so default-deny does not break file pickers, PDF readers or auth flows. Monolith has no allowlist contract at all: MonolithShieldService.kt:165-180 builds the blocked set only from apps whose resolvedTier is not OPEN, so anything unlisted, new or left OPEN passes freely during a session, and the AppCategory enum that could power carve-outs (MonolithModels.kt:225-232, six coarse buckets) is never consulted by the shield loop, which reads only resolvedTier.
  - Fix: Add a recording mode whose rule is a stored allowlist (default-deny) enforced by the shield, with a category/function carve-out layer (file manager, documents/PDF, dialer, input method, package installer, settings) applied inside the enforcement filter before the per-package tier check, so default-deny is safe to ship.
- **[HIGH] YPT has a standalone whole-phone Phone Lock service with a reserved schedule and its own emergency exit; Monolith only ever intercepts tiered packages** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §5.2: phonelock.PhoneLockDetectService is a dedicated whole-phone lock mode — full-screen service_phone_lock.xml overlay, its own foreground notifications (PassionPhoneLockNotification + heads-up PassionHeadUpNotification), a separate ReservePhoneLockNotification foreground service for a lock reserved in advance, schedule held in native prefs flutter.PHONE_LOCK_START_AT / flutter.PHONE_LOCK_FINISH_AT, call-awareness via phonelock.CallReceiver (PHONE_STATE), and a dedicated emergency exit baked into the lock itself (PhoneLockDetectService$c.onClick: phone_lock_emergency + pref flutter.PHONE_LOCK_EMERGENCY_INTENT). Monolith has no equivalent mode anywhere: its only enforcement is per-package tier interception (MonolithShieldService.kt:165-193) — during even a SLEEP-loadout session the launcher, every OPEN-tier app and any unlisted app remain fully usable, and no service locks the device as a whole on a reserved schedule with its own in-lock emergency exit.
  - Fix: Add a true phone-lock mode as its own service: full-screen lock overlay over any foreground package, a reservable start/finish window, and a dedicated emergency exit rendered inside the lock itself — not simulated by tier-rewriting every app.
- **[HIGH] YPT measures 'Allowed Apps Time' inside the recording; Monolith records no session-scoped allowed-use time, so its receipts cannot say what the session actually contained** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §4: the ARSC string set for the recording model includes a distinct 'Allowed Apps Time' measure and 'If use allowed app, back to recording screen 3rd tab' — time spent in permitted apps during a recording is tracked as its own quantity inside that recording, separate from the recording total. Monolith has no equivalent field: FocusSessionEntity (MonolithModels.kt:268-365) stores elapsedSeconds, phantomReachesBlocked and break/penalty counters but no allowed-app seconds, and the only per-app usage figure, BlockedAppEntity.todayUsageMinutes (MonolithModels.kt:238-239), is a whole-day UsageStats sync value in AppCatalogReconcile.kt:100-109, never a session delta. A session spent largely inside an OPEN reference app and a session spent entirely in Monolith therefore produce indistinguishable elapsed figures.
  - Fix: Stamp per-app foreground time at session start and end (or accumulate it in the shield loop for OPEN/PEEK apps) and store an allowedUseSeconds total on the session row, printed on the receipt alongside elapsed and deflections.
- **[HIGH] YPT arms each lock mode with exact alarms and self-guarding receivers; Monolith runs every routine off one inexact chain alarm** — YPT EVIDENCE.md §2/§3.3: the manifest declares both SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and USE_EXACT_ALARM, and each lock mode gets its own alarm receiver — blockapps.BlockAppsAlarmManager and hardmode.HardModeAlarmReceiver — whose observed log strings show state guards before any service start: 'onReceive: no active block, skip service start' and 'BlockAppsService is already running.' Monolith's manifest declares no exact-alarm permission at all, and its one-size chain alarm fires boundaries inexactly via alarmManager.setAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, boundaryMillis, intent) at RoutineScheduler.kt:44 (ReleaseRetryScheduler.kt:42 does the same), with a single generic RoutineAlarmReceiver for every routine.
  - Fix: Declare an exact-alarm permission, schedule routine boundaries exactly, and give scheduled blocking the YPT-shaped treatment: a dedicated alarm receiver per enforcement mode that checks for an active block and an already-running service before starting anything.
## Supplement: Zario head-to-head (from its actual APK)

**Evidence base:** static reverse engineering of Zario (io.zario) — see `apk-re/zario/EVIDENCE.md`. Static analysis only; the APK was never installed or run.

### Head-to-head losses

- **[CRITICAL] Zario's 'AI coach' does not exist as software in the app — it is a calibration pipeline plus onboarding videos; Monolith lacks even the calibration half** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.9: across 13,159 decompiled classes there is no LLM/chat SDK (no OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini client), no chat message model and no chat UI screen. The 'AI' assets are videos — res/raw/zario_ai_chat.mp4 (5,613,932 B) plus zario_ai_dark.mp4 / zario_ai_light.mp4 — played in the welcome flow (WelcomeScreenWithZarioAiModel).
