What actually personalises Zario is a pipeline: a 12-locale survey, then real UsageStats calibration (LoadingAppsScreen, TotalScreenTimeUsage, AppsUsageChoice), then projections stored as prefs (onboardingUsageYearlyUsageTime, onboardingSavedTimeExpectancy) that generate a per-user Personal Program from the backend (zario.app/api/v1). Monolith has no adjudicator (known) — but it also has none of the calibration inputs: it reads UsageStats only to enforce, never to build a per-user program, and its gates are compile-time constants identical for every user (PEEK_DURATION_SECONDS = 120, MonolithRepository.kt:106; (1 - spendCount) token, MonolithWeek.kt:41-42; requiredSeconds = 60, BlockitSuitcaseAndSwitchesViews.kt:534). Zario proves the market's 'AI coaching' claim reduces to calibration + a generated program — and Monolith is missing that cheaper, real thing, not the chatbot.
  - Fix: Build the calibration layer before any 'AI' claim: onboarding usage calibration and a stored per-user projection/program that the gates can actually read, instead of constants.
- **[HIGH] Zario's Circuit Breaker enforces a per-app daily opens budget, not a session: apps are locked by how many times you open them, counted forever** — Zario EVIDENCE §6.2/§7.1: Circuit Breaker state is an engaged flag plus expiry in SharedPrefUtil (setCircuitBreakerEngaged(engaged, expiryTimeMillis)), each controlled app carries a daily max-opens goal (getAppMaxOpensGoal, setAppDateAddedToCb so usage is measured since the app was added), and every interaction is written to a Room action log with enum CBActionType {OPEN, CLOSE, CONTINUE, LEAVE, EXTRA_OPEN}. There is no session to arm — the budget is simply always in force. Monolith's tiers (AppBlockTier LOCKED/PEEK_2M/OPEN) only bite while a session or routine window is active, and nothing in Monolith counts opens per app per day as an enforcement unit: its unit is minutes inside a sealed session. Zario's model catches the behaviour Monolith's model structurally cannot — twenty 'harmless' 30-second checks of a locked app across a day, no session running, each one logged and charged against a budget.
  - Fix: Add an opens-budget rule type alongside the tiers: per-app daily open counts enforced by the existing doors, with the count and its cost shown on the intercept.
- **[HIGH] Zario polices continuous use inside an already-open app (Scroll Stopper); Monolith only polices the doorway** — Zario EVIDENCE §6.1/§7.3: AppMonitorService.scrollStopper(app) fires when now exceeds lastRunningApp.timestamp + appScrollTimeLimitSecs — a per-app continuous-scroll time limit — and routes to Friction or ScrollStopper, counting continues and leaves per day (SCROLLSTOPPER_ALL_CONTINUES_COUNT, scrollStopperNumOfOpensLeftForDay). Monolith's enforcement is launch/window-change only: the accessibility door reacts to window events and the shield door polls the foreground package (MonolithShieldService.kt:193, delay(2000L); MonolithRepository.queryForegroundBlockedApp). Once an OPEN app is in front, no Monolith code measures how long the user has been continuously inside it — the only dwell limit in the app is the 120-second peek lease on the PEEK tier (MonolithRepository.kt:106). A user can scroll an allowed app for three hours mid-'focus' and Monolith has no trigger that can even notice.
  - Fix: Add a continuous-dwell trigger for OPEN-tier apps during sessions: elapsed-in-foreground per app as a first-class intercept condition, not just foreground identity.
- **[HIGH] Zario's enforcement verdict has exactly one author — one detector, one service, one decision tree; Monolith's verdict is split across three components that can disagree** — Zario EVIDENCE §6.1: CheckAppInForeground.execute() is the only detector (UsageStatsManager.queryUsageStats(INTERVAL_BEST_MATCH, now-10000ms, now), sort by lastTimeUsed, take [0]), and AppMonitorService is the only decider, with named decision methods checkIsInsideSchedule() / checkIsSnoozed() / checkIsInFocusTimer() dispatching to executeWhenIsFocusTimer / scrollStopper / openCircuitBreaker / openFrictionScreen. The FGS subtype string declares exactly this one job. Monolith reaches its verdict in three places: MonolithAccessibilityService (window events, Shorts/Reels, browser URL bars at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:382-386), MonolithShieldService's 2-second polling loop reading a tier-filtered blocked set and calling repository.queryForegroundBlockedApp, and the repository's own tier/peek/break filters inside that loop (MonolithShieldService.kt:170-190). Three components, two detection mechanisms, one verdict — each door can and does hold a different picture of what is blocked right now.
  - Fix: Collapse enforcement to one decision path: a single component should own detector + rules + intercept, with the other doors demoted to sensors feeding it.
- **[HIGH] Zario's Friction is a graded state machine with remotely tuned constants; Monolith's Airlock is one fixed wall with fixed numbers** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.2/§19: Friction is modelled as FrictionScreenState(mindfulPauseActive, mindfulPauseTime, screenAfterMindfulPause, frictionText) with five distinct variants — FrictionRegularWithAppLimit, FrictionRegularWithoutAppLimit, FrictionSessionLimit, FrictionLimitHit, LessFrictionScreen — chosen by why you were stopped. Its hardness is data, not code: Remote Config time_holding_locker_free_user=2 vs time_holding_locker_pro_user=5 (seconds of hold-to-unlock), and the CommitmentScreen hold is commitment_pressing_time_milliseconds=3000 with four phases {beforePressing, Pressing, AfterPressing, LastScreenAfterPressing}. Monolith's Airlock has one shape regardless of cause and every number is a hard-coded constant: 120-second peek (MonolithRepository.kt:106), 20-minute cooldown (MonolithRepository.kt:108), 60-second valve (BlockitSuitcaseAndSwitchesViews.kt:534) — no variant for limit-hit vs schedule vs session, and no constant can be tuned without a rebuild.
  - Fix: Model the Airlock as a state machine with a variant per stop-reason, and move its durations out of code into one tunable table.
- **[HIGH] Zario's escape valve is priced in earned XP and never disappears — it shows a price and an insufficient-balance state; Monolith's valve at zero tokens renders nothing** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.5/§9: pausing the whole blocker (Snooze / Reality Escape) costs XP at a stated exchange rate — dialogSnooze_earn_1x_snooze_with_every_100_xp — guarded by REALITY_ESCAPE_XP_THRESHOLD, with a dedicated not-enough state (dialogSnooze_not_enough_xp) and a remaining-time screen while snoozed (RETimeRemainingActivity, activity_reality_escape). The valve is always visible; being broke is a screen that tells you how to earn, not an absence. Monolith's emergency economy is a weekly mint of exactly one token — emergencyBreaksRemainingFromSpendCount = (1 - spendCount).coerceAtLeast(0) (MonolithWeek.kt:41-42) — which never accumulates, cannot be earned, and at zero the exit simply is not offered. Zario's gatekeeper is a priced state machine with a balance; Monolith's is a calendar with a dead end.
  - Fix: Make the emergency exit a priced, earnable balance with an explicit insufficient-balance state, instead of a one-per-week token that vanishes at zero.
- **[MEDIUM] Zario's pause contains a substitute activity — a 12-locale micro-challenge pack offered inside Friction; Monolith's Airlock offers two verbs and dead air** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.2/§7.8: MicroChallengesActivity is fed by res/raw/micro_challenges_<lang>.json for 12 locales, organised by life area (relationship, health, personal_growth, ~16–20 one-minute items each, e.g. 'Hydrate with a glass of water'), and analytics key Friction_clicked_microchallenges shows the challenges are offered inside the Friction pause itself as the alternative action. The pause is designed as substitution: do this instead. Monolith's Airlock (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt) offers exactly RETURN TO FOCUS or EMERGENCY PEEK and nothing to do with the seconds it imposes — the user waits out a numeral. Zario spends the pause; Monolith merely charges it.
  - Fix: Put a substitute action inside the Airlock: a rotating one-minute off-phone task drawn from a local content pack, so the imposed pause has something in it.

### Visual design

- **[MEDIUM] Zario renders its economy on the blocking surfaces themselves — an XP slider on every intercept; Monolith's intercept shows no stake at all** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.1/§9: the blocker surfaces carry the economy in their layouts — cb_xp_slider, screen_blocker_xp_slider, scrollStopper__xp_slider — and Circuit Breaker's state is drawn as an 'ampoule' (ampoule_cb_icon / ampoule.json), a vial that visually holds the blocker's charge. A user hitting a Zario intercept can see what opening costs and what leaving earns, on the surface itself. Monolith's Airlock and shield surfaces render a badge, a countdown numeral and two chips (AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt): no balance, no cost, no accumulated progress is drawn anywhere on the intercept — the token, the streak and the session's value live on other screens the user cannot see at the moment of decision.
  - Fix: Draw the stake on the intercept: token balance / session progress as a persistent element of the Airlock surface, not a fact stored on another screen.
- **[MEDIUM] Zario commissions illustration for failure as well as success — cb_goal_failed_illustration sits beside cb_goal_reached_illustration; Monolith's failures are outcome codes** — Zario EVIDENCE §7.1: the Circuit Breaker goal has two dedicated artwork states, cb_goal_reached_illustration and cb_goal_failed_illustration — breaking your goal gets its own drawn scene, not a red string. Monolith renders failure as a stamped code on the receipt (ELAPSED_SHIELD_GAP and siblings in ReceiptState) in the same mono type as success; no surface in the app draws a distinct visual state for a broken day versus a kept one. Design-wise Zario treats the failure moment as a moment; Monolith treats it as a log line.
  - Fix: Give the broken outcome its own visual state on the receipt — distinct art/weight for a breached session, not the same slip with a different code word.
- **[MEDIUM] Every Zario explainer video is produced in dark and light variants matched to the system theme; Monolith's permission primer is one fixed-palette text board** — Zario EVIDENCE §10/§17: the onboarding media set is doubled per theme — usage_permission_new_video and overlay_permission_new_video and the Zario-AI welcome all exist as *_dark.mp4 / *_light.mp4 pairs, so the film explaining a permission respects the phone's theme. Monolith explains its six special accesses with a single static board (GuardLine / FIX queue) in its own fixed tokens, unchanged by theme, with no motion or demonstration at all. The rival spends production effort exactly where users abandon — the permission ask — and Monolith spends none.
  - Fix: Produce the permission explanations as short themed demonstrations (or at minimum theme-matched illustrated cards) instead of one static board.

### Platform execution

- **[HIGH] Zario asks for two permissions in onboarding and defers the scary ones — Device Admin is an opt-in Strict Mode feature in Settings, not an onboarding toll** — Zario EVIDENCE §10/§6.3/§7.7: the onboarding PermissionsActivity asks Usage Access first, then Overlay, each behind its own PermissionCard with an explainer video; Device Admin, exact-alarm and battery requests do not appear in onboarding at all. Device Admin is requested later, optionally, as Strict Mode (StrictModeManager, StrictModeExplanationModal / StrictModeAlertModal in Settings). Monolith's guard board makes four special accesses the counted price of the core product from the first screen — WatchItemId COUNTED = ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN, NOTIFICATION_LISTENER (WatchStore.kt:80-99), with OVERLAY and BATTERY as two more board items — including the device-admin grant Zario treats as an advanced opt-in. Zario sequences trust: prove value with two grants, sell the invasive one later as a feature. Monolith invoices all of it up front.
  - Fix: Re-sequence the asks: core value on Usage Access + Accessibility alone, and move Device Admin out of the counted guard into an opt-in strict-mode feature.
- **[HIGH] Zario sustains always-on blocking with exactly ONE first-party service in its manifest; Monolith needs three services plus device admin to block only inside sessions** — Zario EVIDENCE §4.2: AppMonitorService is the only first-party service in the entire manifest — no accessibility service, no NotificationListenerService, no VpnService — and it alone sustains the always-on Circuit Breaker, Scroll Stopper, schedules and Focus Timer. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml declares three services (MonolithShieldService FGS, MonolithAccessibilityService, MonolithNotificationListener) plus a DeviceAdmin receiver, and the combined machinery still only enforces while a session or routine is live. The footprint contrast is the finding: one service, always on, versus four components, session-scoped.
  - Fix: Audit which of Monolith's components earn their manifest slot: if one monitor can carry schedules, timers and an always-on list, the three-service split needs a justification it currently doesn't have.
- **[MEDIUM] Zario ships an OEM-specific permission screen inside onboarding (XiaomiPermissionKt); Monolith's permission flow is OEM-blind in the flow itself** — Zario EVIDENCE §10: the permissions step includes a dedicated XiaomiPermissionKt screen — the ask is re-drawn for the OEM whose extra gates (MIUI autostart/background-pop-up) otherwise silently kill blockers. Monolith has no OEM-specific surface anywhere in its permission flow: the same FIX trips fire identical Settings intents on every vendor, so the Xiaomi/Oppo/Vivo user discovers the extra gate only when blocking silently fails later. Zario names the problem at the moment of the ask, per-vendor; Monolith's flow pretends AOSP is the only Android.
  - Fix: Add per-OEM permission screens for the major vendors (Xiaomi/Oppo/Vivo/Huawei) inside the ask flow, keyed off Build.MANUFACTURER.

### Comparative audit

- **[HIGH] Zario cannot touch notifications at all — no listener, no DND policy, nothing; Monolith's held-notification system, flawed as it is, has no counterpart in Zario** — Zario EVIDENCE §3/§6.4/§15/§21: the manifest has no notification-listener component or permission and no ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY; Zario does not silence, hold, read or batch other apps' notifications in any mode. During a Zario block, a locked app's notifications still arrive, buzz and offer a tap-path into the app. Monolith declares MonolithNotificationListener with BIND_NOTIFICATION_LISTENER_SERVICE (AndroidManifest.xml) and captures/holds notifications per session. The execution has known defects, but the capability itself — notification control as part of blocking — exists only on Monolith's side of this comparison.
  - Fix: No action — record as a genuine Monolith advantage; Zario's blocking is app-launch-deep only.
- **[HIGH] Zario blocks apps only — zero website blocking of any kind; Monolith ships a domain blocklist enforced inside browsers** — Zario EVIDENCE §16/§21: no URL/domain blocklist, no browser-filter classes, no VPN/DNS filtering anywhere in first-party code; its WebViewActivity serves Zario's own content (Canny, legal). A user can defeat a Zario lock by opening the same service in a browser and Zario has no opinion about it. Monolith ships BlockedSiteEntity (MonolithModels.kt:544) and enforces it by reading browser URL bars — detectBlockedBrowserUrl with per-browser view ids for Chrome, Brave and Firefox (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:382-386), matched via matchBlockedDomain (MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:67-68). The matcher is brittle substring matching (known), but the enforcement surface itself is one Zario never attempts.
  - Fix: No action — record as a genuine Monolith advantage; keep the site blocker, fix its matcher separately.
- **[HIGH] Only the APK shows what Zario's coach costs in data: usage records uploaded to a backend, two session-recording SDKs, and a server-style secret key embedded in BuildConfig; Monolith phones nothing home** — Zario EVIDENCE §12/§13/§14/§18: per-app usage is synced off-device (ZarioApiService POST appUsage/update/, driven periodically by UpdateBackendAlarmReceiver); the APK embeds UXCam (com.uxcam.service.HttpPostService) and Microsoft Clarity (assets/clarity.js) session-recording/replay, plus Facebook SDK, Amplitude and Firebase analytics; BuildConfig carries a static BEARER_KEY and — observed, value redacted in the evidence file — a server-style RevenueCat secret key (sk_…) compiled into the client. Monolith has no backend, no analytics or recording SDK, and allowBackup=false with full backup exclusion (AndroidManifest.xml): its usage data never leaves the phone. Zario's store page sells a coach; its APK ships a telemetry pipeline with a server credential in it.
  - Fix: No action — record as a genuine Monolith advantage (local-only is a defensible design position against this rival); do not copy Zario's sync/recording stack.
- **[MEDIUM] Monolith is two API levels more current and runs on five more Android generations: targetSdk 36 / minSdk 24 vs Zario's targetSdk 34 / minSdk 29** — Zario EVIDENCE §0: targetSdkVersion 34, minSdkVersion 29 (Android 10 floor). Monolith: targetSdk = 36, minSdk = 24 (app/build.gradle.kts:13-18). The shipping commercial rival is two target levels behind and refuses every device below Android 10, while Monolith carries Android 7–9 users Zario abandons. On platform currency — the axis Monolith usually loses — it is ahead of this rival on both ends.
  - Fix: No action — record as a genuine Monolith advantage; the minSdk-24 compat burden is at least buying reach this rival doesn't have.
- **[MEDIUM] Zario's shipped manifest is sloppier than Monolith's: an ungrantable privileged permission, QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, and a permission string that is actually a mis-declared application attribute** — Zario EVIDENCE §3: the manifest declares READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE (not grantable to a normal Play install — a leftover/OEM-channel declaration), QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, KILL_BACKGROUND_PROCESSES and GET_TASKS, and contains a malformed entry — 'android.requestLegacyExternalStorage' declared as a permission name when it is an application attribute. Dead legacy applock machinery (ServiceApplock / ReceiverApplock / BackgroundManager in com.zario.services, not manifest-declared) also ships in the DEX. Monolith scopes package visibility with a single LAUNCHER <queries> intent (AndroidManifest.xml) and declares none of these. For all Monolith's permission-count problems, its manifest does not ask for permissions it can never be granted or spell its own attributes into the permission list.
  - Fix: No action — record as a genuine Monolith advantage in manifest hygiene; Zario's footprint includes pure cruft.


#

### Second-pass findings — 5 findings (0 critical, 4 high, 1 medium, 0 low)

- **[HIGH] Zario's monitor is engineered to survive Recents swipes and task kills with four stacked resurrection paths; Monolith's shield has none of them** — Zario EVIDENCE.md §4.2/§4.3/§6.1: AppMonitorService is declared stopWithTask=false, the <application> sets excludeFromRecents=true, onStartCommand returns START_STICKY, onTaskRemoved calls RestartAppMonitor.restartAppMonitorService with DELAY_BEFORE_RESTART = 5000, a manifest receiver RestartServiceWhenStopped listens for a custom 'restart-service' action, an AlarmToCheckAppMonitor watchdog re-arms the check, AutoStartReceiver handles BOOT_COMPLETED + QUICKBOOT_POWERON, and the manifest declares REQUEST_COMPANION_RUN_IN_BACKGROUND and REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS (§3). Monolith's MonolithShieldService.kt contains no onTaskRemoved override at all — onDestroy (MonolithShieldService.kt:247-260) only cancels its coroutine scope and clears flags — its manifest declaration (AndroidManifest.xml:58-67) sets no stopWithTask, the application tag sets no excludeFromRecents, and the permission list (AndroidManifest.xml:5-14) declares neither the battery-exemption nor any companion-run permission.
  - Fix: Add the layered resurrection Zario ships: stopWithTask=false and excludeFromRecents on the shield, an onTaskRemoved restart path, a dedicated restart receiver plus a watchdog alarm independent of the session loop, and declare REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS / REQUEST_COMPANION_RUN_IN_BACKGROUND so the asks the app already makes are backed by the manifest.
- **[HIGH] Zario's device-admin policy file declares force-lock and disable-uninstall and is requested in-product for Strict Mode; Monolith's 'Uninstall Guard' admin declares only limit-password and never calls a single policy** — Zario EVIDENCE.md §4.3/§6.3/§7.7: res/xml/device_admin_sample.xml declares disable-keyguard-features, limit-password, force-lock and a <policy disable-uninstall="true"/> element; the AdminReceiver (BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN) backs a Strict Mode that is actually requested in-product via StrictModeManager, the 'STRICT_MODE - requestDeviceAdminPermission:' code path, and StrictModeExplanationModal/StrictModeAlertModal in Settings. Monolith's res/xml/device_admin_receiver.xml declares exactly one policy, <limit-password/>; MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver.kt:13-27 only returns a warning string from onDisableRequested and stamps WatchStore on enable/disable; and the app's sole DevicePolicyManager call anywhere is an isAdminActive() check at MonolithRepository.kt:707-716 — no lockNow(), no disable-uninstall policy — despite the manifest comment at AndroidManifest.xml:140 calling it a 'Kernel-Level Uninstall Guard'.
  - Fix: Either give the admin real policies — declare disable-uninstall and force-lock and wire a Strict-Mode-style in-product request flow with lockNow() as the hard floor when the intercept is escaped — or stop calling the receiver an uninstall guard; Zario shows the policy file and the request flow are both shippable in a consumer blocker.
- **[HIGH] Zario's friction screen changes form by stop-reason and logs every decision as a typed event; Monolith shows one badge-differentiated wall and logs free-text** — Zario APK (EVIDENCE.md §7.2, §6.2): the stop screen is a state machine keyed to why you were stopped — FrictionScreensMode with FrictionRegularWithAppLimit, FrictionRegularWithoutAppLimit, FrictionSessionLimit and FrictionLimitHit composables — and every outcome is written to a Room audit log as a typed CBAction with CBActionType {OPEN, CLOSE, CONTINUE, LEAVE, EXTRA_OPEN}, which feeds the Dashboard's TODAY/LAST7DAYS/LAST30DAYS/EVER per-app stats (§12). Monolith's intercept carries exactly one differentiator, the tier badge string (MonolithShieldService.kt:184-189: EXTRA_INTERCEPT_BADGE), its in-stop content varies only by app category via four canned coachingTip strings (MonolithModels.kt:198-218), and its InterceptLogEntity stores outcome and triggerReason as free-text strings with triggerReason defaulting to 'Habit' (MonolithModels.kt:451-460) — no typed taxonomy of what the user decided at the wall, and no screen that changes shape for limit-hit vs schedule vs session stops.
  - Fix: Give the intercept a reason parameter (limit hit, routine window, session lock, peek expiry) with a distinct layout per reason, and replace the free-text intercept outcome with a typed enum (left / peeked / token-spent / waited-out) that stats and receipts can aggregate.
- **[HIGH] Zario's permission step is resumable and explained per-permission after value is shown; Monolith's primer is dead code and its grant sequence has no resume state** — Zario EVIDENCE.md §10: PermissionsActivity is step 7 of a persisted funnel, after Welcome, survey, Digital Habits calibration, Projections and Personal Program, each permission carries its own explainer video assets (usage_permission_new_video*.mp4, permissions_usage_data_access_video_dark.mp4, overlay_permission_new_video_light/dark.mp4, lottie_usage_permission.json), and onboarding state is resumable via prefs isOnboardingCompleted and lastOnboardingScreen — so a user who leaves for a Settings grant and returns resumes at the same step. Monolith's equivalent explainer, ShieldPermissionPrimerModal at AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:472, is dead: MainActivity.kt:787 records its binding 'stays REMOVED', and no persisted onboarding/permission-step state exists to resume a half-finished grant sequence.
  - Fix: Restore a sequenced, persisted permission step: one permission per screen with a short explainer at the moment of the ask, store the current step, and resume returning users there instead of re-presenting an undifferentiated guard board.
- **[MEDIUM] Manifest count inverts real cost: Zario's 29 declared permissions hide only 2 special-access asks, Monolith's 7 hide 6** — Zario EVIDENCE.md §3: its manifest lists 29 permission strings, but most are normal/auto-granted or junk (INTERNET, WAKE_LOCK, CAMERA, legacy WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, even an ungrantable READ_PRIVILEGED_PHONE_STATE and a malformed android.requestLegacyExternalStorage pseudo-permission) and the 'Notably absent' list confirms no DND, notification-listener, accessibility or VPN special access — the real Settings-trip cost is two grants. Monolith's AndroidManifest.xml:6-14 declares only 7 permissions, yet WatchStore.kt:92-96 enumerates six special-access items (accessibility, usage, device admin, notification listener, overlay, battery), each a separate system Settings journey, and the battery exemption is not even among the 7 declared permissions.
  - Fix: Measure and budget user cost in Settings trips, not manifest lines: cut the special-access count toward Zario's two for the core promise, and declare every permission the app actually prompts for (including the battery exemption) so the manifest honestly reflects the ask.
## Supplement: Flipd head-to-head (from its actual APK)

**Evidence base:** static reverse engineering of Flipd v4.2.20, package com.flipd.app — see `apk-re/flipd/EVIDENCE.md`. Static analysis only; the APK was never installed or run.

### Head-to-head losses

- **[HIGH] Flipd's block is a bounce, not a wall: once a second it relaunches its own timer screen, and the blocked app stays one Recents tap away** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.1: FullLockService.overrideScreen() does exactly one thing when a non-whitelisted app is foreground — startActivity(FLPTimerActivity, FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK). There is no intercept surface at all: no overlay window over the blocked app, no reason prompt, no peek, no emergency negotiation at the moment of temptation; the user lands on Flipd's ordinary timer screen, and the blocked app remains fully usable between the 1-second ticks and one Recents tap behind the bounce. Monolith meets the same reach with a dedicated intercept surface — AirlockInterceptOverlay (app/src/main/java/com/example/ui/components/AirlockAndDisarmOverlays.kt:550) — that presents the session's stated intention and a priced peek/emergency economy before any access. Flipd's enforcement has no moment of decision in it; it is a recurring interruption, not a negotiation.
  - Fix: Keep the Airlock as the differentiator it is: the intercept is where Monolith's intention, peek lease and emergency token live. Do not copy Flipd's bounce model in any 'lite' mode — a block that is only a relaunch teaches users to live in the Recents screen.
- **[HIGH] Flipd's detection, countdown and enforcement are a single polling service — kill FullLockService and the lock, the timer and the watcher die together** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.1 and §4.6: one class, FullLockService (223 decompiled lines), owns everything — a CountDownTimer with timerInterval=1000 whose every tick both counts the session down and calls overrideScreen(), detecting foreground via UsageStatsManager.queryEvents(now-20_000, now) and taking only the last event's package. Detection, session clock and enforcement share one process, one service, one point of failure; the only resurrection path in the APK is RebootReceiver (§3.3), which restarts the lock at boot only if persisted CurrentTimer progress > 0 and focusLock is true — a mid-run death (force-stop, OEM battery killer) is never recovered. Monolith separates the doors: MonolithAccessibilityService (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:70) detects from the accessibility event stream while MonolithShieldService (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/MonolithShieldService.kt:30) independently owns the session. Flipd proves the single-stack version of this architecture is what a shipping product settled for — and its failure mode is total, silent unlock.
  - Fix: Treat Flipd as the cautionary floor, not a model: keep detection and session-keeping in separate components, and note that Flipd has no answer at all for mid-run service death — Monolith's watchdog story, whatever its flaws, is strictly more architecture than the rival ships.
- **[HIGH] In Flipd a session is born social: the timer object itself persists a group code, a live-room id and a live head-count** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.6 and §10: the persisted session state (CurrentTimer) carries groupCode, groupName, isLive, hasLiveRoom, liveSessionID and liveCount as first-class fields, and even saved presets (RemoteShortcut) carry isLive/liveText/liveCount — the home screen shows how many people are focusing on a preset before you start it, and joining a live room is one tap from a room grid (fragment_live_room.xml, /api/Users/LiveSession). Social presence is not a destination in Flipd; it is fields on the timer. Monolith's session record cannot represent another person at all: FocusSessionEntity (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:268) has intention, profileName, durations, HMAC and tamper fields — no user, no group, no room, no audience column exists anywhere in the schema. The gap is at the data-model level, not the UI level: bolting a 'groups' screen onto Monolith later still leaves a session object that was designed for exactly one human.
  - Fix: If any social layer is ever designed, it has to start where Flipd's did — in the session schema (group/room/audience fields written at seal time), not as a screen. Record this as the concrete implementation debt: Monolith's sealed-session model is single-player by construction.
- **[HIGH] A finished Flipd session is published, not filed: it uploads to a feed with comments, reactions and a privacy switch** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.6, §8 and §10: session state carries uploaded/waitingForUpload/discarded flags and sessions sync to Flipd's backend (71 inventoried /api endpoints), where a finished session becomes an activity-feed object — friends see it in FriendActivity/AllUserActivity, can comment (AddActivityComment) and react (ActivityReaction), the owner controls its audience (UpdateActivityPrivacy), and feed notifications report likes/comments/follows on your sessions (FLPFeedNotificationsActivity). A Flipd session's lifecycle ends in circulation. A Monolith session's lifecycle ends in a local receipt whose only action is dismissal (app/src/main/java/com/example/ui/components/ReceiptSheet.kt), filed in a drawer nobody else can ever see. Flipd gets retention from the fact that finishing a session is a social act with witnesses and replies; Monolith's identical effort produces a slip of paper in a locked drawer.
  - Fix: The transferable piece is not 'add a feed' — it is that Flipd treats the completed session as the unit of social currency, with audience control attached. Any future sharing in Monolith should attach to the receipt the same way: publishable object first, privacy switch on it, reactions possible.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's device admin requests literally zero policies — its onEnabled and onDisabled only show a Toast** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §3.3: FLPDeviceAdmin's meta-data policy file is empty — <device-admin><uses-policies/></device-admin> — and the decompiled receiver overrides only onEnabled/onDisabled, each showing a Toast ('Admin enabled'/'Admin disabled'). No lockNow, no password policy, no uninstall policy exists in code or XML; the admin grant enforces nothing whatsoever and functions purely as an extra scary step in the uninstall flow. Monolith's device admin (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:122, MonolithDeviceAdminReceiver) at least declares a policy and is wired into its guard/watch bookkeeping. The honest verdict cuts at Flipd: this is the emptiest possible version of the device-admin theatre — a permission-shaped prop with zero machinery behind it.
  - Fix: Do not imitate: if Monolith keeps a device-admin presence, it should keep at least the pretence of a function. Flipd's empty-policy admin is evidence that users will grant admin rights for literally nothing — which is an argument for Monolith asking only for grants that do work.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd users have checkable public identities — unique username, avatar, study areas — that sessions attach to; Monolith has no user object at all** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §5, §10 and §12: profile setup walks username (with a server uniqueness check, /api/Users/CheckUsernameUnique, plus GetAutoUsername), academic level, areas of study (dedicated DB schemas AreasOfStudy.sq/AreasOfStudyCategory.sq), location and avatar/avatar-colour pickers — every session, group membership and leaderboard row hangs off that public identity. Monolith's data layer (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt) contains entities for tasks, apps, sessions, routines, sites, day notes and guard settings — and nothing that represents the person using it: no name, no profile, no identity the app itself could address. Flipd's accountability features are all downstream of this one modelling decision; Monolith cannot even greet its user, let alone let anyone else find them.
  - Fix: Note the ordering Flipd proves: identity precedes social. A minimal local profile object (name, avatar) is the cheapest first step and is a precondition for every group/room/leaderboard feature the category runs on.

### Visual design

- **[HIGH] Flipd's lock screen and home screen are server-rendered templates — the APK ships shells, not designs** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §5: the two most-seen surfaces in the product are formatted remotely — the lock screen's content comes from /api/ScreenFormat/LockScreenContent and the home screen from /api/ScreenFormat/HomescreenV2. Flipd's team can reword, reorder or redesign the screen a locked-in user stares at without shipping an app update; the local layouts are containers for server decisions. Monolith cannot do this even in principle: it declares no INTERNET permission (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml declares 7 permissions, none of them INTERNET) and every surface is a hard-coded composable, so a single bad line of copy on its intercept requires a full rebuild and reinstall to fix. The honest reverse: Flipd's lock screen is network-dependent design — Monolith's surfaces work in a tunnel, forever, exactly as sealed. But as design infrastructure, Flipd can iterate on its most important screen daily and Monolith cannot iterate on its own at all.
  - Fix: Monolith does not need server UI — it needs the lesson: the intercept/lock surface's copy and ordering should be data (a local format table), not literals buried in composables, so the highest-stakes screen is the easiest one to revise.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's design system is rented — stock DayNight theme, one Material tonal ladder, two commodity fonts — and it still follows the OS, which Monolith's bespoke system refuses to do** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §15: Theme.Flipd's parent is Theme.MaterialComponents.DayNight.DarkActionBar with values-night/color-night/drawable-night resources — dark mode simply follows the system. The brand palette is a five-step Material tonal ladder of a single blue (primary30 #193ca7 through primary90 #dce1ff), and type is Lato + Spectral, two off-the-shelf Google Fonts families. There is almost no original design system here — and every screen inherits OS dark mode, a consistent tonal scale and a coherent serif/sans pairing for free. Monolith hand-built its entire token system instead (app/src/main/java/com/example/ui/theme/Theme.kt:17,42 — two hand-rolled schemes) and still imposes its session-driven night rather than the system's. Flipd demonstrates the uncomfortable trade: a rented system with zero originality beats a bespoke system on the basics users actually notice, starting with 'dark when the phone is dark'.
  - Fix: Steal the boring part: follow the system DayNight by default. Monolith's bespoke palette is only worth its cost if the fundamentals a stock theme gives Flipd for free — system dark mode, one tonal ladder — are matched first.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's resource tree pretends to be translated: ~90 locale folders, 342 strings each, zero of them Flipd's** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §15: the APK carries ~90 values-<locale> resource directories with hundreds of strings each (342 in es/de/fr/ja) — but they are library strings only; not one Flipd-specific key (full_lock_*, premium_benefit*, or any product copy) exists in any of them. Flipd's own UI is English-only behind a resource tree that looks, at a glance, like a 90-language localisation effort. This is design-resource dishonesty only an APK read can catch: the artefact advertises international polish it does not contain. Monolith ships no locale scaffolding at all — its English-only state is at least honestly visible in its resource tree.
  - Fix: No action for Monolith beyond a principle worth keeping: do not let library-generated resource bulk impersonate product work. If localisation ever ships, it should be measurable in product strings, not folder counts.

### Platform execution

- **[HIGH] Flipd asks for its special accesses only inside Focus Lock setup — the rest of the app, timers and social included, runs with none** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.1, §4.5 and §11: onboarding is intro pager → login → profile setup → main, with no permission gauntlet; usage access, overlay and DND policy access are demanded just-in-time when the user first starts a Focus Lock, each behind its own rationale string (full_lock_access_required_text, full_lock_overlay_required_text) plus a fallback string explaining manual Settings navigation (full_lock_no_settings). The entire timer/social/stats product is usable with zero special access — the permissions are gated on the one feature that needs them. Monolith inverts this: its manifest wires an accessibility service (app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:66), a notification listener (:82), a device admin (:122), a special-use foreground shield service (:54) and PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS (:13) into a guard board that must be satisfied before the product delivers value. Flipd's footprint per feature is the discipline: three grants, asked at the point of use, for one feature — everything else asks for nothing.
  - Fix: Copy the gating shape, not the features: any Monolith capability that works without special access should be reachable without it, and each remaining grant should be asked inside the flow that spends it, with Flipd-style rationale copy and a manual-path fallback.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's app-enumeration permission is a typo: declared without the android.permission. prefix, it names a permission that does not exist** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §2: the manifest declares the literal string QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES with no android.permission. prefix, which Android resolves as com.flipd.app.QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES — a permission that does not exist and grants nothing; the whitelist picker's actual enumeration rides on the <queries> intent declarations sitting next to it. A shipping release's manifest contains a dead permission line its own authors never noticed, because the feature kept working through the other mechanism. Monolith's manifest is overreaching in places, but every permission it declares is at least a real one that does what it says. Only a manifest-level read catches this class of defect — store listings and feature comparisons never would.
  - Fix: Worth a one-line audit habit for Monolith: diff declared permissions against what the platform actually grants. Flipd proves even a mature, popular app ships silently dead declarations for years.
- **[MEDIUM] Only 2,079 of Flipd's 19,261 classes are Flipd's — and several of its 23 permissions serve SDKs, not focus** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §0, §2 and §14: 19,261 DEX classes, 2,079 of them com.flipd.*; Intercom alone contributes 1,830 classes and 13 of the 49 manifest activities, RevenueCat 1,177 classes, Firebase 533. The permission list carries the same rent: AD_ID and the install-referrer binding exist for attribution, ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION has no identified core feature, and READ_PHONE_STATE has no identified use at all in the decompiled app code (both marked unknown-purpose in the evidence). Flipd's platform footprint is mostly other companies' machinery, and part of its scary-permission surface is rented too. Monolith ships zero third-party SDKs — every component in its manifest is its own — so its footprint, whatever else is wrong with it, is entirely product. The contrast matters for trust: Flipd asks for location and phone state on behalf of vendors; Monolith's asks, however numerous, are at least for itself.
  - Fix: Keep Monolith's zero-SDK property as a stated constraint in any future feature work: Flipd shows the end-state of the alternative — a focus app whose binary and permission list mostly belong to Intercom, RevenueCat and attribution vendors.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's release build ships its own scaffolding: a debugger wait inside the lock service, an exported preview activity, test link hosts, debug logging left on** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §0, §3.1, §4.1 and §13: FullLockService.onCreate() contains if (Debug.isDebuggerConnected()) Debug.waitForDebugger(); — the enforcement service itself will stall for a debugger in production. The manifest exports a Jetpack Compose PreviewActivity (a development surface, exported=true) and auto-verifies App Links for test hosts flipd.test-app.link and flipd-alternate.test-app.link alongside the production domains, with Branch live AND test keys in manifest meta-data. RevenueCat is configured with setDebugLogsEnabled(true) in the release build. Any one of these is a leftover; together they show a release pipeline with no pre-ship artefact review. Monolith's shipped artefacts have their own template junk, but nothing in its manifest exports a dev surface or waits for a debugger inside its shield.
  - Fix: A concrete checklist item for Monolith's first real release: grep the built APK's manifest for exported non-launcher components and test hosts, and grep the DEX for waitForDebugger/debug-log flags. Flipd is the proof that 'popular and shipping' does not mean anyone did this.

### Comparative audit

- **[HIGH] Flipd's record is a diary, not evidence: sessions can be added by hand and edited after the fact — and its leaderboards rank exactly that** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §5 and §13: Flipd ships FLPAddTimeActivity (manual session entry) and FLPEditSessionActivity (edit/delete past sessions) — post-hoc session editing is so central it is literally premium benefit #5, 'Add, edit, and delete sessions'. Three of its four timer types (time-block, stopwatch, Pomodoro) block nothing at all; they are self-reported timers. So the raw material of Flipd's streaks, stats and group leaderboards (§7, §10) is time the user declares, can invent retroactively, and can rewrite — the leaderboard ranks honour-system data. Monolith's session is the opposite construction: sealed at arm time and HMAC-signed (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/CryptoIntegrityManager.kt:53 signSessionState), with shield-gap and tamper state latched into the record (FocusSessionEntity, app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:268) and no edit path in the product. Whatever Monolith's record-keeping lacks in circulation, it is the only one of the two that could survive being doubted.
  - Fix: Hold this line in any social future: if Monolith ever ranks or shares sessions, the sealed, uneditable record is its credibility advantage over Flipd's editable diary. Do not add manual session entry or post-hoc editing to chase parity with Flipd's stats — it would spend the one property that makes Monolith's numbers mean more.
- **[HIGH] Flipd has no website blocking at all — no VPN, no DNS, no URL machinery anywhere in the DEX; a browser is just another bounced app** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.3 and §16 (checked-and-absent inventory): no VpnService, no DNS filtering, no browser interception, no URL/domain strings or blocklist anywhere in DEX or resources. In a Focus Lock, Chrome is simply a non-whitelisted package that gets bounced like a game — Flipd cannot express 'YouTube blocked, docs allowed', cannot see a single URL, and offers zero granularity inside the browser where a large share of distraction actually happens. Monolith ships a real per-domain site blocker: user rules are persisted as BlockedSiteEntity (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:543) and enforced against the browser's actual URL via its accessibility door (MonolithAccessibilityService, app/src/main/java/com/example/service/MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:70). Monolith's matcher has known flaws, but the capability class exists in its code and is provably absent — not paywalled, not hidden, absent — from Flipd's.
  - Fix: Count website blocking as a genuine Monolith lead over Flipd, not a commodity feature: a social timer with a bounce is competing in a different enforcement league. Parity pressure should run the other way — Flipd would need a VPN or accessibility layer it has never shipped to match this.
- **[HIGH] Flipd cannot start a lock by the clock: its 'shortcuts' are saved presets with at most one reminder each, and there is no schedule engine anywhere** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §6: what Flipd calls shortcuts are saved timer presets on the home screen (RemoteShortcut: duration, tag, theme, isLive) — not launcher shortcuts and not schedules. Each can carry at most one reminder (a single reminder table row, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM). Beyond that there is nothing: no schedule tables, no recurring windows, no day masks, and no WorkManager/JobScheduler usage of Flipd's own (the JobScheduler references in the DEX belong to Firebase data-transport). A Flipd lock can only ever be started by a human tap or resumed after reboot. Monolith has a full routine engine: RoutineEntity (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:550) with start/end minutes, daysMask, loadout binding, pause-until and edit-horizon, fired by its own scheduler/alarm chain — recurring, unattended, judged afterwards. On automation, the comparison is not close: Flipd has a reminder; Monolith has a timetable.
  - Fix: Routines are a structural Monolith advantage worth protecting in prioritisation: Flipd's preset-plus-reminder is what a focus app ships when it has no scheduler, and its users must re-decide to focus every single day. Monolith's routine engine, for all its audited flaws, removes that daily decision.
- **[HIGH] Flipd's lock can never be total: ~90 packages are hard-coded always-allowed — Spotify, Uber and payment apps included — whatever the user wants** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.2: FullLockService.allowedApps is a hard-coded static list of roughly 90 package names that always pass during Focus Lock, and it is not a safety floor — alongside dialers and keyboards it permanently exempts Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal, SoundCloud, Uber and Uber Driver, Lyft, Paytm and Google Pay (India), Outlook and Teams. A Flipd user who knows music or ride-hailing is their escape route cannot lock those apps at any price; the exemption is the vendor's choice, compiled in. Worse, the user's own whitelist is consulted as isWhitelisted(pkg, premiumFlag) with the flag derived from RevenueCat customer info in the tick path (§4.1) — even the custom list is entangled with subscription state. Monolith's tiers are the opposite philosophy: every installed app carries a user-set LOCKED/PEEK/OPEN rule (blocked_apps, app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:231) and no content app is exempt by vendor decree. Flipd's lock has a ceiling on how locked it can be; Monolith's does not.
  - Fix: User sovereignty over the rule set is a real Monolith strength — keep exemptions limited to genuine system functions, and never let a vendor-curated allowlist of content apps into the enforcement path. If a safety floor is added, it should be user-visible and user-editable, the two things Flipd's is not.


#

### Second-pass findings — 7 findings (0 critical, 4 high, 3 medium, 0 low)

- **[HIGH] Monolith's fallback door reads daily-aggregate lastTimeUsed with an 8-second cutoff; Flipd's reads the real UsageEvents stream on a 20-second window every 1 second** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.1: FullLockService ticks every 1000 ms and calls getRecentActivity(), which runs UsageStatsManager.queryEvents(now-20_000 ms, now), filters through isEventActive(UsageEvents.Event) and returns the last event's package name — typed foreground events on a 20 s window at 1 s cadence. Monolith's shield door never reads events at all: MonolithRepository.kt:564-578 queryForegroundBlockedApp() calls queryUsageStats(INTERVAL_DAILY, start, end) and filters to packages whose lastTimeUsed >= (end - 8_000L), taking maxByOrNull { lastTimeUsed }, and MonolithShieldService.kt:193 polls that only every delay(2000L). A blocked app opened and settled into use has a lastTimeUsed older than 8 s, so the shield door — the only door left when accessibility is off, dead or revoked — goes blind to it for the rest of its stay, while the service's protecting witness (MonolithShieldService.kt:160-166) still certifies the session as protected.
  - Fix: Replace the shield door's queryUsageStats/lastTimeUsed guess with UsageStatsManager.queryEvents on a look-back window (the rival's mechanism), drop the 8-second recency cutoff, and shorten the poll to ~1 s; until then, stop letting the shield's protecting witness certify a session it cannot actually see into.
- **[HIGH] Flipd keeps the lock up during a call by allowlisting the telecom packages; Monolith suspends every door — including its uninstall guard — for the whole call** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.1-4.2: the exemption is per-package inside the blocking check — overrideScreen() bounces a foreground package only if isWhitelisted(pkg) is false, and the dialer/incallui/telecom packages are on the built-in allowlist, so during a call the lock stays up for every other app. Monolith exempts by global audio state in both doors: MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:190 returns from onAccessibilityEvent entirely when isCallActive() (AudioManager MODE_RINGTONE/MODE_IN_CALL/MODE_IN_COMMUNICATION, defined at :297) — before the Settings/installer guard, the Shorts/Reels sniper, the site blocker and the per-app check all run — and the shield door does the same at MonolithRepository.kt:566, where queryForegroundBlockedApp() returns null whenever isPhoneOrVoipCallActive(). Any ringing or in-progress WhatsApp/Telegram/cellular call is therefore a complete enforcement holiday, including for the uninstall guard, for as long as the call lasts.
  - Fix: Move the call exemption from a global AudioManager early-return to a per-package exemption evaluated inside each door's block decision (exempt the dialer/incall/telecom packages and the call's own app, as Flipd's allowlist does), so the Settings guard, sniper, site blocker and app tiers keep enforcing while a call is in progress.
- **[HIGH] Flipd's timer and its lock are two separate, per-session choices; Monolith fuses them — every session is a maximum-enforcement lock** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4/§4.6/§18: plain time-block, stopwatch and Pomodoro sessions 'block nothing — they are self-reported timers that record time'; blocking exists only in Focus Lock mode, toggled per session at FLPFocusSetupActivity, and the choice is persisted on the running session itself as CurrentTimer.focusLock — RebootReceiver (§3.3) resumes a lock after reboot only if getCurrentProgress() > 0 AND getFocusLock() is true, so a non-lock timer never resurrects as a lock. Monolith has no such flag anywhere: FocusSessionEntity (app/src/main/java/com/example/data/MonolithModels.kt:267) carries isStopwatchMode, totalStudyBlocks and routine fields but no lock/blocking toggle; startSession (MonolithRepository.kt:1321-1329) takes only intention/profileName/durationMinutes/studyBlocksCount/routineId, and every seal unconditionally starts the shield (SessionSealTransition.kt:242, MonolithShieldService.startShield).
  - Fix: Add a persisted per-session lock flag (default off for a first/manual timer) so a session can be a pure logged timer — counting toward history and totals with no shield — and make shield start, reboot resume and receipt judgement all read that flag instead of assuming every session row is a blocking session.
- **[HIGH] Flipd sessions start from saved user-authored recipes (duration + goal + tag + reminder + lock variant); Monolith has no session-recipe object at all** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §6/§5: 'shortcuts' are user-authored saved session recipes stored in a SQLDelight shortcut table (with a goal INTEGER column) and synced via /api/CreateShortcut|EditShortcut|DeleteShortcut|RearrangeShortcuts; each RemoteShortcut carries duration, goal, isStopwatch, tag, themeName, isLive/liveText/liveCount and its own RemoteReminder (reminder table, reminderEnabled, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM), and the home screen renders distinct rows including list_item_focus_lock_shortcut.xml — one tap replays the whole recipe, lock included. Monolith's nearest objects cannot hold a recipe: StudyModePreset is a 4-entry compile-time enum (MonolithModels.kt:61-72), and selecting one only copies workMinutes and defaultBlocks into the dial (MonolithViewModel.kt:1459-1464) — its breakMinutes are never even read; FocusProfileEntity (MonolithModels.kt:251-265) has name/defaultMinutes/blockedCategoriesCsv/schedule fields but no goal, tag, reminder or lock-variant field, and no user-authored preset object exists in the schema at all.
  - Fix: Introduce a persisted user-authored session-preset entity carrying duration/mode, block count, loadout, goal minutes, tag and an optional reminder, rendered as one-tap rows on the Deck; let startSession consume a preset id so repeat sessions stop requiring a full wheel-and-blocks re-specification every time.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's lock has a compiled-in ~90-package floor (keyboards, telecom stack, payments, ride-hailing) that no session can override; Monolith's tier economy has no floor at all** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §4.2: FullLockService.allowedApps is a hard-coded static list of ~90 packages always allowed during Focus Lock — dialer/contacts/incallui/telecom stacks, SMS apps, calendars, cameras, notes, calculators, clocks, Google Maps, Uber/Lyft, and payment apps (Paytm family, Google Pay India) — plus a separate 3-entry keyboardPackageNames list (Gboard, Samsung IME, SwiftKey), so typing inside an allowed app and paying/getting a ride home can never be locked away in any session. Monolith has no floor in either door: every catalogued package passes through the tier economy, and the strictest preset, applySmartLoadout's SLEEP branch (MonolithRepository.kt:1152-1164), LOCKs everything whose package/name does not contain the substrings dialer/phone/clock/alarm/maps — payment apps, ride-hailing, camera and messaging included, with no per-session way to recover them except ending or rewriting the loadout.
  - Fix: Add a compiled-in, non-editable always-allowed floor in both enforcement doors for input methods, the telecom/incall stack, and payment/ride-hailing packages, checked before the tier lookup — the categories Flipd's list proves users need mid-lock — instead of letting a substring loadout decide whether the user can type, pay or get home.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd models multitasking as a declared, counted session mode; Monolith can only record cross-task movement as deflections** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §5/§4.6: sessions can be flagged as multitasking work — a multitask_label/multitask_button in the timer UI, persisted on CurrentTimer as isMultitasking plus a multitaskingCount — so a session that legitimately rotates between tasks/apps is recorded as that kind of session and counted as such. Monolith's code contains zero occurrences of 'multitask' (grep over app/src/main/java returns nothing): FocusSessionEntity bonds a session to a single task (taskId, MonolithModels.kt:323, plus FocusTaskEntity.startedAtSessionElapsedSec), and the only counters for leaving the bonded task/app are punitive ones — phantomReachesBlocked (MonolithModels.kt:298) and InterceptLogEntity rows recording deflections. Rotation between two legitimate tasks or reference apps can only ever be written into Monolith's record as urges stopped, never as a declared mode of working.
  - Fix: Add a declared multitasking mode to the session row (flag + rotation count): when set, movement between the session's bonded tasks and OPEN/PEEK apps is recorded as multitasking rather than as phantom reaches/intercepts, so receipts and history can represent split-focus work honestly instead of scoring it as resistance.
- **[MEDIUM] Flipd's reboot footprint is one receiver with one condition; Monolith wakes on six system actions, pre-unlock, and runs a full reconcile on a clock change** — Flipd EVIDENCE.md §3.3: its only boot component is RebootReceiver (BOOT_COMPLETED, priority 100), and decompiled behaviour restarts the lock only if CurrentTimer.getCurrentProgress() > 0 && CurrentTimer.getFocusLock() — no persisted lock, no work, and no other actions are registered; nothing in Flipd's manifest is directBootAware. Monolith's MonolithBootReceiver is registered for six actions (AndroidManifest.xml, receiver block: LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, BOOT_COMPLETED, QUICKBOOT_POWERON, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, TIME_SET, TIMEZONE_CHANGED) with android:directBootAware="true" — a flag also set on MainActivity, the shield service, the accessibility service, the notification listener and both other receivers. MonolithBootReceiver.kt:27-58 runs a forced RoutineHeartbeat.tick plus database access and a possible shield restart on every boot/package-replace, and MonolithBootReceiver.kt:60-73 runs another forced full tick merely because the user changed the clock or timezone. Every Monolith install pays cold-start, pre-unlock background work for events Flipd proves a focus app can simply ignore.
  - Fix: Cut the wake surface to Flipd's shape: act on BOOT_COMPLETED only when a persisted active session or armed routine actually exists, drop directBootAware from components that have no pre-unlock job, and handle TIME_SET/TIMEZONE_CHANGED lazily at next natural tick instead of forcing a full reconcile from a broadcast receiver.
## Supplement: Freedom head-to-head (from its actual APK)

**Evidence base:** static reverse engineering of Freedom (to.freedom.android2) — see `apk-re/freedom/EVIDENCE.md`. Static analysis only; the APK was never installed or run.

### Head-to-head losses

- **[CRITICAL] Freedom sessions start and stop remotely — the Android app is an endpoint of an account session system; Monolith's sessions exist only on the phone that created them** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §10: its device-admin description string states the design outright — 'Ensures Freedom runs in the background, allowing sessions to start and stop remotely.' The native layer is built as a stateless executor for that system: SessionInfo holds a stub state and SessionForegroundService aborts with 'the properties are not configured by Flutter. Abort' until the app layer pushes a session (§6.1, §8.2); a scheduled start is delivered by UpdateSessionStatusWorker firing a forced updateSessionStatus event at startAtMillis so the account-side schedule can arm the phone (§10); sign-in on Android is Google SSO and even Apple SSO via a WebView flow (§15.1) — because the session belongs to the account, not the handset. Monolith has no account, no remote arm, no endpoint model: RoutineEntity (MonolithModels.kt:550) and the on-device RoutineScheduler (RoutineScheduler.kt:23) mean a session or routine can only be created, edited or started on the phone itself, by hand, in the app. A user who leaves their phone in another room — the canonical focus scenario — can start a Freedom session from their laptop; in Monolith there is no 'from anywhere else' at all.
  - Fix: Decide whether Monolith sessions are phone-local by design or by default. If by default, the first step is the executor split Freedom already has: session state as a self-contained pushed configuration (apps/sites/end/break) that a local scheduler is only one possible source of.
- **[HIGH] Freedom learns how to block a new browser on-device; Monolith's browser/surface knowledge is compiled in and can only change with an app update** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §7.6: the accessibility service contains a 1,577-line WindowExplorer — while a session is active it walks a target app's full accessibility tree (vibrating as it goes as a progress haptic), produces a Report of node/view-id/URL-extraction paths, saves it AES-encrypted, sends it to the app layer as an explorationEvent, and — critically — merges any discovered scanBrowserOptions into the persisted local scan config (LocalScanOptionsManager.mergeExplorationOptions → internal.default/localBrowserScanOptions) and applies them to WebScanner immediately. Blocking knowledge is therefore self-healing data that improves on the device. Monolith has no learning path at all: the browsers and surfaces it can police are literal constants compiled into MonolithAccessibilityService.kt — the shorts/reels view-id list at :335-343 (five hard-coded YouTube/Instagram resource ids) and the urlBarViewIds loop at :390. When YouTube renames a view id or a user runs an unlisted browser, Monolith's enforcement silently stops working until a developer edits Kotlin, ships an update, and the user installs it; Freedom's equivalent fix is a scan-config merge that happens on the phone.
  - Fix: Move Monolith's browser/surface rules out of Kotlin constants into a persisted, updatable rule store (per-browser URL-bar extraction rules, per-app surface view-ids), and add a diagnostic walk that can discover and persist a working extraction rule for an unknown browser instead of silently not blocking it.
- **[HIGH] Freedom blocks surfaces inside other apps from runtime-supplied view-id rules; Monolith's only in-app surface blocking is a hard-coded list for exactly two packages** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §7.4: AppScanner deserialises scannedAppsJson into AppScanSettings keyed by provider package — if the foreground app is a provider app and any listed viewId is present in its window while the target app is in the session's block set, the surface is blocked (AppSuccess) without blocking the host app. The rules arrive as JSON from the app layer at session-configure time, so the set of blockable in-app surfaces is data, not code. Monolith's entire in-app surface enforcement is MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:112-115 (shortsSniperArmed gates on exactly two package names, com.google.android.youtube and com.instagram.android) plus the five literal resource ids at :335-343 and text/desc matching for 'shorts'/'reels' at :355-357. There is no rule model: no third app can ever get a surface rule, no surface other than short-video feeds can be targeted, and every rule change is a code change. Freedom treats 'block the feed, not the app' as a general mechanism; Monolith treats it as one hand-built exception for two apps.
  - Fix: Generalise the sniper into a data-driven surface-rule model (provider package + view-id set + action) stored in Room and editable/extensible without code changes, starting with the existing YouTube/Instagram rules expressed as data.
- **[HIGH] A separate companion app can read and rewrite Freedom's configuration through a signature-permission provider; nothing outside Monolith can impose or audit its configuration** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §16 and §3: the manifest requests the signature-level permission to.freedom.freedomCompanion.permission.OVERRIDES and queries provider to.freedom.freedomCompanion.overrides; a dedicated MethodChannel (freedom/companion_config) implements readOverrides and writeOverrides against content://to.freedom.freedomCompanion.overrides/document — a whole second app exists whose job is to impose configuration on the blocker from outside it. That is an external control plane: the person being blocked and the person holding the configuration can be different people, enforced by Android's signature permission model. Monolith's manifest (read in full) declares no provider, no override permission and no companion channel of any kind — every rule in Monolith is settable only from inside Monolith, by the same hands the rules are meant to restrain, and no second device or person can hold, impose or even inspect the configuration.
  - Fix: If Monolith ever serves a second person (parent, partner, coach), copy the mechanism, not just the idea: a signature-permission content-provider override document is how Freedom makes external control tamper-resistant on stock Android.
- **[MEDIUM] Freedom's detector reports its own health (first/last node, last block, slow-scan warning); Monolith's detector has no health surface at all** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §6.4 and §17: the native availability contract (BlockingEngineState) carries a debugInfo built from SessionInfo.collectDebugInfo() — foreground-service status plus a scanning status report with enabled / first-node / last-node / last-block / last-block-success timestamps, and the scanner itself flags a health failure when node checking exceeds 100 ms ('Node checking is Too long'). Detector liveness is a designed, queryable product surface. Monolith's detection is a delay(2000L) loop in MonolithShieldService.kt:193 fed by UsageStatsManager queries (MonolithRepository.kt:534-538) with no equivalent: nothing in the app records when the detector last saw a window, last blocked anything, or whether its scans are running at all, so a dead detector and a healthy one present identically to the user.
  - Fix: Record and expose detector-health facts (last scan tick, last foreground observation, last successful block) from the shield/accessibility path, and surface a stale-detector state in the guard line instead of letting a silent detector impersonate a working one.

### Visual design

- **[HIGH] Freedom ships five purpose-built icon fonts as one icon system; Monolith has no icon system at all — zero Icon composables in the entire UI** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §21: its Flutter FontManifest ships five bespoke icon fonts in the core package — 'Device Icons', 'Navigation Icons', 'Onboarding Icons', 'Social Icons' and 'Practical Icons' — so every surface (devices, navigation, onboarding, social, utilities) draws glyphs from a single designed iconography with consistent stroke and metaphor. Monolith: a grep for 'Icon(' across the whole app/src/main/java/com/example/ui tree returns 0 matches, and res/drawable contains nothing but ic_launcher_background.xml and ic_launcher_foreground.xml. There is no icon font, no vector-drawable set, no Material Icons usage — every glyph-like mark in the interface is a text character or a hand-drawn Canvas shape inside individual components, so iconography is whatever each screen improvised. Freedom's icons are a system; Monolith's are punctuation.
  - Fix: Adopt one icon vocabulary (a single icon font or a curated vector set) and route every glyph in the UI through it, replacing per-component text characters and one-off Canvas drawings.

### Platform execution

- **[HIGH] Freedom offers the accessibility button/shortcut as a second activation path for its service; Monolith has no shortcut integration of any kind** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §18: among its nine native permission managers sits AccessibilityShortcutManager, which reads and writes the secure settings accessibility_shortcut_target_service and accessibility_button_targets and deep-links to Accessibility Settings — Freedom can be bound to the system's accessibility shortcut/button, giving the user a system-level gesture to summon or toggle the service and giving setup a second route when the standard toggle path is awkward. Monolith: a case-insensitive grep for 'shortcut' across all of app/src/main/java, app/src/main/res and AndroidManifest.xml returns zero matches. The accessibility service can only ever be reached through the standard Settings toggle, and once bound there is no system gesture associated with it at all. Freedom treats the platform's shortcut surface as part of the product; Monolith doesn't know it exists.
  - Fix: Register Monolith's accessibility service as an accessibility-shortcut/button target so the service has a system-level activation path besides the Settings toggle.
- **[HIGH] When a permission goes missing mid-session, Freedom's session notification becomes the repair tool — Monolith's shield notification can only state a title** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §8.2 and §6.4: Freedom computes a native availability state from six permission managers — active, disabled (only when Accessibility is missing), restricted (anything else missing) — and when permissions are missing, its persistent session notification (id 51) gains a big-text warning plus action buttons labelled 'Enable blocking' / 'Block notifications' that deep-link to exactly the right settings screen via getActionForMissingPermission. The one surface a user can always reach — the ongoing notification — is the recovery path. Monolith's shield notification is built at MonolithShieldService.kt:223-225 with a content title and text and no actions anywhere in the service (no addAction call exists in the file): it can announce a session but cannot fix anything, so a permission revoked or lost mid-session leaves the user to hunt through the app's own guard screens while the notification watches.
  - Fix: Give the shield foreground notification the same job: detect missing grants at render time and attach per-permission action buttons that open the exact settings page, instead of a static title/text notification.
- **[MEDIUM] Freedom runs a commercial blocker at targetSdk 36 with no SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and no PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS in its manifest; Monolith declares both** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §3 (explicit negatives, verified from the decoded manifest): no android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, no android.permission.PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS, no QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES — window content comes from its accessibility service, detection is accessibility-only (§7.3), and installed-app enumeration works through PackageManager launcher queries (§14). The two most sensitive permissions in Monolith's manifest — SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW (AndroidManifest.xml:11) and PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS (AndroidManifest.xml:12-14) — are permissions Freedom's entire shipping product does without. Monolith asks the user (and any reviewer) for overlay and usage-access rights that a direct competitor proves are unnecessary for the same job: detection, website blocking and app blocking all included.
  - Fix: Treat Freedom's manifest as the burden of proof: any Monolith permission Freedom ships without (overlay, usage stats) needs a named feature that dies without it, or it should be dropped from the manifest.

### Comparative audit

- **[HIGH] Freedom's block has no native face and silently evaporates if its Flutter engine isn't listening; Monolith's intercept is native and always renders** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §5 and §7.2: the native block is only a keypress — GLOBAL_ACTION_BACK on first offence, escalating to GLOBAL_ACTION_HOME on a repeat offence against the same app — after which a sessionEvent (appBlocked/webBlocked) is sent to the Dart layer, and what the user sees next is entirely Dart's business. But services obtain the plugin via FreedomPlatformPlugin.getPluginFromEngine(...) and events are discarded when Dart hasn't enabled them ('Discard event of type: …'); the engine also logs an error when the plugin is not registered in the cached freedom_flutter_engine. So Freedom's block screen has a hard runtime dependency on a live Flutter engine: no engine, no screen — the user is ejected to home with no reason shown, no choice offered, nothing recorded on-device. Monolith's Airlock intercept is a native Compose surface in the same process as its enforcement: it renders its wall, countdown and choices unconditionally, with no second runtime to be absent. On the single most important screen in the category, the commercial app is the fragile one.
  - Fix: Keep Monolith's intercept native and self-contained — this is a genuine structural advantage worth protecting in any future rewrite; do not move block rendering behind a bridge, engine or web layer.
- **[HIGH] Freedom's release build logs blocked packages and extracted URLs to logcat and embeds session-replay analytics; Monolith ships no tracker or log pipeline at all** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §20 and §19.2: the shipping release BuildConfig has RELEASE_LOGS_ENABLED=TRUE and ACCESSIBILITY_LOGS_ENABLED=TRUE, and the accessibility service, scanners and matchers log verbosely — blocked package names, extracted URLs/hosts, view-tree scan results — to logcat, readable by any process with log access on the device. A Papertrail channel method lets the app layer supply a syslog host/port and ship logs off-device when debug logging is on. The binary also embeds Microsoft Clarity (clarity_flutter) including a WebViewTrackingBridge — session-replay analytics — alongside Braze, Kochava attribution and Firebase Analytics (§19.2). Monolith ships none of this: no third-party analytics or replay SDK, no remote log shipping, no verbose production logging of what the user tried to open. Whatever Monolith's other privacy faults, on telemetry surface the local hobby codebase is materially cleaner than the commercial product it is compared against.
  - Fix: Record this as a deliberate Monolith advantage: keep the no-third-party-telemetry line, and if diagnostics are ever added, keep them on-device and content-free (no packages, no URLs) — Freedom shows exactly where the commercial norm leads.
- **[MEDIUM] Freedom's boot and keep-alive machinery is theatre — the boot receiver only logs and the keep-alive worker only checks an engine exists; Monolith's boot path actually re-arms** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §10: BootCompletedReceiver 'does nothing but log' ('On Boot finished broadcast is received'); KeepAliveWorker.doWork 'is nearly a no-op — it only checks whether freedom_flutter_engine exists in the engine registry and returns success'; and WorkManager's own RescheduleReceiver is declared disabled in the manifest. After a reboot, nothing in Freedom's native layer re-arms or even verifies an in-progress session — recovery waits entirely on the Dart side being restarted by something else. Monolith's MonolithBootReceiver (MonolithBootReceiver.kt:25-37) handles LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, BOOT_COMPLETED, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED and TIME_SET, re-derives shield state inside goAsync() and restarts protection — imperfect, but a real native resumption path. The app with the full-time reliability team shipped a boot receiver that writes a log line; the solo project shipped one that restarts the shield.
  - Fix: No action for Monolith beyond not regressing it: keep boot resumption native. Freedom's arrangement is the cautionary example of an executor architecture whose owner (the app layer) may never wake up.
- **[MEDIUM] Monolith keeps a signed, durable on-device session record; Freedom's Android layer holds one transient session in a static holder and remembers nothing** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §5.4, §6.1 and §17: the native session is a single SessionInfo object pushed as JSON, explicitly a 'stub' until configured; native persistence is three small SharedPreferences files (debug flag, learned browser scan options, the user's previous DND filter, a break-notification dedup timestamp) and an installed-apps cache. There is no on-device session history, no record of past blocks beyond events streamed to Dart, and no integrity protection on the session state in the Android binary. Monolith persists every session in Room and HMAC-signs session state at CryptoIntegrityManager.kt:53 (signSessionState, verified at :83), producing numbered, frozen receipts per session. Freedom's phone forgets everything the account doesn't hold; Monolith's phone is itself the archive — signed, inspectable and independent of any server.
  - Fix: Treat the on-device signed archive as a differentiator to keep: it survives account loss, server shutdown and offline use in a way Freedom's executor model structurally cannot.


### Second-pass findings — 4 findings (1 critical, 3 high, 0 medium, 0 low)

- **[CRITICAL] Freedom sessions can block the entire web except named exceptions; Monolith can only blacklist a hand-listed set of domains** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §6.1/§7.5: the native session contract SessionInfo.Properties carries blockEverything plus uris and excludedUris, and UrlMatcher.BlockProperties {blockAll, blockedUrls, excludedUrls} is enforced by DefaultUrlMatcher by parsing the host — an excluded host is exempt, blockAll blocks any host, otherwise parent domains are walked against the blocked set. A Freedom session can therefore run the web in allowlist mode: everything blocked except named exceptions. Monolith's entire web matcher is MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:67-68, matchBlockedDomain(urlText, domains) = domains.firstOrNull { urlText.contains(it) }, fed only the stored site list at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:254-265; there is no block-all flag and no exclusion set anywhere in the door, and the code's own comment at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:254-259 states an emptied list blocks no websites — any unlisted or mirror domain browses freely in a 'locked' session.
  - Fix: Add a native block-everything web mode to the session model with an explicit excluded-host allowlist, enforced by parsed-host/domain matching in the accessibility door, so a session can allow only study sites instead of enumerating every distracting domain.
- **[HIGH] Freedom ejects with escalating BACK-then-HOME and no self-launch; Monolith's app block only launches itself over the blocked app** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §7.2/§3: on a blocked app FreedomAccessibilityService calls pauseScanning() (500ms, PAUSE_BETWEEN_BLOCKS_MILLIS) then performGlobalAction(GLOBAL_ACTION_BACK) on first offence and performGlobalAction(GLOBAL_ACTION_HOME) on a repeat offence against the same app (lastBlockedAppId comparison); websites get soft BACK; the APK declares no SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and contains no native block screen — enforcement ejects the user from the blocked app itself and escalates. Monolith's per-app tier door does no ejection at all: MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:288 merely calls launchInterceptScreen(), which at MonolithAccessibilityService.kt:416-428 builds an Intent to its own MainActivity (FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK|SINGLE_TOP) and startActivity()s it, leaving the blocked app underneath; the shield door does the same at MonolithShieldService.kt:178-192. A repeat attempt gets the identical self-launch, never a BACK, never a HOME.
  - Fix: Make the accessibility door eject first (GLOBAL_ACTION_BACK, escalating to GLOBAL_ACTION_HOME on a repeat offence against the same package within the session, tracked explicitly) and treat the intercept activity as explanation only, not as the enforcement mechanism itself.
- **[HIGH] Freedom's break is a native sub-session with an exact-alarm, deduped 'break over' notification; Monolith's Safe Break is just two countdown fields on the session row with no alarm and no return notification** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §6.1/§8.2/§11: a break is a first-class session state — SessionInfo endsBreak=true with empty apps/uris — and SessionForegroundService treats its start as a pause (foreground notification removed, DND released, keep-alive cancelled, wake lock released) while BreakEndedNotificationScheduler maintains an AlarmManager setExactAndAllowWhileIdle alarm (request code 902913001, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM) for the break's endDateTime, deduped by the break_ended_notification_ledger (last_notified_break_end_millis) so the HIGH-importance 'Break's over. Back to your session.' notification (id 820000001, channel BreakEnded) fires exactly once even if the process was dead. Monolith's break is only two fields on the session row — MonolithModels.kt FocusSessionEntity isInSafeBreak/safeBreakSecondsRemaining — with a fixed length (MonolithRepository.kt:110 SAFE_BREAK_DURATION_SECONDS = 600) counted down inside updateSessionProgress ticks (MonolithRepository.kt, isInSafeBreak branch ~1991-2020); grep shows AlarmManager is used only by RoutineScheduler.kt and ReleaseRetryScheduler.kt, never for a break end, and there is no break-ended notification or dedup ledger.
  - Fix: Make break end a scheduled event, not a tick side-effect: arm an exact (setExactAndAllowWhileIdle) alarm at break start for the break's end instant, post a dedicated break-ended notification from its receiver, and dedup it with a persisted last-notified ledger so a dead/stalled process cannot silently swallow the return point.
- **[HIGH] Freedom's engine publishes an explicit permission-criticality taxonomy — only Accessibility is fatal — while Monolith's Guard count conflates critical and cosmetic grants** — Freedom EVIDENCE.md §6.4: BlockingEngineState is computed natively from six permission managers and exposed as JSON {availability, missingPermissions, debugInfo}, where availability is 'active' (none missing), 'disabled' (only when Accessibility is missing) or 'restricted' (anything else missing) — the UI is told exactly which single grant kills blocking and which merely degrade it. Monolith instead counts four grants into its header Guard line — ACCESSIBILITY, USAGE_ACCESS, DEVICE_ADMIN and NOTIFICATION_LISTENER are all 'counted' (app/src/main/java/com/example/service/WatchStore.kt:80-99) — yet its actual warrant depends only on accessibility binding and usage access (WatchStore.kt:304-308). A user reading Monolith's board cannot tell that the device-admin FIX trip (an uninstall guard) and the notification-listener trip are non-fatal, while Freedom's state machine makes that distinction a first-class, machine-readable fact.
  - Fix: Adopt a three-state availability model like Freedom's: publish {state, missingPermissions} from the watch layer, mark only accessibility (+usage) as blocking-fatal, and label device-admin/notification-listener/overlay/battery as degraded-mode items on the board so users triage the one Settings trip that actually matters first.
